“When asked, ‘Venerable Gotama, is happiness and suffering self-made?’ you say, ‘Do not say so, Timbaruka.’ When asked, ‘Then, Venerable Gotama, is happiness and suffering made by another?’ you say, ‘Do not say so, Timbaruka.’ When asked, ‘Then, Venerable Gotama, is happiness and suffering both self-made and made by another?’ you say, ‘Do not say so, Timbaruka.’ When asked, ‘Then, Venerable Gotama, is happiness and suffering not self-made, not other-made, and arisen without a cause?’ you say, ‘Do not say so, Timbaruka.’ When asked, ‘Then, Venerable Gotama, is there no happiness and suffering?’ you say, ‘It is not, Timbaruka, that there is no happiness and suffering; there is indeed happiness and suffering, Timbaruka.’ When asked, ‘In that case, does the Venerable Gotama not know or see happiness and suffering?’ you say, ‘It is not, Timbaruka, that I do not know or see happiness and suffering. I know happiness and suffering, Timbaruka; I see happiness and suffering, Timbaruka.’ May the Venerable Gotama explain happiness and suffering to me. May the Venerable Gotama teach happiness and suffering to me.”

“‘Sā vedanā, so vedayatī’ti kho, timbaruka, ādito sato ‘sayaṃkataṃ sukhadukkha’nti evampāhaṃ na vadāmi. ‘Aññā vedanā, añño vedayatī’ti [T 2.0028] kho, timbaruka, vedanābhitunnassa sato ‘paraṃkataṃ sukhadukkha’nti evampāhaṃ na vadāmi. Ete te, timbaruka, ubho ante anupagamma majjhena tathāgato dhammaṃ deseti – ‘avijjāpaccayā saṅkhārā; saṅkhārapaccayā viññāṇaṃ…pe… evametassa kevalassa dukkhakkhandhassa samudayo hoti. Avijjāya tveva asesavirāganirodhā saṅkhāranirodho; saṅkhāranirodhā viññāṇanirodho…pe… evametassa kevalassa dukkhakkhandhassa nirodho hotī’”ti.

“Timbaruka, regarding the view, ‘The feeling is the same as the one who feels,’ which, being present from the outset, implies ‘happiness and suffering are self-made’—this I do not say. Timbaruka, regarding the view, ‘The feeling is one thing, and the one who feels is another,’ which, for one afflicted by feeling, implies ‘happiness and suffering are made by another’—this I do not say. Avoiding both these extremes, Timbaruka, the Tathāgata teaches the Dhamma by the middle way: ‘With ignorance as a condition, formations come to be; with formations as a condition, consciousness comes to be… Thus is the origin of this whole mass of suffering. But with the remainderless fading away and cessation of that very ignorance, comes the cessation of formations; with the cessation of formations comes the cessation of consciousness… Thus is the cessation of this whole mass of suffering.’”

Evaṃ vutte, timbaruko paribbājako bhagavantaṃ etadavoca – “abhikkantaṃ, bho gotama…pe… esāhaṃ bhavantaṃ gotamaṃ saraṇaṃ gacchāmi dhammañca bhikkhusaṅghañca. Upāsakaṃ maṃ bhavaṃ gotamo dhāretu ajjatagge pāṇupetaṃ saraṇaṃ gata”nti. Aṭṭhamaṃ.

When this was said, the wanderer Timbaruka said this to the Blessed One: “Excellent, Venerable Gotama! Excellent, Venerable Gotama! ... I go for refuge to the Venerable Gotama, to the Dhamma, and to the Saṅgha of bhikkhus. May the Venerable Gotama remember me as a lay follower who has gone for refuge for life from this day forward.” The Eighth.

9. Bālapaṇḍitasuttaṃ

9. The Discourse on the Fool and the Wise Person

19. Sāvatthiyaṃ viharati…pe… “avijjānīvaraṇassa, bhikkhave, bālassa taṇhāya sampayuttassa [P 2.0024] evamayaṃ kāyo samudāgato. Iti ayañceva kāyo bahiddhā ca nāmarūpaṃ, itthetaṃ dvayaṃ[V 1.0023], dvayaṃ paṭicca phasso saḷevāyatanāni [M 1.0263] saḷāyatanāni (ka.), yehi phuṭṭho bālo sukhadukkhaṃ paṭisaṃvedayati etesaṃ vā aññatarena”.

19. Dwelling at Sāvatthī… “Bhikkhus, for a fool hindered by ignorance and conjoined with craving, this body has thus arisen. Thus, there is this very body and external name-and-form; in this way, this is a pair. Dependent on the pair, there is contact at the six sense bases. Touched by these, or by one or another of them, the fool experiences pleasure and pain.”

“Avijjānīvaraṇassa, bhikkhave, paṇḍitassa taṇhāya sampayuttassa evamayaṃ kāyo samudāgato. Iti ayañceva kāyo bahiddhā ca nāmarūpaṃ, itthetaṃ dvayaṃ, dvayaṃ paṭicca phasso saḷevāyatanāni, yehi phuṭṭho paṇḍito sukhadukkhaṃ paṭisaṃvedayati etesaṃ vā aññatarena”.

“Bhikkhus, for a wise person hindered by ignorance and conjoined with craving, this body has thus arisen. Thus, there is this very body and external name-and-form; in this way, this is a pair. Dependent on the pair, there is contact at the six sense bases. Touched by these, or by one or another of them, the wise person experiences pleasure and pain.”

“Tatra[T 2.0029], bhikkhave, ko viseso ko adhippayāso adhippāyo (sī. pī. ka.), adhippāyaso (syā. kaṃ.) adhi + pa + yasu + ṇa + sī = adhippayāso kiṃ nānākaraṇaṃ paṇḍitassa bālenā”ti? “Bhagavaṃmūlakā no, bhante, dhammā, bhagavaṃnettikā, bhagavaṃpaṭisaraṇā. Sādhu vata, bhante, bhagavantaṃyeva paṭibhātu etassa bhāsitassa attho. Bhagavato sutvā bhikkhū dhāressantī”ti.

“In that case, bhikkhus, what is the distinction, what is the difference, what is the distinguishing feature of the wise person from the fool?” “Venerable sir, for us the teachings have the Blessed One as their root, the Blessed One as their guide, the Blessed One as their refuge. It would be good, venerable sir, if the meaning of this utterance were to become clear to the Blessed One himself. Having heard it from the Blessed One, the bhikkhus will bear it in mind.”

“Tena hi, bhikkhave, suṇātha, sādhukaṃ manasi karotha, bhāsissāmī”ti. “Evaṃ, bhante”ti kho te bhikkhū bhagavato paccassosuṃ. Bhagavā etadavoca –

“In that case, bhikkhus, listen, attend carefully, I will speak.” “Yes, venerable sir,” those bhikkhus responded to the Blessed One. The Blessed One said this:

“Yāya ca, bhikkhave, avijjāya nivutassa bālassa yāya ca taṇhāya sampayuttassa ayaṃ kāyo samudāgato, sā ceva avijjā bālassa appahīnā sā ca taṇhā aparikkhīṇā. Taṃ kissa hetu? Na, bhikkhave, bālo acari brahmacariyaṃ sammā dukkhakkhayāya. Tasmā bālo kāyassa bhedā kāyūpago hoti, so kāyūpago samāno na parimuccati jātiyā jarāmaraṇena sokehi paridevehi dukkhehi domanassehi upāyāsehi. Na parimuccati dukkhasmāti vadāmi.

“Bhikkhus, the ignorance by which the fool is veiled, and the craving with which he is conjoined—it is from these that this body has arisen. That very ignorance has not been abandoned by the fool, and that craving is not exhausted. For what reason? Because, bhikkhus, the fool has not lived the holy life for the complete destruction of suffering. Therefore, at the breaking up of the body, the fool goes to another body. Being one who goes to a body, he is not freed from birth, aging, and death; from sorrow, lamentation, pain, distress, and despair. He is not freed from suffering, I say.

“Yāya ca, bhikkhave, avijjāya nivutassa paṇḍitassa yāya ca taṇhāya sampayuttassa ayaṃ kāyo samudāgato, sā ceva avijjā paṇḍitassa pahīnā, sā ca taṇhā parikkhīṇā. Taṃ kissa hetu? Acari, bhikkhave, paṇḍito brahmacariyaṃ [P 2.0025] sammā dukkhakkhayāya. Tasmā paṇḍito kāyassa bhedā na kāyūpago hoti. So akāyūpago samāno parimuccati jātiyā jarāmaraṇena sokehi paridevehi dukkhehi domanassehi upāyāsehi. Parimuccati dukkhasmāti vadāmi. Ayaṃ [M 1.0264] kho[T 2.0030], bhikkhave, viseso[V 1.0024], ayaṃ adhippayāso, idaṃ nānākaraṇaṃ paṇḍitassa bālena yadidaṃ brahmacariyavāso”ti. Navamaṃ.

“Bhikkhus, it is because of that ignorance with which the wise person is veiled and that craving with which he is conjoined that this body has arisen. That very ignorance has been abandoned by the wise person, and that craving is exhausted. For what reason? Because, bhikkhus, the wise person has lived the holy life rightly for the complete destruction of suffering. Therefore, with the breakup of the body, the wise person does not go to another body. Not being one who goes to a body, he is freed from birth, aging, and death; from sorrow, lamentation, pain, distress, and despair. He is freed from suffering, I say. This, bhikkhus, is the distinction, this is the superior quality, this is the difference between the wise person and the fool: namely, the living of the holy life.”

10. Paccayasuttaṃ

10. The Discourse on Conditions

20. Sāvatthiyaṃ viharati…pe… “paṭiccasamuppādañca vo, bhikkhave, desessāmi paṭiccasamuppanne ca dhamme. Taṃ suṇātha, sādhukaṃ manasi karotha, bhāsissāmī”ti. “Evaṃ, bhante”ti kho te bhikkhū bhagavato paccassosuṃ. Bhagavā etadavoca –

20. At Sāvatthī. “Bhikkhus, I will teach you dependent origination and dependently arisen phenomena. Listen to that and attend carefully, I will speak.” “Yes, venerable sir,” those bhikkhus replied to the Blessed One. The Blessed One said this:

“Katamo ca, bhikkhave, paṭiccasamuppādo? Jātipaccayā, bhikkhave, jarāmaraṇaṃ. Uppādā vā tathāgatānaṃ anuppādā vā tathāgatānaṃ, ṭhitāva sā dhātu dhammaṭṭhitatā dhammaniyāmatā idappaccayatā. Taṃ tathāgato abhisambujjhati abhisameti. Abhisambujjhitvā abhisametvā ācikkhati deseti paññāpeti paṭṭhapeti vivarati vibhajati uttānīkaroti. ‘Passathā’ti cāha – ‘jātipaccayā, bhikkhave, jarāmaraṇaṃ’”.

“And what, bhikkhus, is dependent origination? With birth as condition, bhikkhus, aging and death come to be. Whether Tathāgatas arise or do not arise, this element stands, this stability of the Dhamma, this fixed course of the Dhamma, this specific conditionality. The Tathāgata awakens to this and comprehends it. Having awakened to it and comprehended it, he points it out, teaches it, proclaims it, establishes it, discloses it, analyzes it, and elucidates it. And he says, ‘See! With birth as condition, bhikkhus, there is aging and death.’”

“Bhavapaccayā, bhikkhave, jāti…pe… upādānapaccayā, bhikkhave, bhavo… taṇhāpaccayā, bhikkhave, upādānaṃ… vedanāpaccayā, bhikkhave, taṇhā… phassapaccayā, bhikkhave, vedanā… saḷāyatanapaccayā, bhikkhave, phasso… nāmarūpapaccayā, bhikkhave, saḷāyatanaṃ… viññāṇapaccayā, bhikkhave, nāmarūpaṃ… saṅkhārapaccayā, bhikkhave, viññāṇaṃ… avijjāpaccayā, bhikkhave, saṅkhārā uppādā vā tathāgatānaṃ anuppādā vā tathāgatānaṃ, ṭhitāva sā dhātu dhammaṭṭhitatā dhammaniyāmatā idappaccayatā. Taṃ tathāgato abhisambujjhati abhisameti[P 2.0026]. Abhisambujjhitvā abhisametvā ācikkhati [T 2.0031] deseti paññāpeti paṭṭhapeti vivarati vibhajati uttānīkaroti. ‘Passathā’ti cāha ‘avijjāpaccayā, bhikkhave, saṅkhārā’. Iti kho, bhikkhave, yā tatra tathatā avitathatā anaññathatā idappaccayatā – ayaṃ vuccati, bhikkhave, paṭiccasamuppādo.

“With becoming as condition, bhikkhus, there is birth… with clinging as condition, bhikkhus, there is becoming… with craving as condition, bhikkhus, there is clinging… with feeling as condition, bhikkhus, there is craving… with contact as condition, bhikkhus, there is feeling… with the six sense bases as condition, bhikkhus, there is contact… with name-and-form as condition, bhikkhus, there are the six sense bases… with consciousness as condition, bhikkhus, there is name-and-form… with formations as condition, bhikkhus, there is consciousness… with ignorance as condition, bhikkhus, there are formations. Whether Tathāgatas arise or do not arise, this element stands, this stability of the Dhamma, this fixed course of the Dhamma, this specific conditionality. The Tathāgata awakens to this and comprehends it. Having awakened to it and comprehended it, he points it out, teaches it, proclaims it, establishes it, discloses it, analyzes it, and elucidates it. And he says, ‘See! With ignorance as condition, bhikkhus, there are formations.’ Thus, bhikkhus, that which is suchness, un-erroneousness, not-otherness, this specific conditionality—this is called, bhikkhus, dependent origination.”

“Katame ca, bhikkhave, paṭiccasamuppannā dhammā? Jarāmaraṇaṃ, bhikkhave, aniccaṃ saṅkhataṃ paṭiccasamuppannaṃ khayadhammaṃ vayadhammaṃ virāgadhammaṃ nirodhadhammaṃ. Jāti, bhikkhave, aniccā saṅkhatā paṭiccasamuppannā [V 1.0025] khayadhammā vayadhammā virāgadhammā nirodhadhammā. Bhavo, bhikkhave, anicco saṅkhato paṭiccasamuppanno khayadhammo vayadhammo virāgadhammo nirodhadhammo. Upādānaṃ bhikkhave…pe… taṇhā, bhikkhave… vedanā, bhikkhave… phasso, bhikkhave… saḷāyatanaṃ, bhikkhave… nāmarūpaṃ, bhikkhave… viññāṇaṃ[M 1.0265], bhikkhave… saṅkhārā, bhikkhave… avijjā, bhikkhave, aniccā saṅkhatā paṭiccasamuppannā khayadhammā vayadhammā virāgadhammā nirodhadhammā. Ime vuccanti, bhikkhave, paṭiccasamuppannā dhammā.

“And what, bhikkhus, are the dependently arisen phenomena? Aging and death, bhikkhus, are impermanent, conditioned, dependently arisen, subject to destruction, subject to vanishing, subject to fading away, subject to cessation. Birth, bhikkhus, is impermanent, conditioned, dependently arisen, subject to destruction, subject to vanishing, subject to fading away, subject to cessation. Becoming, bhikkhus, is impermanent, conditioned, dependently arisen, subject to destruction, subject to vanishing, subject to fading away, subject to cessation. Clinging, bhikkhus… Craving, bhikkhus… Feeling, bhikkhus… Contact, bhikkhus… The six sense bases, bhikkhus… Name-and-form, bhikkhus… Consciousness, bhikkhus… Formations, bhikkhus… Ignorance, bhikkhus, is impermanent, conditioned, dependently arisen, subject to destruction, subject to vanishing, subject to fading away, subject to cessation. These, bhikkhus, are called the dependently arisen phenomena.”

“Yato kho, bhikkhave, ariyasāvakassa ‘ayañca paṭiccasamuppādo, ime ca paṭiccasamuppannā dhammā’ yathābhūtaṃ sammappaññāya sudiṭṭhā honti, so vata pubbantaṃ vā paṭidhāvissati – ‘ahosiṃ nu kho ahaṃ nu khvāhaṃ (syā. kaṃ. pī. ka.) atītamaddhānaṃ, nanu kho ahosiṃ atītamaddhānaṃ, kiṃ nu kho ahosiṃ atītamaddhānaṃ, kathaṃ nu kho ahosiṃ atītamaddhānaṃ, kiṃ hutvā kiṃ ahosiṃ [T 2.0032] nu kho ahaṃ atītamaddhāna’nti; aparantaṃ vā upadhāvissati apadhāvissati (ka.) – ‘bhavissāmi nu kho ahaṃ anāgatamaddhānaṃ, nanu kho bhavissāmi anāgatamaddhānaṃ[P 2.0027], kiṃ nu kho bhavissāmi anāgatamaddhānaṃ, kathaṃ nu kho bhavissāmi anāgatamaddhānaṃ, kiṃ hutvā kiṃ bhavissāmi nu kho ahaṃ anāgatamaddhāna’nti; etarahi vā paccuppannaṃ addhānaṃ ajjhattaṃ kathaṃkathī bhavissati – ‘ahaṃ nu khosmi, no nu khosmi, kiṃ nu khosmi, kathaṃ nu khosmi, ayaṃ nu kho satto kuto āgato, so kuhiṃ gamissatī’ti – netaṃ ṭhānaṃ vijjati. Taṃ kissa hetu? Tathāhi, bhikkhave, ariyasāvakassa ayañca paṭiccasamuppādo ime ca paṭiccasamuppannā dhammā yathābhūtaṃ sammappaññāya sudiṭṭhā”ti. Dasamaṃ.

“Bhikkhus, when a noble disciple has clearly seen with right wisdom, as it really is, this dependent origination and these dependently arisen phenomena, it is impossible that he will run back to the past, thinking: ‘Did I exist in the past? Did I not exist in the past? What was I in the past? How was I in the past? Having been what, what did I become in the past?’ Or that he will run forward to the future, thinking: ‘Will I exist in the future? Will I not exist in the future? What will I be in the future? How will I be in the future? Having been what, what will I become in the future?’ Or that he will now be inwardly perplexed about the present, thinking: ‘Am I? Am I not? What am I? How am I? From where has this being come? Where will it go?’ Such a case does not exist. For what reason? Because, bhikkhus, the noble disciple has clearly seen with right wisdom, as it really is, this dependent origination and these dependently arisen phenomena.”

Āhāravaggo dutiyo.

The Second Chapter on Nutriment.

Tassuddānaṃ –

The summary verse:

Āhāraṃ phagguno ceva, dve ca samaṇabrāhmaṇā;

Kaccānagotto dhammakathikaṃ, acelaṃ timbarukena ca;

Bālapaṇḍitato ceva, dasamo paccayena cāti.

Nutriment, and Phagguna, and two on Ascetics and Brahmins; Kaccānagotta, the Dhamma Speaker, the Naked Ascetic, and Timbaruka; Both the Fool and the Wise, and the tenth on Conditions.

3. Dasabalavaggo

3. The Chapter on the Ten Powers

1. Dasabalasuttaṃ

1. The Discourse on the Ten Powers

21. Sāvatthiyaṃ [T 2.0033][M 1.0266] viharati…pe… “dasabalasamannāgato, bhikkhave, tathāgato catūhi ca vesārajjehi samannāgato āsabhaṃ ṭhānaṃ paṭijānāti, parisāsu [V 1.0026] sīhanādaṃ nadati, brahmacakkaṃ pavatteti – iti [P 2.0028] rūpaṃ iti rūpassa samudayo iti rūpassa atthaṅgamo, iti vedanā iti vedanāya samudayo iti vedanāya atthaṅgamo, iti saññā iti saññāya samudayo iti saññāya atthaṅgamo, iti saṅkhārā iti saṅkhārānaṃ samudayo iti saṅkhārānaṃ atthaṅgamo, iti viññāṇaṃ iti viññāṇassa samudayo iti viññāṇassa atthaṅgamo. Iti imasmiṃ sati idaṃ hoti, imassuppādā idaṃ uppajjati. Imasmiṃ asati idaṃ na hoti, imassa nirodhā idaṃ nirujjhati. Yadidaṃ avijjāpaccayā saṅkhārā; saṅkhārapaccayā viññāṇaṃ…pe… evametassa kevalassa dukkhakkhandhassa samudayo hoti. Avijjāya tveva asesavirāganirodhā saṅkhāranirodho; saṅkhāranirodhā viññāṇanirodho…pe… evametassa kevalassa dukkhakkhandhassa nirodho hotī”ti. Paṭhamaṃ.

21. At Sāvatthī... 'Bhikkhus, the Tathāgata, endowed with the ten powers and with the four kinds of fearlessness, claims the pre-eminent, unshakeable position, roars the lion’s roar in the assemblies, and sets rolling the supreme wheel: ‘This is form, this is the origin of form, this is the cessation of form. This is feeling, this is the origin of feeling, this is the cessation of feeling. This is perception, this is the origin of perception, this is the cessation of perception. These are formations, this is the origin of formations, this is the cessation of formations. This is consciousness, this is the origin of consciousness, this is the cessation of consciousness. When this exists, that comes to be; with the arising of this, that arises. When this does not exist, that does not come to be; with the cessation of this, that ceases. That is: with ignorance as condition, formations come to be; with formations as condition, consciousness comes to be... and so on... Thus is the origin of this whole mass of suffering. But with the remainderless fading away and cessation of ignorance, there is the cessation of formations; with the cessation of formations, there is the cessation of consciousness... and so on... Thus is the cessation of this whole mass of suffering.' First.

2. Dutiyadasabalasuttaṃ

2. The Second Discourse on the Ten Powers

22. Sāvatthiyaṃ viharati…pe… “dasabalasamannāgato, bhikkhave, tathāgato catūhi ca vesārajjehi samannāgato āsabhaṃ ṭhānaṃ paṭijānāti, parisāsu sīhanādaṃ nadati, brahmacakkaṃ pavattetti – ‘iti rūpaṃ iti rūpassa samudayo iti rūpassa atthaṅgamo, iti vedanā iti vedanāya samudayo iti vedanāya [T 2.0034] atthaṅgamo, iti saññā iti saññāya samudayo iti saññāya atthaṅgamo, iti saṅkhārā iti saṅkhārānaṃ samudayo iti saṅkhārānaṃ atthaṅgamo, iti viññāṇaṃ iti viññāṇassa samudayo iti viññāṇassa atthaṅgamo. Iti imasmiṃ sati idaṃ hoti, imassuppādā idaṃ uppajjati; imasmiṃ asati idaṃ na hoti imassa nirodhā idaṃ nirujjhati. Yadidaṃ avijjāpaccayā saṅkhārā; saṅkhārapaccayā viññāṇaṃ…pe… [V 1.0027] evametassa kevalassa dukkhakkhandhassa samudayo hoti. Avijjāya tveva asesavirāganirodhā saṅkhāranirodho; saṅkhāranirodhā viññāṇanirodho…pe… evametassa kevalassa dukkhakkhandhassa nirodho hoti’”.

22. At Sāvatthī... 'Bhikkhus, the Tathāgata, endowed with the ten powers and with the four kinds of fearlessness, claims the pre-eminent, unshakeable position, roars the lion’s roar in the assemblies, and sets rolling the supreme wheel: ‘This is form, this is the origin of form, this is the cessation of form. This is feeling, this is the origin of feeling, this is the cessation of feeling. This is perception, this is the origin of perception, this is the cessation of perception. These are formations, this is the origin of formations, this is the cessation of formations. This is consciousness, this is the origin of consciousness, this is the cessation of consciousness. When this exists, that comes to be; with the arising of this, that arises. When this does not exist, that does not come to be; with the cessation of this, that ceases. That is: with ignorance as condition, formations come to be; with formations as condition, consciousness comes to be... and so on... Thus is the origin of this whole mass of suffering. But with the remainderless fading away and cessation of ignorance, there is the cessation of formations; with the cessation of formations, there is the cessation of consciousness... and so on... Thus is the cessation of this whole mass of suffering.'

“Evaṃ svākkhāto, bhikkhave, mayā dhammo uttāno vivaṭo pakāsito chinnapilotiko. Evaṃ svākkhāte kho, bhikkhave, mayā dhamme uttāne vivaṭe pakāsite chinnapilotike alameva saddhāpabbajitena kulaputtena vīriyaṃ ārabhituṃ – ‘kāmaṃ taco ca nhāru nahāru (sī. syā. kaṃ. pī.) ca aṭṭhi [M 1.0267] ca avasissatu, sarīre upasussatu avasussatu ma. ni. 2.184 maṃsalohitaṃ. Yaṃ taṃ purisathāmena purisavīriyena purisaparakkamena pattabbaṃ, na taṃ apāpuṇitvā vīriyassa saṇṭhānaṃ bhavissatī’”ti.

'Bhikkhus, the Dhamma has been well proclaimed by me—it is manifest, uncovered, revealed, and free of patchwork. In this Dhamma, so well proclaimed by me—manifest, uncovered, revealed, and free of patchwork—it is indeed fitting for a clansman who has gone forth in faith to arouse his energy thus: ‘Willingly, let only skin, sinews, and bone remain, and let the flesh and blood in my body dry up; but there will be no relaxing of my energy until I have attained what can be attained by manly strength, manly energy, and manly exertion.’

“Dukkhaṃ[P 2.0029], bhikkhave, kusīto viharati vokiṇṇo pāpakehi akusalehi dhammehi, mahantañca sadatthaṃ parihāpeti. Āraddhavīriyo ca kho, bhikkhave, sukhaṃ viharati pavivitto pāpakehi akusalehi dhammehi, mahantañca sadatthaṃ paripūreti. Na, bhikkhave, hīnena [T 2.0035] aggassa patti hoti. Aggena ca kho, bhikkhave, aggassa patti hoti. Maṇḍapeyyamidaṃ, bhikkhave, brahmacariyaṃ, satthā sammukhībhūto. Tasmātiha, bhikkhave, vīriyaṃ ārabhatha appattassa pattiyā, anadhigatassa adhigamāya, asacchikatassa sacchikiriyāya. ‘Evaṃ no ayaṃ amhākaṃ pabbajjā avañjhā bhavissati saphalā saudrayā. Yesañca yesaṃ (sī. syā. kaṃ.), yesaṃ hi (pī. ka.) mayaṃ paribhuñjāma cīvara-piṇḍapātasenāsana-gilānappaccayabhesajjaparikkhāraṃ tesaṃ te kārā amhesu mahapphalā bhavissanti mahānisaṃsā’ti – evañhi vo, bhikkhave, sikkhitabbaṃ. Attatthaṃ vā hi, bhikkhave, sampassamānena alameva appamādena sampādetuṃ; paratthaṃ vā hi, bhikkhave, sampassamānena alameva appamādena sampādetuṃ; ubhayatthaṃ vā hi, bhikkhave, sampassamānena alameva appamādena sampādetu”nti. Dutiyaṃ.

Bhikkhus, the lazy person dwells in suffering, mingled with evil, unwholesome states, and causes his own great good to diminish. But the energetic person dwells in happiness, secluded from evil, unwholesome states, and fulfills his own great good. Bhikkhus, the supreme is not attained through what is inferior; it is through the supreme that the supreme is attained. Bhikkhus, this holy life is a choice drink, and the Teacher is present before you. Therefore, bhikkhus, arouse your energy for attaining the unattained, for achieving the unachieved, for realizing the unrealized, thinking: ‘In this way, this going forth of ours will not be barren, but fruitful and prosperous. And for those whose robes, almsfood, lodging, and medicinal provisions we use, their acts of service toward us will be of great fruit and great benefit.’ It is in this way, bhikkhus, that you should train yourselves. Bhikkhus, for one who sees his own good, it is indeed fitting to strive with diligence. For one who sees the good of others, it is indeed fitting to strive with diligence. For one who sees the good of both, it is indeed fitting to strive with diligence. Second.

3. Upanisasuttaṃ

3. The Discourse on Supporting Conditions

23. Sāvatthiyaṃ viharati…pe… “jānato ahaṃ, bhikkhave, passato āsavānaṃ khayaṃ vadāmi, no ajānato no apassato. Kiñca, bhikkhave, jānato kiṃ passato āsavānaṃ khayo hoti[V 1.0028]? Iti rūpaṃ iti rūpassa samudayo iti rūpassa atthaṅgamo, iti vedanā…pe… iti saññā… iti saṅkhārā… iti viññāṇaṃ iti viññāṇassa samudayo iti viññāṇassa atthaṅgamoti. Evaṃ kho, bhikkhave, jānato evaṃ passato āsavānaṃ khayo hoti”.

23. At Sāvatthī. “Bhikkhus, I declare the destruction of the taints for one who knows and sees, not for one who does not know and does not see. Knowing what, bhikkhus, seeing what, does the destruction of the taints come about? ‘This is form, this is the origin of form, this is the cessation of form. This is feeling… This is perception… These are formations… This is consciousness, this is the origin of consciousness, this is the cessation of consciousness.’ It is for one who knows and sees thus, bhikkhus, that the destruction of the taints comes about.”

“Yampissa [P 2.0030] taṃ, bhikkhave, khayasmiṃ khayeññāṇaṃ, tampi saupanisaṃ vadāmi, no anupanisaṃ. Kā ca, bhikkhave, khayeñāṇassa upanisā? ‘Vimuttī’tissa [T 2.0036] vacanīyaṃ. Vimuttimpāhaṃ vimuttimpahaṃ (sī. syā. kaṃ.), bhikkhave, saupanisaṃ vadāmi, no anupanisaṃ. Kā ca, bhikkhave, vimuttiyā [M 1.0268] upanisā? ‘Virāgo’tissa vacanīyaṃ. Virāgampāhaṃ, bhikkhave, saupanisaṃ vadāmi, no anupanisaṃ. Kā ca, bhikkhave, virāgassa upanisā? ‘Nibbidā’tissa vacanīyaṃ. Nibbidampāhaṃ, bhikkhave, saupanisaṃ vadāmi, no anupanisaṃ. Kā ca, bhikkhave, nibbidāya upanisā? ‘Yathābhūtañāṇadassana’ntissa vacanīyaṃ. Yathābhūtañāṇadassanampāhaṃ, bhikkhave, saupanisaṃ vadāmi, no anupanisaṃ. Kā ca, bhikkhave, yathābhūtañāṇadassanassa upanisā? ‘Samādhī’tissa vacanīyaṃ. Samādhimpāhaṃ, bhikkhave, saupanisaṃ vadāmi, no anupanisaṃ.

“Bhikkhus, that knowledge of destruction in one for whom the taints are destroyed—that too, I say, has a supporting condition; it is not without a supporting condition. And what, bhikkhus, is the supporting condition for the knowledge of destruction? ‘Liberation,’ it should be said. Liberation too, bhikkhus, I say, has a supporting condition; it is not without a supporting condition. And what, bhikkhus, is the supporting condition for liberation? ‘Dispassion,’ it should be said. Dispassion too, bhikkhus, I say, has a supporting condition; it is not without a supporting condition. And what, bhikkhus, is the supporting condition for dispassion? ‘Disenchantment,’ it should be said. Disenchantment too, bhikkhus, I say, has a supporting condition; it is not without a supporting condition. And what, bhikkhus, is the supporting condition for disenchantment? ‘The knowledge and vision of things as they really are,’ it should be said. The knowledge and vision of things as they really are too, bhikkhus, I say, has a supporting condition; it is not without a supporting condition. And what, bhikkhus, is the supporting condition for the knowledge and vision of things as they really are? ‘Concentration,’ it should be said. Concentration too, bhikkhus, I say, has a supporting condition; it is not without a supporting condition.

“Kā ca, bhikkhave, samādhissa upanisā? ‘Sukha’ntissa vacanīyaṃ. Sukhampāhaṃ, bhikkhave, saupanisaṃ vadāmi, no anupanisaṃ. Kā ca, bhikkhave, sukhassa upanisā? ‘Passaddhī’tissa vacanīyaṃ. Passaddhimpāhaṃ, bhikkhave, saupanisaṃ vadāmi, no anupanisaṃ. Kā ca, bhikkhave, passaddhiyā upanisā? ‘Pītī’tissa vacanīyaṃ. Pītimpāhaṃ, bhikkhave, saupanisaṃ vadāmi, no anupanisaṃ. Kā ca, bhikkhave, pītiyā upanisā? ‘Pāmojja’ntissa vacanīyaṃ. Pāmojjampāhaṃ, bhikkhave, saupanisaṃ vadāmi, no anupanisaṃ. Kā ca, bhikkhave, pāmojjassa upanisā? ‘Saddhā’tissa vacanīyaṃ. Saddhampāhaṃ, bhikkhave, saupanisaṃ vadāmi, no anupanisaṃ.

“And what, bhikkhus, is the supporting condition for concentration? ‘Happiness,’ it should be said. Happiness too, bhikkhus, I say, has a supporting condition; it is not without a supporting condition. And what, bhikkhus, is the supporting condition for happiness? ‘Tranquility,’ it should be said. Tranquility too, bhikkhus, I say, has a supporting condition; it is not without a supporting condition. And what, bhikkhus, is the supporting condition for tranquility? ‘Rapture,’ it should be said. Rapture too, bhikkhus, I say, has a supporting condition; it is not without a supporting condition. And what, bhikkhus, is the supporting condition for rapture? ‘Gladness,’ it should be said. Gladness too, bhikkhus, I say, has a supporting condition; it is not without a supporting condition. And what, bhikkhus, is the supporting condition for gladness? ‘Faith,’ it should be said. Faith too, bhikkhus, I say, has a supporting condition; it is not without a supporting condition.

“Kā [P 2.0031] ca, bhikkhave, saddhāya upanisā? ‘Dukkha’ntissa vacanīyaṃ. Dukkhampāhaṃ, bhikkhave, saupanisaṃ vadāmi, no anupanisaṃ. Kā ca, bhikkhave, dukkhassa upanisā? ‘Jātī’tissa vacanīyaṃ. Jātimpāhaṃ[T 2.0037], bhikkhave, saupanisaṃ vadāmi, no anupanisaṃ. Kā ca, bhikkhave, jātiyā upanisā? ‘Bhavo’tissa vacanīyaṃ. Bhavampāhaṃ, bhikkhave, saupanisaṃ vadāmi[V 1.0029], no anupanisaṃ. Kā ca, bhikkhave, bhavassa upanisā? ‘Upādāna’ntissa vacanīyaṃ. Upādānampāhaṃ, bhikkhave, saupanisaṃ vadāmi, no anupanisaṃ. Kā ca, bhikkhave, upādānassa upanisā? ‘Taṇhā’tissa vacanīyaṃ. Taṇhampāhaṃ, bhikkhave, saupanisaṃ vadāmi, no anupanisaṃ.

“And what, bhikkhus, is the supporting condition for faith? ‘Suffering,’ it should be said. Suffering too, bhikkhus, I say, has a supporting condition; it is not without a supporting condition. And what, bhikkhus, is the supporting condition for suffering? ‘Birth,’ it should be said. Birth too, bhikkhus, I say, has a supporting condition; it is not without a supporting condition. And what, bhikkhus, is the supporting condition for birth? ‘Existence,’ it should be said. Existence too, bhikkhus, I say, has a supporting condition; it is not without a supporting condition. And what, bhikkhus, is the supporting condition for existence? ‘Clinging,’ it should be said. Clinging too, bhikkhus, I say, has a supporting condition; it is not without a supporting condition. And what, bhikkhus, is the supporting condition for clinging? ‘Craving,’ it should be said. Craving too, bhikkhus, I say, has a supporting condition; it is not without a supporting condition.

“Kā ca, bhikkhave, taṇhāya upanisā? ‘Vedanā’tissa vacanīyaṃ…pe… ‘phasso’tissa vacanīyaṃ… ‘saḷāyatana’ntissa vacanīyaṃ… ‘nāmarūpa’ntissa vacanīyaṃ… ‘viññāṇa’ntissa vacanīyaṃ… ‘saṅkhārā’tissa vacanīyaṃ. Saṅkhārepāhaṃ, bhikkhave, saupanise vadāmi, no anupanise. Kā ca, bhikkhave, saṅkhārānaṃ upanisā? ‘Avijjā’tissa vacanīyaṃ.

“And what, bhikkhus, is the supporting condition for craving? ‘Feeling,’ it should be said… ‘Contact,’ it should be said… ‘The six sense bases,’ it should be said… ‘Name-and-form,’ it should be said… ‘Consciousness,’ it should be said… ‘Formations,’ it should be said. Formations too, bhikkhus, I say, have supporting conditions; they are not without supporting conditions. And what, bhikkhus, is the supporting condition for formations? ‘Ignorance,’ it should be said.

“Iti [M 1.0269] kho, bhikkhave, avijjūpanisā saṅkhārā, saṅkhārūpanisaṃ viññāṇaṃ, viññāṇūpanisaṃ nāmarūpaṃ, nāmarūpūpanisaṃ saḷāyatanaṃ, saḷāyatanūpaniso phasso, phassūpanisā vedanā, vedanūpanisā taṇhā, taṇhūpanisaṃ upādānaṃ, upādānūpaniso bhavo, bhavūpanisā jāti, jātūpanisaṃ dukkhaṃ, dukkhūpanisā saddhā, saddhūpanisaṃ pāmojjaṃ, pāmojjūpanisā pīti, pītūpanisā passaddhi, passaddhūpanisaṃ sukhaṃ, sukhūpaniso samādhi, samādhūpanisaṃ yathābhūtañāṇadassanaṃ, yathābhūtañāṇadassanūpanisā [P 2.0032] nibbidā, nibbidūpaniso virāgo, virāgūpanisā vimutti, vimuttūpanisaṃ khayeñāṇaṃ.

“Thus, bhikkhus, formations have ignorance as their supporting condition; consciousness has formations as its supporting condition; name-and-form has consciousness as its supporting condition; the six sense bases have name-and-form as their supporting condition; contact has the six sense bases as its supporting condition; feeling has contact as its supporting condition; craving has feeling as its supporting condition; clinging has craving as its supporting condition; existence has clinging as its supporting condition; birth has existence as its supporting condition; suffering has birth as its supporting condition; faith has suffering as its supporting condition; gladness has faith as its supporting condition; rapture has gladness as its supporting condition; tranquility has rapture as its supporting condition; happiness has tranquility as its supporting condition; concentration has happiness as its supporting condition; the knowledge and vision of things as they really are has concentration as its supporting condition; disenchantment has the knowledge and vision of things as they really are as its supporting condition; dispassion has disenchantment as its supporting condition; liberation has dispassion as its supporting condition; the knowledge of destruction has liberation as its supporting condition.

“Seyyathāpi, bhikkhave, uparipabbate thullaphusitake deve vassante [T 2.0038] taṃ udakaṃ yathāninnaṃ pavattamānaṃ pabbatakandarapadarasākhā paripūreti. Pabbatakandarapadarasākhāparipūrā kusobbhe kussubbhe (sī. syā. kaṃ.), kusubbhe (pī.) ṇvādi 129 suttaṃ oloketabbaṃ paripūrenti. Kusobbhā paripūrā mahāsobbhe paripūrenti. Mahāsobbhā paripūrā kunnadiyo paripūrenti. Kunnadiyo paripūrā mahānadiyo paripūrenti. Mahānadiyo paripūrā mahāsamuddaṃ paripūrenti.

“Bhikkhus, it is just as when it rains with heavy drops on a mountain top, the water flows down to a low-lying area and fills the mountain clefts, crevices, and gullies. When the mountain clefts, crevices, and gullies are full, they fill the small pools. When the small pools are full, they fill the large pools. When the large pools are full, they fill the small rivers. When the small rivers are full, they fill the great rivers. When the great rivers are full, they fill the great ocean.

“Evameva kho, bhikkhave, avijjūpanisā saṅkhārā, saṅkhārūpanisaṃ viññāṇaṃ, viññāṇūpanisaṃ nāmarūpaṃ, nāmarūpūpanisaṃ saḷāyatanaṃ, saḷāyatanūpaniso phasso, phassūpanisā vedanā, vedanūpanisā taṇhā, taṇhūpanisaṃ upādānaṃ, upādānūpaniso bhavo, bhavūpanisā jāti, jātūpanisaṃ [V 1.0030] dukkhaṃ, dukkhūpanisā saddhā, saddhūpanisaṃ pāmojjaṃ, pāmojjūpanisā pīti, pītūpanisā passaddhi, passaddhūpanisaṃ sukhaṃ, sukhūpaniso samādhi, samādhūpanisaṃ yathābhūtañāṇadassanaṃ, yathābhūtañāṇadassanūpanisā nibbidā, nibbidūpaniso virāgo, virāgūpanisā vimutti, vimuttūpanisaṃ khayeñāṇa”nti. Tatiyaṃ.

“Just so, bhikkhus, formations have ignorance as their supporting condition; consciousness has formations as its supporting condition; name-and-form has consciousness as its supporting condition; the six sense bases have name-and-form as their supporting condition; contact has the six sense bases as its supporting condition; feeling has contact as its supporting condition; craving has feeling as its supporting condition; clinging has craving as its supporting condition; existence has clinging as its supporting condition; birth has existence as its supporting condition; suffering has birth as its supporting condition; faith has suffering as its supporting condition; gladness has faith as its supporting condition; rapture has gladness as its supporting condition; tranquility has rapture as its supporting condition; happiness has tranquility as its supporting condition; concentration has happiness as its supporting condition; the knowledge and vision of things as they really are has concentration as its supporting condition; disenchantment has the knowledge and vision of things as they really are as its supporting condition; dispassion has disenchantment as its supporting condition; liberation has dispassion as its supporting condition; the knowledge of destruction has liberation as its supporting condition.” The third.

4. Aññatitthiyasuttaṃ

4. The Discourse Concerning Those of Other Views

24. Rājagahe viharati veḷuvane. Atha kho āyasmā sāriputto pubbaṇhasamayaṃ nivāsetvā pattacīvaramādāya rājagahaṃ piṇḍāya pāvisi. Atha kho āyasmato sāriputtassa etadahosi – “atippago kho tāva rājagahe piṇḍāya carituṃ. Yaṃnūnāhaṃ yena aññatitthiyānaṃ paribbājakānaṃ ārāmo tenupasaṅkameyya”nti.

24. He was dwelling at Rājagaha, in the Bamboo Grove. Then, the Venerable Sāriputta, having dressed in the morning, took his bowl and robe and entered Rājagaha for alms-food. Then this thought occurred to the Venerable Sāriputta: ‘It is still too early to wander for alms-food in Rājagaha. What if I were to approach the park of the wanderers of other views?’”

Atha [M 1.0270] kho āyasmā sāriputto yena aññatitthiyānaṃ paribbājakānaṃ [P 2.0033] ārāmo tenupasaṅkami; upasaṅkamitvā [T 2.0039] tehi aññatitthiyehi paribbājakehi saddhiṃ sammodi. Sammodanīyaṃ kathaṃ sāraṇīyaṃ vītisāretvā ekamantaṃ nisīdi. Ekamantaṃ nisinnaṃ kho āyasmantaṃ sāriputtaṃ te aññatitthiyā paribbājakā etadavocuṃ –

Then the Venerable Sāriputta approached the park of the wanderers of other views. Having approached, he exchanged greetings with those wanderers of other views. Having concluded the pleasant and memorable talk, he sat down to one side. To the Venerable Sāriputta, who was seated to one side, those wanderers of other views said this:

“Santāvuso, sāriputta, eke samaṇabrāhmaṇā kammavādā sayaṃkataṃ dukkhaṃ paññapenti. Santi panāvuso sāriputta, eke samaṇabrāhmaṇā kammavādā paraṃkataṃ dukkhaṃ paññapenti. Santāvuso sāriputta, eke samaṇabrāhmaṇā kammavādā sayaṃkatañca paraṃkatañca dukkhaṃ paññapenti. Santi panāvuso sāriputta, eke samaṇabrāhmaṇā kammavādā asayaṃkāraṃ aparaṃkāraṃ adhiccasamuppannaṃ dukkhaṃ paññapenti. Idha, panāvuso sāriputta, samaṇo gotamo kiṃvādī kimakkhāyī? Kathaṃ byākaramānā ca mayaṃ vuttavādino ceva samaṇassa gotamassa assāma, na ca samaṇaṃ gotamaṃ abhūtena abbhācikkheyyāma, dhammassa cānudhammaṃ byākareyyāma, na ca koci sahadhammiko vādānupāto vādānuvādo (ka.) dī. ni. 1.381 gārayhaṃ ṭhānaṃ āgaccheyyā”ti?

“Friend Sāriputta, there are some ascetics and brahmins, proponents of kamma, who declare suffering to be self-made. Friend Sāriputta, there are some ascetics and brahmins, proponents of kamma, who declare suffering to be made by another. Friend Sāriputta, there are some ascetics and brahmins, proponents of kamma, who declare suffering to be both self-made and made by another. Friend Sāriputta, there are some ascetics and brahmins, proponents of kamma, who declare suffering to be not self-made and not other-made, having arisen without a cause. Now, in this regard, friend Sāriputta, what is the ascetic Gotama's doctrine? What does he proclaim? How should we answer so that we would be reporting what was said by the ascetic Gotama, and not misrepresent the ascetic Gotama with what is false, and so that we would explain the Dhamma in accordance with the Dhamma, and no legitimate consequence of our statement would provide grounds for censure?”

“Paṭiccasamuppannaṃ kho, āvuso, dukkhaṃ vuttaṃ bhagavatā. Kiṃ paṭicca? Phassaṃ paṭicca. Iti [V 1.0031] vadaṃ vuttavādī ceva bhagavato assa, na ca bhagavantaṃ abhūtena abbhācikkheyya, dhammassa cānudhammaṃ byākareyya, na ca koci sahadhammiko vādānupāto gārayhaṃ ṭhānaṃ āgaccheyya.

“Friends, suffering has been declared by the Blessed One to be dependently arisen. Dependent on what? Dependent on contact. One who speaks thus would be reporting what was said by the Blessed One, and would not misrepresent the Blessed One with what is false; one would explain the Dhamma in accordance with the Dhamma, and no legitimate consequence of the statement would provide grounds for censure.”

“Tatrāvuso, ye te samaṇabrāhmaṇā kammavādā sayaṃkataṃ dukkhaṃ paññapenti tadapi phassapaccayā. Yepi te samaṇabrāhmaṇā kammavādā paraṃkataṃ dukkhaṃ paññapenti tadapi phassapaccayā. Yepi te samaṇabrāhmaṇā kammavādā sayaṃkatañca paraṃkatañca dukkhaṃ paññapenti tadapi phassapaccayā. Yepi [T 2.0040][P 2.0034] te samaṇabrāhmaṇā kammavādā asayaṃkāraṃ aparaṃkāraṃ adhiccasamuppannaṃ dukkhaṃ paññapenti tadapi phassapaccayā.

“Friends, among them, those ascetics and brahmins who are proponents of kamma and declare suffering to be self-made—that too is conditioned by contact. Those ascetics and brahmins who are proponents of kamma and declare suffering to be made by another—that too is conditioned by contact. Those ascetics and brahmins who are proponents of kamma and declare suffering to be both self-made and made by another—that too is conditioned by contact. Those ascetics and brahmins who are proponents of kamma and declare suffering to be not self-made and not other-made, having arisen without a cause—that too is conditioned by contact.”

“Tatrāvuso, ye te samaṇabrāhmaṇā kammavādā sayaṃkataṃ dukkhaṃ paññapenti, te vata aññatra phassā paṭisaṃvedissantīti netaṃ ṭhānaṃ vijjati. Yepi te samaṇabrāhmaṇā kammavādā paraṃkataṃ dukkhaṃ paññapenti, te vata aññatra phassā paṭisaṃvedissantīti netaṃ ṭhānaṃ vijjati. Yepi te [M 1.0271] samaṇabrāhmaṇā kammavādā sayaṃkatañca paraṃkatañca dukkhaṃ paññapenti, te vata aññatra phassā paṭisaṃvedissantīti netaṃ ṭhānaṃ vijjati. Yepi te samaṇabrāhmaṇā kammavādā asayaṃkāraṃ aparaṃkāraṃ adhiccasamuppannaṃ dukkhaṃ paññapenti, te vata aññatra phassā paṭisaṃvedissantīti netaṃ ṭhānaṃ vijjatī”ti.

“Friends, among them, for those ascetics and brahmins who are proponents of kamma and declare suffering to be self-made, that they will experience it apart from contact—this is not possible. For those ascetics and brahmins who are proponents of kamma and declare suffering to be made by another, that they will experience it apart from contact—this is not possible. For those ascetics and brahmins who are proponents of kamma and declare suffering to be both self-made and made by another, that they will experience it apart from contact—this is not possible. For those ascetics and brahmins who are proponents of kamma and declare suffering to be not self-made and not other-made, having arisen without a cause, that they will experience it apart from contact—this is not possible.”

Assosi kho āyasmā ānando āyasmato sāriputtassa tehi aññatitthiyehi paribbājakehi saddhiṃ imaṃ kathāsallāpaṃ. Atha kho āyasmā ānando rājagahe piṇḍāya caritvā pacchābhattaṃ piṇḍapātapaṭikkanto yena bhagavā tenupasaṅkami; upasaṅkamitvā bhagavantaṃ abhivādetvā ekamantaṃ nisīdi. Ekamantaṃ nisinno kho āyasmā ānando yāvatako āyasmato sāriputtassa tehi aññatitthiyehi paribbājakehi saddhiṃ ahosi kathāsallāpo taṃ sabbaṃ bhagavato ārocesi.

The Venerable Ānanda heard this conversation between the Venerable Sāriputta and those wanderers of other views. Then the Venerable Ānanda, having wandered for alms-food in Rājagaha, on his return from the alms-round after the meal, approached the Blessed One. Having approached, he paid homage to the Blessed One and sat down to one side. Seated to one side, the Venerable Ānanda reported to the Blessed One the entire conversation that had taken place between the Venerable Sāriputta and those wanderers of other views.

“Sādhu sādhu, ānanda, yathā taṃ sāriputto sammā byākaramāno [T 2.0041] byākareyya. Paṭiccasamuppannaṃ kho, ānanda, dukkhaṃ vuttaṃ mayā. Kiṃ paṭicca? Phassaṃ paṭicca. Iti vadaṃ vuttavādī ceva me assa, na ca maṃ abhūtena abbhācikkheyya, dhammassa cānudhammaṃ byākareyya, na ca koci sahadhammiko vādānupāto gārayhaṃ ṭhānaṃ āgaccheyya.

“Good, good, Ānanda! It is just as Sāriputta, answering correctly, should have answered. Ānanda, suffering has been declared by me to be dependently arisen. Dependent on what? Dependent on contact. One who speaks thus would be reporting what was said by me, and would not misrepresent me with what is false; one would explain the Dhamma in accordance with the Dhamma, and no legitimate consequence of the statement would provide grounds for censure.”

“Tatrānanda[V 1.0032], ye te samaṇabrāhmaṇā kammavādā sayaṃkataṃ dukkhaṃ paññapenti tadapi phassapaccayā. Yepi [P 2.0035] te…pe… yepi te…pe… yepi te samaṇabrāhmaṇā kammavādā asayaṃkāraṃ aparaṃkāraṃ adhiccasamuppannaṃ dukkhaṃ paññapenti tadapi phassapaccayā.

“In that regard, Ānanda, those ascetics and brahmins who are proponents of kamma and declare suffering to be self-made—that too is conditioned by contact. Those ascetics and brahmins who are proponents of kamma and declare suffering to be made by another—that too is conditioned by contact. Those ascetics and brahmins who are proponents of kamma and declare suffering to be both self-made and made by another—that too is conditioned by contact. Those ascetics and brahmins who are proponents of kamma and declare suffering to be not self-made, not other-made, and arisen without a cause—that too is conditioned by contact.”

“Tatrānanda, yepi te samaṇabrāhmaṇā kammavādā sayaṃkataṃ dukkhaṃ paññapenti, te vata aññatra phassā paṭisaṃvedissantīti netaṃ ṭhānaṃ vijjati. Yepi te…pe… yepi te…pe… yepi te samaṇabrāhmaṇā kammavādā asayaṃkāraṃ aparaṃkāraṃ adhiccasamuppannaṃ dukkhaṃ paññapenti, te vata aññatra phassā paṭisaṃvedissantīti netaṃ ṭhānaṃ vijjati.

“In that regard, Ānanda, for those ascetics and brahmins who are proponents of kamma and declare suffering to be self-made, it is impossible that they would experience it apart from contact. For those ascetics and brahmins who are proponents of kamma and declare suffering to be made by another, it is impossible that they would experience it apart from contact. For those ascetics and brahmins who are proponents of kamma and declare suffering to be both self-made and made by another, it is impossible that they would experience it apart from contact. For those ascetics and brahmins who are proponents of kamma and declare suffering to be not self-made, not other-made, and arisen without a cause, it is impossible that they would experience it apart from contact.”

“Ekamidāhaṃ, ānanda, samayaṃ idheva rājagahe viharāmi veḷuvane kalandakanivāpe. Atha khvāhaṃ, ānanda, pubbaṇhasamayaṃ nivāsetvā pattacīvaramādāya rājagahaṃ piṇḍāya pāvisiṃ. Tassa mayhaṃ, ānanda, etadahosi – ‘atippago [M 1.0272] kho tāva rājagahe piṇḍāya carituṃ. Yaṃnūnāhaṃ yena aññatitthiyānaṃ paribbājakānaṃ ārāmo tenupasaṅkameyya’”nti.

On one occasion, Ānanda, I was staying right here in Rājagaha, in the Bamboo Grove, the Squirrels' Feeding Place. Then, Ānanda, in the morning, having dressed and taken my bowl and robe, I entered Rājagaha for alms. It occurred to me, Ānanda: 'It is still too early to go for alms in Rājagaha. What if I were to approach the park of the wandering ascetics of other persuasions?'

“Atha khvāhaṃ, ānanda, yena aññatitthiyānaṃ paribbājakānaṃ ārāmo tenupasaṅkamiṃ; upasaṅkamitvā tehi aññatitthiyehi paribbājakehi [T 2.0042] saddhiṃ sammodiṃ. Sammodanīyaṃ kathaṃ sāraṇīyaṃ vītisāretvā ekamantaṃ nisīdiṃ. Ekamantaṃ nisinnaṃ kho maṃ, ānanda, te aññatitthiyā paribbājakā etadavocuṃ –

Then, Ānanda, I approached the park of the wandering ascetics of other persuasions. Having approached, I exchanged greetings with those wandering ascetics of other persuasions. After concluding the courteous and memorable talk, I sat down to one side. Seated to one side, Ānanda, those wandering ascetics of other persuasions said this to me:

‘Santāvuso gotama, eke samaṇabrāhmaṇā kammavādā sayaṃkataṃ dukkhaṃ paññapenti. Santi panāvuso gotama, eke samaṇabrāhmaṇā kammavādā paraṃkataṃ dukkhaṃ paññapenti. Santāvuso gotama, eke samaṇabrāhmaṇā kammavādā sayaṃkatañca paraṃkatañca dukkhaṃ paññapenti. Santi panāvuso gotama, eke samaṇabrāhmaṇā kammavādā asayaṃkāraṃ aparaṃkāraṃ adhiccasamuppannaṃ dukkhaṃ paññapenti. Idha no āyasmā gotamo kiṃvādī kimakkhāyī? Kathaṃ byākaramānā ca mayaṃ vuttavādino ceva āyasmato gotamassa assāma, na ca āyasmantaṃ gotamaṃ abhūtena abbhācikkheyyāma[P 2.0036], dhammassa cānudhammaṃ byākareyyāma, na ca koci sahadhammiko vādānupāto gārayhaṃ ṭhānaṃ āgaccheyyā’”ti?

‘Friend Gotama, there are some ascetics and brahmins, proponents of kamma, who declare suffering as self-made. There are also, friend Gotama, some ascetics and brahmins, proponents of kamma, who declare suffering as made by another. There are, friend Gotama, some ascetics and brahmins, proponents of kamma, who declare suffering as both self-made and made by another. There are also, friend Gotama, some ascetics and brahmins, proponents of kamma, who declare suffering as not self-made, not other-made, and arisen without a cause. In this regard, what is the Venerable Gotama's doctrine, what does he proclaim? And how should we explain so that we would be repeating what has been said by the Venerable Gotama, and not misrepresent the Venerable Gotama with what is untrue, and so we would explain in accordance with the Dhamma, and no reasonable, co-doctrinal basis for criticism would arise?’

“Evaṃ [V 1.0033] vuttāhaṃ, ānanda, te aññatitthiye paribbājake etadavocaṃ – ‘paṭiccasamuppannaṃ kho, āvuso, dukkhaṃ vuttaṃ mayā. Kiṃ paṭicca? Phassaṃ paṭicca. Iti vadaṃ vuttavādī ceva me assa, na ca maṃ abhūtena abbhācikkheyya, dhammassa cānudhammaṃ byākareyya, na ca koci sahadhammiko vādānupāto gārayhaṃ ṭhānaṃ āgaccheyyā’”ti.

When this was said, Ānanda, I said this to those wandering ascetics of other persuasions: 'Friends, it has been stated by me that suffering is dependently arisen. Dependent on what? Dependent on contact. One who says this would be repeating what was said by me, and would not be misrepresenting me with what is untrue, and would be explaining in accordance with the Dhamma, and no reasonable, co-doctrinal basis for criticism would arise.'

“Tatrāvuso, ye te samaṇabrāhmaṇā kammavādā sayaṃkataṃ dukkhaṃ paññapenti tadapi phassapaccayā. Yepi te…pe… yepi te…pe… [T 2.0043] yepi te samaṇabrāhmaṇā kammavādā asayaṃkāraṃ aparaṃkāraṃ adhiccasamuppannaṃ dukkhaṃ paññapenti tadapi phassapaccayā.

In that regard, friends, for those ascetics and brahmins who are proponents of kamma and declare suffering to be self-made—that too is conditioned by contact. And for those… and for those… and for those ascetics and brahmins who are proponents of kamma and declare suffering to be not self-made, not other-made, and arisen without a cause—that too is conditioned by contact.

“Tatrāvuso, ye te samaṇabrāhmaṇā kammavādā sayaṃkataṃ dukkhaṃ paññapenti, te vata aññatra phassā paṭisaṃvedissantīti netaṃ ṭhānaṃ vijjati. Yepi te…pe… yepi te…pe… yepi te samaṇabrāhmaṇā kammavādā asayaṃkāraṃ aparaṃkāraṃ adhiccasamuppannaṃ dukkhaṃ paññapenti, te vata aññatra phassā paṭisaṃvedissantīti netaṃ ṭhānaṃ vijjatī”ti. “Acchariyaṃ bhante, abbhutaṃ bhante[M 1.0273]! Yatra hi nāma ekena padena sabbo attho vutto bhavissati. Siyā nu kho, bhante, esevattho vitthārena vuccamāno gambhīro ceva assa gambhīrāvabhāso cā”ti?

‘In that regard, friends, for those ascetics and brahmins who are proponents of kamma and declare suffering to be self-made, it is impossible that they would experience it apart from contact. And for those… and for those… and for those ascetics and brahmins who are proponents of kamma and declare suffering to be not self-made, not other-made, and arisen without a cause, it is impossible that they would experience it apart from contact.’ ‘Marvelous, venerable sir! Amazing, venerable sir! How the entire meaning has been stated with a single phrase! Venerable sir, could it be that this very meaning, when explained in detail, would be both profound and have the appearance of profundity?’

“Tena hānanda, taññevettha paṭibhātū”ti. “Sace maṃ, bhante, evaṃ puccheyyuṃ – ‘jarāmaraṇaṃ, āvuso ānanda, kiṃnidānaṃ kiṃsamudayaṃ kiṃjātikaṃ kiṃpabhava’nti? Evaṃ puṭṭhohaṃ, bhante, evaṃ byākareyyaṃ – ‘jarāmaraṇaṃ kho, āvuso, jātinidānaṃ jātisamudayaṃ jātijātikaṃ jātipabhava’nti. Evaṃ puṭṭhohaṃ, bhante, evaṃ byākareyyaṃ.

‘Then, Ānanda, let that very meaning become clear to you.’ ‘Venerable sir, if they were to ask me: “Friend Ānanda, what is the source, what is the origin, what is the birth, what is the provenance of aging and death?”—being asked thus, venerable sir, I would explain thus: “Friends, aging and death have birth as their source, birth as their origin, birth as their birth, birth as their provenance.” Being asked thus, venerable sir, I would explain thus.

“Sace [P 2.0037] maṃ, bhante, evaṃ puccheyyuṃ – ‘jāti panāvuso ānanda, kiṃnidānā kiṃsamudayā kiṃjātikā kiṃpabhavā’ti? Evaṃ puṭṭhohaṃ, bhante, evaṃ byākareyyaṃ – ‘jāti kho, āvuso, bhavanidānā bhavasamudayā bhavajātikā bhavappabhavā’ti. Evaṃ puṭṭhohaṃ, bhante, evaṃ byākareyyaṃ[T 2.0044].

‘Venerable sir, if they were to ask me: “But, friend Ānanda, what is the source, what is the origin, what is the birth, what is the provenance of birth?”—being asked thus, venerable sir, I would explain thus: “Friends, birth has becoming as its source, becoming as its origin, becoming as its birth, becoming as its provenance.” Being asked thus, venerable sir, I would explain thus.

“Sace maṃ, bhante, evaṃ puccheyyuṃ – ‘bhavo panāvuso ānanda, kiṃnidāno kiṃsamudayo kiṃjātiko kiṃpabhavo’ti? Evaṃ puṭṭhohaṃ, bhante, evaṃ byākareyyaṃ – ‘bhavo kho, āvuso, upādānanidāno [V 1.0034] upādānasamudayo upādānajātiko upādānappabhavo’ti. Evaṃ puṭṭhohaṃ, bhante, evaṃ byākareyyaṃ.

‘Venerable sir, if they were to ask me: “But, friend Ānanda, what is the source, what is the origin, what is the birth, what is the provenance of becoming?”—being asked thus, venerable sir, I would explain thus: “Friends, becoming has clinging as its source, clinging as its origin, clinging as its birth, clinging as its provenance.” Being asked thus, venerable sir, I would explain thus.

“Sace maṃ, bhante, evaṃ puccheyyuṃ – upādānaṃ panāvuso…pe… taṇhā panāvuso…pe… vedanā panāvuso…pe… sace maṃ, bhante, evaṃ puccheyyuṃ – ‘phasso panāvuso ānanda, kiṃnidāno kiṃsamudayo kiṃjātiko kiṃpabhavo’ti? Evaṃ puṭṭhohaṃ, bhante, evaṃ byākareyyaṃ – ‘phasso kho, āvuso, saḷāyatananidāno saḷāyatanasamudayo saḷāyatanajātiko saḷāyatanappabhavo’ti. ‘Channaṃtveva, āvuso, phassāyatanānaṃ asesavirāganirodhā phassanirodho; phassanirodhā vedanānirodho; vedanānirodhā taṇhānirodho; taṇhānirodhā upādānanirodho; upādānanirodhā bhavanirodho; bhavanirodhā jātinirodho; jātinirodhā jarāmaraṇaṃ sokaparidevadukkhadomanassupāyāsā nirujjhanti. Evametassa kevalassa dukkhakkhandhassa nirodho hotī’ti. Evaṃ puṭṭhohaṃ, bhante, evaṃ byākareyya”nti. Catutthaṃ.

“Venerable Sir, if they were to ask me thus: ‘Friend, as for clinging… and so on… as for craving… and so on… as for feeling… and so on….’ Venerable Sir, if they were to ask me thus: ‘Friend Ānanda, as for contact, what is its source, what is its origin, what is its birth, what is its provenance?’—being asked thus, Venerable Sir, I would answer thus: ‘Friends, contact has the six sense bases as its source, the six sense bases as its origin, the six sense bases as its birth, the six sense bases as its provenance.’ ‘Friends, through the remainderless fading away and cessation of just these six bases for contact, there is the cessation of contact. With the cessation of contact, there is the cessation of feeling. With the cessation of feeling, there is the cessation of craving. With the cessation of craving, there is the cessation of clinging. With the cessation of clinging, there is the cessation of becoming. With the cessation of becoming, there is the cessation of birth. With the cessation of birth, aging and death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair cease. Thus there is the cessation of this entire mass of suffering.’ Being asked thus, Venerable Sir, I would answer thus.”

5. Bhūmijasuttaṃ

5. The Bhūmija Sutta

25. Sāvatthiyaṃ [M 1.0274] viharati. Atha kho āyasmā bhūmijo sāyanhasamayaṃ paṭisallānā vuṭṭhito yenāyasmā sāriputto tenupasaṅkami; upasaṅkamitvā [P 2.0038] āyasmatā sāriputtena saddhiṃ sammodi. Sammodanīyaṃ kathaṃ sāraṇīyaṃ vītisāretvā ekamantaṃ nisīdi. Ekamantaṃ nisinno kho [T 2.0045] āyasmā bhūmijo āyasmantaṃ sāriputtaṃ etadavoca –

25. He was dwelling in Sāvatthī. Then, the Venerable Bhūmija, having arisen from solitary seclusion in the evening, approached the Venerable Sāriputta. Having approached, he exchanged joyful greetings with the Venerable Sāriputta. Having concluded the joyful and memorable talk, he sat down to one side. The Venerable Bhūmija, having sat down to one side, said this to the Venerable Sāriputta:

“Santāvuso sāriputta, eke samaṇabrāhmaṇā kammavādā sayaṃkataṃ sukhadukkhaṃ paññapenti. Santi panāvuso sāriputta, eke samaṇabrāhmaṇā kammavādā paraṃkataṃ sukhadukkhaṃ paññapenti. Santāvuso sāriputta, eke samaṇabrāhmaṇā kammavādā sayaṃkatañca paraṃkatañca sukhadukkhaṃ paññapenti. Santi panāvuso sāriputta, eke samaṇabrāhmaṇā kammavādā asayaṃkāraṃ aparaṃkāraṃ adhiccasamuppannaṃ sukhadukkhaṃ paññapenti. Idha no, āvuso sāriputta, bhagavā kiṃvādī kimakkhāyī[V 1.0035], kathaṃ byākaramānā ca mayaṃ vuttavādino ceva bhagavato assāma, na ca bhagavantaṃ abhūtena abbhācikkheyyāma, dhammassa cānudhammaṃ byākareyyāma, na ca koci sahadhammiko vādānupāto gārayhaṃ ṭhānaṃ āgaccheyyā”ti?

“Friend Sāriputta, there are some ascetics and brahmins who are proponents of kamma who declare that pleasure and pain are self-made. Friend Sāriputta, there are some ascetics and brahmins who are proponents of kamma who declare that pleasure and pain are made by another. Friend Sāriputta, there are some ascetics and brahmins who are proponents of kamma who declare that pleasure and pain are both self-made and made by another. Friend Sāriputta, there are some ascetics and brahmins who are proponents of kamma who declare that pleasure and pain, being not self-made and not made by another, arise without a cause. In this matter, Friend Sāriputta, what is our Blessed One's teaching? What does he proclaim? And how should we answer so that we would be stating what was said by the Blessed One, and would not misrepresent the Blessed One with what is untrue, and would explain the teaching in accordance with the teaching, and so that no consequential argument from a co-religionist would arrive at a censurable point?”

“Paṭiccasamuppannaṃ kho, āvuso, sukhadukkhaṃ vuttaṃ bhagavatā. Kiṃ paṭicca? Phassaṃ paṭicca. Iti vadaṃ vuttavādī ceva bhagavato assa, na ca bhagavantaṃ abhūtena abbhācikkheyya, dhammassa cānudhammaṃ byākareyya, na ca koci sahadhammiko vādānupāto gārayhaṃ ṭhānaṃ āgaccheyya.

“Friend, the Blessed One has stated that pleasure and pain are dependently arisen. Dependent on what? Dependent on contact. One who says this would be stating what was said by the Blessed One, and would not misrepresent the Blessed One with what is untrue, and would explain the teaching in accordance with the teaching, and no consequential argument from a co-religionist would arrive at a censurable point.”

“Tatrāvuso, ye te samaṇabrāhmaṇā kammavādā sayaṃkataṃ sukhadukkhaṃ paññapenti, tadapi phassapaccayā. Yepi te…pe… yepi te…pe… yepi te samaṇabrāhmaṇā kammavādā asayaṃkāraṃ aparaṃkāraṃ adhiccasamuppannaṃ sukhadukkhaṃ paññapenti, tadapi phassapaccayā.

“Therein, friend, as for those ascetics and brahmins who are proponents of kamma and declare that pleasure and pain are self-made—that too is conditioned by contact. As for those… and as for those… and as for those ascetics and brahmins who are proponents of kamma and declare that pleasure and pain, being not self-made and not made by another, arise without a cause—that too is conditioned by contact.

“Tatrāvuso, ye te samaṇabrāhmaṇā kammavādā sayaṃkataṃ sukhadukkhaṃ [T 2.0046] paññapenti, te vata aññatra phassā paṭisaṃvedissantīti netaṃ ṭhānaṃ vijjati. Yepi te…pe. [P 2.0039]… yepi te…pe… yepi te samaṇabrāhmaṇā kammavādā asayaṃkāraṃ aparaṃkāraṃ adhiccasamuppannaṃ sukhadukkhaṃ paññapenti, te vata aññatra phassā paṭisaṃvedissantīti netaṃ ṭhānaṃ vijjatī”ti.

“Therein, friend, as for those ascetics and brahmins who are proponents of kamma and declare that pleasure and pain are self-made—that they will experience it apart from contact, this possibility does not exist. As for those… and as for those… and as for those ascetics and brahmins who are proponents of kamma and declare that pleasure and pain, being not self-made and not made by another, arise without a cause—that they will experience it apart from contact, this possibility does not exist.”

Assosi [M 1.0275] kho āyasmā ānando āyasmato sāriputtassa āyasmatā bhūmijena saddhiṃ imaṃ kathāsallāpaṃ. Atha kho āyasmā ānando yena bhagavā tenupasaṅkami; upasaṅkamitvā bhagavantaṃ abhivādetvā ekamantaṃ nisīdi. Ekamantaṃ nisinno kho āyasmā ānando yāvatako āyasmato sāriputtassa āyasmatā bhūmijena saddhiṃ ahosi kathāsallāpo taṃ sabbaṃ bhagavato ārocesi.

The Venerable Ānanda heard this conversation of the Venerable Sāriputta with the Venerable Bhūmija. Then the Venerable Ānanda approached the Blessed One. Having approached and paid homage to the Blessed One, he sat down to one side. Having sat down to one side, the Venerable Ānanda related to the Blessed One the entire conversation that had taken place between the Venerable Sāriputta and the Venerable Bhūmija.

“Sādhu sādhu, ānanda, yathā taṃ sāriputto sammā byākaramāno byākareyya. Paṭiccasamuppannaṃ kho, ānanda, sukhadukkhaṃ vuttaṃ mayā. Kiṃ paṭicca? Phassaṃ paṭicca. Iti vadaṃ vuttavādī ceva me assa, na ca maṃ abhūtena abbhācikkheyya, dhammassa cānudhammaṃ byākareyya, na ca koci sahadhammiko vādānupāto gārayhaṃ ṭhānaṃ āgaccheyya.

“Excellent, excellent, Ānanda! Sāriputta has answered correctly, just as one should answer. Ānanda, pleasure and pain have been stated by me to be dependently arisen. Dependent on what? Dependent on contact. One who says this would be stating what was said by me, and would not misrepresent me with what is untrue, and would explain the teaching in accordance with the teaching, and no consequential argument from a co-religionist would arrive at a censurable point.”

“Tatrānanda[V 1.0036], ye te samaṇabrāhmaṇā kammavādā sayaṃkataṃ sukhadukkhaṃ paññapenti tadapi phassapaccayā. Yepi te…pe… yepi te…pe… yepi te samaṇabrāhmaṇā kammavādā asayaṃkāraṃ aparaṃkāraṃ adhiccasamuppannaṃ sukhadukkhaṃ paññapenti tadapi phassapaccayā.

“Therein, Ānanda, as for those ascetics and brahmins who are proponents of kamma and declare that pleasure and pain are self-made—that too is conditioned by contact. As for those… and as for those… and as for those ascetics and brahmins who are proponents of kamma and declare that pleasure and pain, being not self-made and not made by another, arise without a cause—that too is conditioned by contact.

“Tatrānanda[T 2.0047], ye te samaṇabrāhmaṇā kammavādā sayaṃkataṃ sukhadukkhaṃ paññapenti, te vata aññatra phassā paṭisaṃvedissantīti netaṃ ṭhānaṃ vijjati. Yepi te…pe… yepi te…pe… yepi te samaṇabrāhmaṇākammavādā asayaṃkāraṃ aparaṃkāraṃ adhiccasamuppannaṃ sukhadukkhaṃ paññapenti, te vata aññatra phassā paṭisaṃvedissantīti netaṃ ṭhānaṃ vijjati.

“Therein, Ānanda, as for those ascetics and brahmins who are proponents of kamma and declare that pleasure and pain are self-made—that they will experience it apart from contact, this possibility does not exist. As for those… and as for those… and as for those ascetics and brahmins who are proponents of kamma and declare that pleasure and pain, being not self-made and not made by another, arise without a cause—that they will experience it apart from contact, this possibility does not exist.

“Kāye vā hānanda, sati kāyasañcetanāhetu uppajjati ajjhattaṃ [P 2.0040] sukhadukkhaṃ. Vācāya vā hānanda, sati vacīsañcetanāhetu uppajjati ajjhattaṃ sukhadukkhaṃ. Mane vā hānanda, sati manosañcetanāhetu uppajjati ajjhattaṃ sukhadukkhaṃ avijjāpaccayā ca.

“Ānanda, when there is a body, internal pleasure and pain arises on account of bodily volition. Ānanda, when there is speech, internal pleasure and pain arises on account of verbal volition. Ānanda, when there is a mind, internal pleasure and pain arises on account of mental volition. And this is conditioned by ignorance.

“Sāmaṃ vā taṃ, ānanda, kāyasaṅkhāraṃ abhisaṅkharoti, yaṃpaccayāssa yaṃpaccayāya (syā. kaṃ.), yaṃpaccayā yaṃ (ka.) taṃ uppajjati ajjhattaṃ sukhadukkhaṃ. Pare vā taṃ pare vāssa taṃ (sī. pī.), pare vāyataṃ (syā. kaṃ.), ānanda, kāyasaṅkhāraṃ abhisaṅkharonti, yaṃpaccayāssa taṃ uppajjati ajjhattaṃ sukhadukkhaṃ. Sampajāno vā taṃ, ānanda, kāyasaṅkhāraṃ abhisaṅkharoti yaṃpaccayāssa taṃ uppajjati ajjhattaṃ sukhadukkhaṃ. Asampajāno [M 1.0276] vā taṃ, ānanda, kāyasaṅkhāraṃ abhisaṅkharoti yaṃpaccayāssa taṃ uppajjati ajjhattaṃ sukhadukkhaṃ.

“Ānanda, one oneself forms that bodily formation on account of which that internal pleasure and pain arises for one. Or others, Ānanda, form that bodily formation on account of which that internal pleasure and pain arises for one. Or, Ānanda, one with clear comprehension forms that bodily formation on account of which that internal pleasure and pain arises for one. Or, Ānanda, one without clear comprehension forms that bodily formation on account of which that internal pleasure and pain arises for one.

“Sāmaṃ vā taṃ, ānanda, vacīsaṅkhāraṃ abhisaṅkharoti yaṃpaccayāssa taṃ uppajjati ajjhattaṃ sukhadukkhaṃ. Pare [T 2.0048] vā taṃ, ānanda, vacīsaṅkhāraṃ abhisaṅkharonti yaṃpaccayāssa taṃ uppajjati ajjhattaṃ sukhadukkhaṃ. Sampajāno vā taṃ, ānanda…pe… asampajāno vā taṃ, ānanda, vacīsaṅkhāraṃ abhisaṅkharoti yaṃpaccayāssa taṃ uppajjati ajjhattaṃ sukhadukkhaṃ.

Ānanda, one by oneself forms that verbal formation on account of which that internal pleasure and pain arises for one. Or others, Ānanda, form that verbal formation on account of which that internal pleasure and pain arises for one. Or, Ānanda, one with clear comprehension... Or, Ānanda, one without clear comprehension forms that verbal formation on account of which that internal pleasure and pain arises for one.

“Sāmaṃ vā taṃ, ānanda, manosaṅkhāraṃ abhisaṅkharoti yaṃpaccayāssa taṃ uppajjati ajjhattaṃ sukhadukkhaṃ. Pare vā taṃ, ānanda, manosaṅkhāraṃ abhisaṅkharonti yaṃpaccayāssa taṃ uppajjati ajjhattaṃ sukhadukkhaṃ. Sampajāno vā taṃ, ānanda…pe… asampajāno vā taṃ, ānanda, manosaṅkhāraṃ abhisaṅkharoti yaṃpaccayāssa taṃ uppajjati ajjhattaṃ sukhadukkhaṃ.

Ānanda, one by oneself forms that mental formation on account of which that internal pleasure and pain arises for one. Or others, Ānanda, form that mental formation on account of which that internal pleasure and pain arises for one. Or, Ānanda, one with clear comprehension... Or, Ānanda, one without clear comprehension forms that mental formation on account of which that internal pleasure and pain arises for one.

“Imesu[V 1.0037], ānanda, dhammesu avijjā anupatitā. Avijjāya tveva, ānanda, asesavirāganirodhā so kāyo na hoti yaṃpaccayāssa taṃ uppajjati ajjhattaṃ sukhadukkhaṃ. Sā vācā na hoti yaṃpaccayāssa taṃ uppajjati ajjhattaṃ sukhadukkhaṃ. So mano na hoti yaṃpaccayāssa taṃ uppajjati [P 2.0041] ajjhattaṃ sukhadukkhaṃ. Khettaṃ taṃ na hoti…pe… vatthu taṃ na hoti…pe… āyatanaṃ taṃ na hoti…pe… adhikaraṇaṃ taṃ na hoti yaṃpaccayāssa taṃ uppajjati ajjhattaṃ sukhadukkha”nti. Pañcamaṃ.

Ānanda, ignorance pervades these phenomena. With the remainderless fading away and cessation of that very ignorance, Ānanda, that bodily volition, on account of which that internal pleasure and pain arises for one, does not come to be. That verbal volition, on account of which that internal pleasure and pain arises for one, does not come to be. That mental volition, on account of which that internal pleasure and pain arises for one, does not come to be. That is not the field... that is not the ground... that is not the basis... that is not the cause, on account of which that internal pleasure and pain arises for one.” The fifth.

6. Upavāṇasuttaṃ

6. The Upavāṇa Sutta

26. Sāvatthiyaṃ viharati. Atha kho āyasmā upavāṇo yena bhagavā tenupasaṅkami; upasaṅkamitvā bhagavantaṃ abhivādetvā ekamantaṃ nisīdi. Ekamantaṃ nisinno kho āyasmā upavāṇo bhagavantaṃ etadavoca [T 2.0049] –

26. At Sāvatthī. Then the Venerable Upavāṇa approached the Blessed One, paid homage to him, and sat down to one side. As he was sitting to one side, the Venerable Upavāṇa said to the Blessed One:

“Santi, bhante, eke samaṇabrāhmaṇā sayaṃkataṃ dukkhaṃ paññapenti. Santi pana, bhante, eke samaṇabrāhmaṇā paraṃkataṃ dukkhaṃ paññapenti. Santi pana, bhante, eke samaṇabrāhmaṇā sayaṃkatañca paraṃkatañca dukkhaṃ paññapenti. Santi pana, bhante, eke samaṇabrāhmaṇā asayaṃkāraṃ aparaṃkāraṃ adhiccasamuppannaṃ dukkhaṃ paññapenti. Idha no, bhante, bhagavā kiṃvādī kimakkhāyī kathaṃ byākaramānā ca mayaṃ vuttavādino ceva bhagavato assāma, na ca bhagavantaṃ abhūtena [M 1.0277] abbhācikkheyyāma, dhammassa cānudhammaṃ byākareyyāma, na ca koci sahadhammiko vādānupāto gārayhaṃ ṭhānaṃ āgaccheyyā”ti?

“Venerable sir, there are some ascetics and brahmins who declare suffering to be self-made. There are some ascetics and brahmins, venerable sir, who declare suffering to be made by another. There are some ascetics and brahmins, venerable sir, who declare suffering to be both self-made and made by another. There are some ascetics and brahmins, venerable sir, who declare suffering to be not self-made, not made by another, and arisen without a cause. In this matter, venerable sir, what is the Blessed One's doctrine, what does he proclaim? How should we explain so that we would be stating what was spoken by the Blessed One, not misrepresenting the Blessed One with what is untrue, and would explain the Dhamma in accordance with the Dhamma, so that no legitimate ensuing assertion and talk would provide grounds for censure?”

“Paṭiccasamuppannaṃ kho, upavāṇa, dukkhaṃ vuttaṃ mayā. Kiṃ paṭicca? Phassaṃ paṭicca. Iti vadaṃ vuttavādī ceva me assa, na ca maṃ abhūtena abbhācikkheyya, dhammassa cānudhammaṃ byākareyya, na ca koci sahadhammiko vādānupāto gārayhaṃ ṭhānaṃ āgaccheyya.

“Upavāṇa, I have declared suffering to be dependently arisen. Dependent on what? Dependent on contact. One who speaks thus would be stating what was spoken by me, would not be misrepresenting me with what is untrue, and would be explaining the Dhamma in accordance with the Dhamma, so that no legitimate ensuing assertion and talk would provide grounds for censure.”

“Tatra, upavāṇa, ye te samaṇabrāhmaṇā sayaṃkataṃ dukkhaṃ paññapenti, tadapi phassapaccayā. Yepi te…pe… yepi te…pe… yepi te samaṇabrāhmaṇā asayaṃkāraṃ aparaṃkāraṃ adhiccasamuppannaṃ dukkhaṃ paññapenti tadapi phassapaccayā.

“Therein, Upavāṇa, for those ascetics and brahmins who declare suffering to be self-made—that too is conditioned by contact. For those who declare it to be made by another… for those who declare it to be both self-made and made by another… and for those ascetics and brahmins who declare suffering to be not self-made, not made by another, and arisen without a cause—that too is conditioned by contact.”

“Tatra[V 1.0038][P 2.0042], upavāṇa, ye te samaṇabrāhmaṇā sayaṃkataṃ dukkhaṃ paññapenti, te vata añña phassā paṭisaṃvedissantīti [T 2.0050] netaṃ ṭhānaṃ vijjati. Yepi te…pe… yepi te…pe… yepi te samaṇabrāhmaṇā asayaṃkāraṃ aparaṃkāraṃ adhiccasamuppannaṃ dukkhaṃ paññapenti, te vata aññatra phassā paṭisaṃvedissantīti netaṃ ṭhānaṃ vijjatī”ti. Chaṭṭhaṃ.

“Therein, Upavāṇa, for those ascetics and brahmins who declare suffering to be self-made, it is impossible that they will experience it apart from contact. For those who declare it to be made by another… for those who declare it to be both self-made and made by another… and for those ascetics and brahmins who declare suffering to be not self-made, not made by another, and arisen without a cause, it is impossible that they will experience it apart from contact.” The sixth.

7. Paccayasuttaṃ

7. The Discourse on Conditions

27. Sāvatthiyaṃ viharati…pe… “avijjāpaccayā, bhikkhave, saṅkhārā; saṅkhārapaccayā viññāṇaṃ…pe… evametassa kevalassa dukkhakkhandhassa samudayo hoti.

27. At Sāvatthī... “Bhikkhus, with ignorance as a condition, volitional formations come to be; with volitional formations as a condition, consciousness comes to be... Thus is the arising of this whole mass of suffering.

“Katamañca, bhikkhave, jarāmaraṇaṃ? Yā tesaṃ tesaṃ sattānaṃ tamhi tamhi sattanikāye jarā jīraṇatā khaṇḍiccaṃ pāliccaṃ valittacatā āyuno saṃhāni indriyānaṃ paripāko – ayaṃ vuccati jarā. Yā tesaṃ tesaṃ sattānaṃ tamhā tamhā sattanikāyā cuti cavanatā bhedo antaradhānaṃ maccu maraṇaṃ kālakiriyā khandhānaṃ bhedo kaḷevarassa nikkhepo; idaṃ vuccati maraṇaṃ. Iti ayañca jarā idañca maraṇaṃ. Idaṃ vuccati, bhikkhave, jarāmaraṇaṃ. Jātisamudayā jarāmaraṇasamudayo; jātinirodhā jarāmaraṇanirodho. Ayameva ariyo aṭṭhaṅgiko maggo jarāmaraṇanirodhagāminī paṭipadā. Seyyathidaṃ – sammādiṭṭhi, sammāsaṅkappo, sammāvācā, sammākammanto, sammāājīvo, sammāvāyāmo, sammāsati, sammāsamādhi.

“And what, bhikkhus, is aging-and-death? Whatever, for the various beings in the various orders of beings, is the aging, decrepitude, brokenness of teeth, grayness of hair, wrinkledness of skin, decline of life, and decay of the faculties—this is called aging. Whatever, for the various beings from the various orders of beings, is the passing away, the falling away, the breaking up, the disappearance, death, dying, the making of time, the breaking up of the aggregates, the casting off of the corpse—this is called death. Thus, this is aging and this is death. This, bhikkhus, is called aging-and-death. With the arising of birth, there is the arising of aging-and-death. With the cessation of birth, there is the cessation of aging-and-death. This very Noble Eightfold Path is the practice leading to the cessation of aging-and-death, namely: right view, right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration.”

“Katamā [M 1.0278] ca, bhikkhave, jāti…pe… katamo ca, bhikkhave, bhavo… katamañca, bhikkhave, upādānaṃ… katamā [P 2.0043] ca, bhikkhave, taṇhā… katamā ca, bhikkhave, vedanā… katamo ca, bhikkhave[T 2.0051], phasso… katamañca, bhikkhave, saḷāyatanaṃ… katamañca, bhikkhave, nāmarūpaṃ… katamañca, bhikkhave, viññāṇaṃ…?

“And what, bhikkhus, is birth? ... And what, bhikkhus, is becoming? ... And what, bhikkhus, is clinging? ... And what, bhikkhus, is craving? ... And what, bhikkhus, is feeling? ... And what, bhikkhus, is contact? ... And what, bhikkhus, is the sixfold sense base? ... And what, bhikkhus, is name-and-form? ... And what, bhikkhus, is consciousness?”

“Katame [V 1.0039] ca, bhikkhave, saṅkhārā? Tayome, bhikkhave, saṅkhārā – kāyasaṅkhāro, vacīsaṅkhāro, cittasaṅkhāro. Ime vuccanti, bhikkhave, saṅkhārā. Avijjāsamudayā saṅkhārasamudayo; avijjānirodhā saṅkhāranirodho. Ayameva ariyo aṭṭhaṅgiko maggo saṅkhāranirodhagāminī paṭipadā. Seyyathidaṃ – sammādiṭṭhi…pe… sammāsamādhi.

“And what, bhikkhus, are formations? There are these three formations, bhikkhus: the bodily formation, the verbal formation, and the mental formation. These, bhikkhus, are called formations. With the origin of ignorance, there is the origin of formations. With the cessation of ignorance, there is the cessation of formations. This very Noble Eightfold Path is the practice leading to the cessation of formations, namely: right view... right concentration.”

“Yato kho, bhikkhave, ariyasāvako evaṃ paccayaṃ pajānāti, evaṃ paccayasamudayaṃ pajānāti, evaṃ paccayanirodhaṃ pajānāti, evaṃ paccayanirodhagāminiṃ paṭipadaṃ pajānāti. Ayaṃ vuccati, bhikkhave, ariyasāvako diṭṭhisampanno itipi, dassanasampanno itipi, āgato imaṃ saddhammaṃ itipi, passati imaṃ saddhammaṃ itipi, sekkhena ñāṇena samannāgato itipi, sekkhāya vijjāya samannāgato itipi, dhammasotaṃ samāpanno itipi, ariyo nibbedhikapañño itipi, amatadvāraṃ āhacca tiṭṭhati itipī”ti. Sattamaṃ.

“When, bhikkhus, a noble disciple thus knows the condition, thus knows the arising of the condition, thus knows the cessation of the condition, and thus knows the practice leading to the cessation of the condition, this noble disciple, bhikkhus, is called one accomplished in view, one accomplished in vision, one who has arrived at this true Dhamma, one who sees this true Dhamma, one endowed with the knowledge of a trainee, one endowed with the true knowledge of a trainee, one who has attained the stream of the Dhamma, a noble one with penetrative wisdom, one who stands having reached the door to the Deathless.”

8. Bhikkhusuttaṃ

8. The Bhikkhu Sutta

28. Sāvatthiyaṃ viharati…pe… “tatra kho…pe… idha, bhikkhave, bhikkhu jarāmaraṇaṃ pajānāti, jarāmaraṇasamudayaṃ pajānāti, jarāmaraṇanirodhaṃ pajānāti, jarāmaraṇanirodhagāminiṃ paṭipadaṃ pajānāti, jātiṃ pajānāti…pe… bhavaṃ pajānāti… upādānaṃ pajānāti… taṇhaṃ [P 2.0044] pajānāti… vedanaṃ pajānāti… phassaṃ pajānāti… saḷāyatanaṃ pajānāti… nāmarūpaṃ pajānāti… viññāṇaṃ pajānāti… saṅkhāre pajānāti, saṅkhārasamudayaṃ pajānāti[T 2.0052], saṅkhāranirodhaṃ pajānāti, saṅkhāranirodhagāminiṃ paṭipadaṃ pajānāti.

28. Dwelling at Sāvatthī. ... On that occasion... 'Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu understands aging-and-death, he understands the origin of aging-and-death, he understands the cessation of aging-and-death, he understands the path leading to the cessation of aging-and-death. He understands birth... he understands becoming... he understands clinging... he understands craving... he understands feeling... he understands contact... he understands the six sense bases... he understands name-and-form... he understands consciousness... he understands formations, he understands the origin of formations, he understands the cessation of formations, he understands the path leading to the cessation of formations.'

“Katamañca, bhikkhave, jarāmaraṇaṃ? Yā tesaṃ tesaṃ sattānaṃ tamhi tamhi sattanikāye jarā jīraṇatā khaṇḍiccaṃ pāliccaṃ valittacatā āyuno saṃhāni indriyānaṃ paripāko – ayaṃ vuccati jarā. Yā tesaṃ tesaṃ sattānaṃ tamhā tamhā sattanikāyā cuti cavanatā bhedo antaradhānaṃ maccu maraṇaṃ kālakiriyā khandhānaṃ bhedo kaḷevarassa nikkhepo; idaṃ vuccati [M 1.0279] maraṇaṃ. Iti ayaṃ ca jarā idañca maraṇaṃ. Idaṃ vuccati, bhikkhave, jarāmaraṇaṃ. Jātisamudayā [V 1.0040] jarāmaraṇasamudayo; jātinirodhā jarāmaraṇanirodho. Ayameva ariyo aṭṭhaṅgiko maggo jarāmaraṇanirodhagāminī paṭipadā. Seyyathidaṃ – sammādiṭṭhi…pe… sammāsamādhi.

“And what, bhikkhus, is aging-and-death? Whatever, for the various beings in the various orders of beings, is aging, decrepitude, brokenness of teeth, grayness of hair, wrinkledness of skin, the decline of the life-span, the decay of the sense faculties—this is called aging. Whatever, for the various beings in the various orders of beings, is the passing away, the falling away, the breaking up, the disappearance, death, dying, the completion of the time-period, the breaking up of the aggregates, the laying down of the corpse—this is called death. Thus, this aging and this death: this, bhikkhus, is called aging-and-death. With the origin of birth, there is the origin of aging-and-death. With the cessation of birth, there is the cessation of aging-and-death. This very Noble Eightfold Path is the path leading to the cessation of aging-and-death, that is: Right View... Right Concentration.”

“Katamā ca, bhikkhave, jāti…pe… katamo ca, bhikkhave, bhavo… katamañca, bhikkhave, upādānaṃ… vedanā… phasso… saḷāyatanaṃ… nāmarūpaṃ… viññāṇaṃ….

“And what, bhikkhus, is birth? ... And what, bhikkhus, is becoming? ... And what, bhikkhus, is clinging? ... And what, bhikkhus, is craving? ... And what is feeling? ... And what is contact? ... And what is the sixfold sense base? ... And what is name-and-form? ... And what is consciousness?”

“Katame ca, bhikkhave, saṅkhārā? Tayome, bhikkhave, saṅkhārā – kāyasaṅkhāro, vacīsaṅkhāro, cittasaṅkhāro. Ime vuccanti, bhikkhave, saṅkhārā. Avijjāsamudayā saṅkhārasamudayo; avijjānirodhā saṅkhāranirodho. Ayameva ariyo aṭṭhaṅgiko maggo saṅkhāranirodhagāminī paṭipadā. Seyyathidaṃ – sammādiṭṭhi…pe… sammāsamādhi.

“And what, bhikkhus, are formations? There are these three formations, bhikkhus: the bodily formation, the verbal formation, and the mental formation. These, bhikkhus, are called formations. With the origin of ignorance, there is the origin of formations. With the cessation of ignorance, there is the cessation of formations. This very Noble Eightfold Path is the path leading to the cessation of formations, that is: Right View... Right Concentration.”

“Yato kho, bhikkhave, bhikkhu evaṃ jarāmaraṇaṃ pajānāti, evaṃ jarāmaraṇasamudayaṃ pajānāti, evaṃ jarāmaraṇanirodhaṃ [T 2.0053] pajānāti, evaṃ jarāmaraṇanirodhagāminiṃ paṭipadaṃ pajānāti, evaṃ jātiṃ pajānāti…pe… bhavaṃ… upādānaṃ… taṇhaṃ… vedanaṃ… phassaṃ… saḷāyatanaṃ… nāmarūpaṃ… viññāṇaṃ [P 2.0045]… saṅkhāre… saṅkhārasamudayaṃ… saṅkhāranirodhaṃ… evaṃ saṅkhāranirodhagāminiṃ paṭipadaṃ pajānāti.
