Householder, one who destroys life, on account of destroying life, generates fear and enmity in the present life and generates fear and enmity in the life to come, and he experiences mental suffering and displeasure. For one who abstains from destroying life, that fear and enmity is thus pacified.

“Yaṃ, gahapati, adinnādāyī adinnādānapaccayā diṭṭhadhammikampi bhayaṃ veraṃ pasavati, samparāyikampi bhayaṃ veraṃ pasavati, cetasikampi dukkhaṃ domanassaṃ paṭisaṃvedayati, adinnādānā paṭiviratassa evaṃ taṃ bhayaṃ veraṃ vūpasantaṃ hoti.

“Householder, one who takes what is not given, on account of taking what is not given, generates fear and enmity in the present life and generates fear and enmity in the life to come, and he experiences mental suffering and displeasure. For one who abstains from taking what is not given, that fear and enmity is thus pacified.

“Yaṃ[P 2.0069], gahapati, kāmesumicchācārī kāmesumicchācārapaccayā [T 2.0083] diṭṭhadhammikampi bhayaṃ veraṃ pasavati, samparāyikampi bhayaṃ veraṃ pasavati, cetasikampi dukkhaṃ domanassaṃ paṭisaṃvedayati, kāmesumicchācārā paṭiviratassa evaṃ taṃ bhayaṃ veraṃ vūpasantaṃ hoti.

“Householder, one who engages in sexual misconduct, on account of sexual misconduct, generates fear and enmity in the present life and generates fear and enmity in the life to come, and he experiences mental suffering and displeasure. For one who abstains from sexual misconduct, that fear and enmity is thus pacified.

“Yaṃ, gahapati, musāvādī musāvādapaccayā diṭṭhadhammikampi bhayaṃ veraṃ pasavati, samparāyikampi bhayaṃ veraṃ pasavati, cetasikampi dukkhaṃ domanassaṃ paṭisaṃvedayati, musāvādā paṭiviratassa evaṃ taṃ bhayaṃ veraṃ vūpasantaṃ hoti.

“Householder, one who speaks falsehood, on account of speaking falsehood, generates fear and enmity in the present life and generates fear and enmity in the life to come, and he experiences mental suffering and displeasure. For one who abstains from speaking falsehood, that fear and enmity is thus pacified.

“Yaṃ, gahapati, surāmerayamajjapamādaṭṭhāyī surāmerayamajjapamādaṭṭhānapaccayā diṭṭhadhammikampi bhayaṃ veraṃ pasavati, samparāyikampi bhayaṃ veraṃ pasavati, cetasikampi dukkhaṃ domanassaṃ paṭisaṃvedayati, surāmerayamajjapamādaṭṭhānā paṭiviratassa evaṃ taṃ bhayaṃ veraṃ vūpasantaṃ hoti. Imāni pañca bhayāni verāni vūpasantāni honti.

“Householder, one who partakes of liquor, wine, and intoxicants which are the basis for heedlessness, on account of partaking of liquor, wine, and intoxicants which are the basis for heedlessness, generates fear and enmity in the present life and generates fear and enmity in the life to come, and he experiences mental suffering and displeasure. For one who abstains from partaking of liquor, wine, and intoxicants which are the basis for heedlessness, that fear and enmity is thus pacified. These are the five fears and enmities that are pacified.

“Katamehi catūhi sotāpattiyaṅgehi samannāgato hoti? Idha, gahapati, ariyasāvako buddhe aveccappasādena samannāgato hoti – ‘itipi so bhagavā arahaṃ sammāsambuddho vijjācaraṇasampanno sugato lokavidū anuttaro purisadammasārathi satthā devamanussānaṃ buddho bhagavā’”ti.

“With which four factors of stream-entry is he endowed? Here, householder, a noble disciple is endowed with unwavering confidence in the Buddha: ‘Thus is the Blessed One: an Arahant, a perfectly enlightened one, accomplished in knowledge and conduct, the Well-Gone One, knower of the world, an unsurpassed trainer of persons to be tamed, teacher of gods and humans, the Buddha, the Blessed One.’

“Dhamme [V 1.0062] aveccappasādena samannāgato hoti – ‘svākkhāto bhagavatā dhammo sandiṭṭhiko akāliko ehipassiko opaneyyiko paccattaṃ veditabbo viññūhī’”ti.

“He is endowed with unwavering confidence in the Dhamma: ‘The Dhamma is well-proclaimed by the Blessed One, visible here and now, immediate, inviting one to come and see, leading onward, to be experienced personally by the wise.’

“Saṅghe [M 1.0299] aveccappasādena samannāgato hoti – ‘suppaṭipanno bhagavato sāvakasaṅgho, ujuppaṭipanno bhagavato sāvakasaṅgho, ñāyappaṭipanno bhagavato sāvakasaṅgho, sāmīcippaṭipanno bhagavato sāvakasaṅgho[T 2.0084], yadidaṃ cattāri purisayugāni aṭṭha purisapuggalā, esa bhagavato sāvakasaṅgho [P 2.0070] āhuneyyo pāhuneyyo dakkhiṇeyyo añjalikaraṇīyo anuttaraṃ puññakkhettaṃ lokassā’”ti.

“He is endowed with unwavering confidence in the Saṅgha: ‘The Saṅgha of the Blessed One’s disciples is practicing the good way, practicing the straight way, practicing the methodical way, practicing the proper way—that is, the four pairs of persons, the eight types of individuals. This Saṅgha of the Blessed One’s disciples is worthy of offerings, worthy of hospitality, worthy of gifts, worthy of reverential salutation, an unsurpassed field of merit for the world.’

“Ariyakantehi sīlehi samannāgato hoti akhaṇḍehi acchiddehi asabalehi akammāsehi bhujissehi viññuppasatthehi aparāmaṭṭhehi samādhisaṃvattanikehi. Imehi catūhi sotāpattiyaṅgehi samannāgato hoti.

“He is endowed with virtues dear to the noble ones—unbroken, unperforated, unspotted, unmottled, liberating, praised by the wise, ungrasped, and conducive to concentration. With these four factors of stream-entry is he endowed.

“Katamo cassa ariyo ñāyo paññāya sudiṭṭho hoti suppaṭividdho? Idha, gahapati, ariyasāvako paṭiccasamuppādaññeva sādhukaṃ yoniso manasi karoti – ‘iti imasmiṃ sati idaṃ hoti, imasmiṃ asati idaṃ na hoti; imassuppādā idaṃ uppajjati, imassa nirodhā idaṃ nirujjhati. Yadidaṃ avijjāpaccayā saṅkhārā; saṅkhārapaccayā viññāṇaṃ…pe… evametassa kevalassa dukkhakkhandhassa samudayo hoti. Avijjāya tveva asesavirāganirodhā saṅkhāranirodho; saṅkhāranirodhā viññāṇanirodho…pe… evametassa kevalassa dukkhakkhandhassa nirodho hotī’”ti. Ayamassa ariyo ñāyo paññāya sudiṭṭho hoti suppaṭividdho.

“And what is the noble principle that has been well seen and well penetrated by him with wisdom? Here, householder, a noble disciple gives careful and wise attention to dependent origination itself: ‘When this is, that is; with the arising of this, that arises. When this is not, that is not; with the cessation of this, that ceases. That is: with ignorance as condition, volitional formations arise; with volitional formations as condition, consciousness arises… Such is the origin of this whole mass of suffering. But with the remainderless fading away and cessation of ignorance comes the cessation of volitional formations; with the cessation of volitional formations comes the cessation of consciousness… Such is the cessation of this whole mass of suffering.’ This is the noble principle that has been well seen and well penetrated by him with wisdom.

“Yato kho, gahapati, ariyasāvakassa imāni pañca bhayāni verāni vūpasantāni honti, imehi catūhi sotāpattiyaṅgehi samannāgato hoti, ayañcassa ariyo ñāyo paññāya sudiṭṭho hoti suppaṭividdho, so ākaṅkhamāno attanāva attānaṃ byākareyya – ‘khīṇanirayomhi [T 2.0085] khīṇatiracchānayoni khīṇapettivisayo khīṇāpāyaduggativinipāto, sotāpannohamasmi avinipātadhammo niyato sambodhiparāyano’”ti.

“When, householder, for a noble disciple these five fears and enmities are pacified, he is endowed with these four factors of stream-entry, and this noble principle has been well seen and well penetrated by him with wisdom, he may, if he wishes, declare of himself: ‘Hell is exhausted for me; the animal birth is exhausted; the sphere of ghosts is exhausted; the planes of misery, bad destinations, and downfall are exhausted. I am a stream-enterer, not subject to downfall, assured, and destined for full enlightenment.’”

2. Dutiyapañcaverabhayasuttaṃ

2. The Second Discourse on the Five Fears and Enmities

42. Sāvatthiyaṃ [V 1.0063] viharati…pe… “yato [P 2.0071] kho, bhikkhave, ariyasāvakassa pañca bhayāni verāni vūpasantāni honti, catūhi ca sotāpattiyaṅgehi samannāgato hoti, ariyo cassa ñāyo paññāya sudiṭṭho hoti [M 1.0300] suppaṭividdho, so ākaṅkhamāno attanāva attānaṃ byākareyya – ‘khīṇanirayomhi khīṇatiracchānayoni khīṇapettivisayo khīṇāpāyaduggativinipāto, sotāpannohamasmi avinipātadhammo niyato sambodhiparāyano’”ti.

42. At Sāvatthī… “When, bhikkhus, for a noble disciple five fears and enmities have subsided, he is endowed with the four factors of stream-entry, and the noble method has been well seen and well penetrated by his wisdom, then, if he wishes, he may declare of himself: ‘Hell is exhausted for me, the animal realm is exhausted, the realm of petas is exhausted, the plane of misery, the bad destination, the downfall is exhausted. I am a stream-enterer, not subject to downfall, certain, and destined for enlightenment.’”

“Katamāni pañca bhayāni verāni vūpasantāni honti? Yaṃ, bhikkhave, pāṇātipātī …pe… yaṃ, bhikkhave, adinnādāyī…pe… yaṃ, bhikkhave, kāmesumicchācārī… yaṃ, bhikkhave, musāvādī… yaṃ, bhikkhave, surāmerayamajjapamādaṭṭhāyī…pe… imāni pañca bhayāni verāni vūpasantāni honti.

“What are the five fears and enmities that have subsided? Bhikkhus, whatever fear and enmity one who destroys life generates... and so on... whatever fear and enmity one who takes what is not given generates... whatever fear and enmity one who engages in sexual misconduct generates... whatever fear and enmity one who speaks falsely generates... whatever fear and enmity one who partakes of wine, liquor, and intoxicants which are the basis for heedlessness generates... These are the five fears and enmities that have subsided.

“Katamehi catūhi sotāpattiyaṅgehi samannāgato hoti? Idha, bhikkhave, ariyasāvako buddhe…pe… dhamme… saṅghe… ariyakantehi sīlehi samannāgato hoti. Imehi catūhi sotāpattiyaṅgehi samannāgato hoti.

“With which four factors of stream-entry is he endowed? Here, bhikkhus, a noble disciple is endowed with unwavering confidence in the Buddha… in the Dhamma… in the Saṅgha… and he is endowed with the virtues dear to the noble ones. With these four factors of stream-entry is he endowed.

“Katamo cassa ariyo ñāyo paññāya sudiṭṭho hoti suppaṭividdho[T 2.0086]? Idha, bhikkhave, ariyasāvako paṭiccasamuppādaññeva sādhukaṃ yoniso manasi karoti…pe… ayamassa ariyo ñāyo paññāya sudiṭṭho hoti suppaṭividdho.

“And what is the noble method that has been well seen and well penetrated by his wisdom? Here, bhikkhus, a noble disciple attends well and wisely to dependent origination itself… This is the noble method that has been well seen and well penetrated by his wisdom.

“Yato kho, bhikkhave, ariyasāvakassa imāni pañca bhayāni verāni vūpasantāni honti, imehi ca catūhi sotāpattiyaṅgehi samannāgato hoti, ayañcassa ariyo ñāyo paññāya sudiṭṭho hoti suppaṭividdho, so ākaṅkhamāno attanāva attānaṃ byākareyya – ‘khīṇanirayomhi khīṇatiracchānayoni khīṇapettivisayo khīṇāpāyaduggativinipāto, sotāpannohamasmi avinipātadhammo niyato sambodhiparāyano’”ti. Dutiyaṃ.

“When, bhikkhus, for a noble disciple these five fears and enmities have subsided, and he is endowed with these four factors of stream-entry, and this noble method has been well seen and well penetrated by his wisdom, then, if he wishes, he may declare of himself: ‘Hell is exhausted for me, the animal realm is exhausted, the realm of petas is exhausted, the plane of misery, the bad destination, the downfall is exhausted. I am a stream-enterer, not subject to downfall, certain, and destined for enlightenment.’” The Second.

3. Dukkhasuttaṃ

3. 3. The Discourse on Suffering

43. Sāvatthiyaṃ [V 1.0064] viharati…pe… “dukkhassa[P 2.0072], bhikkhave, samudayañca atthaṅgamañca desessāmi. Taṃ suṇātha, sādhukaṃ manasi karotha; bhāsissāmī”ti. “Evaṃ, bhante”ti kho te bhikkhū bhagavato paccassosuṃ. Bhagavā etadavoca –

43. At Sāvatthī… “Bhikkhus, I will teach you the arising and the cessation of suffering. Listen to that, attend carefully; I will speak.” “Yes, Venerable Sir,” those bhikkhus replied to the Blessed One. The Blessed One said this:

“Katamo ca, bhikkhave, dukkhassa samudayo? Cakkhuñca paṭicca rūpe ca uppajjati cakkhuviññāṇaṃ. Tiṇṇaṃ saṅgati phasso. Phassapaccayā vedanā; vedanāpaccayā taṇhā. Ayaṃ kho, bhikkhave, dukkhassa samudayo.

“And what, bhikkhus, is the arising of suffering? Dependent on the eye and forms, eye-consciousness arises. The meeting of the three is contact. With contact as condition, feeling arises; with feeling as condition, craving arises. This, bhikkhus, is the arising of suffering.

“Sotañca [M 1.0301] paṭicca sadde ca uppajjati sotaviññāṇaṃ…pe… ghānañca paṭicca gandhe ca…pe… jivhañca paṭicca rase ca…pe… kāyañca paṭicca phoṭṭhabbe ca…pe… manañca paṭicca dhamme ca uppajjati manoviññāṇaṃ. Tiṇṇaṃ saṅgati phasso. Phassapaccayā vedanā; vedanāpaccayā taṇhā. Ayaṃ [T 2.0087] kho, bhikkhave, dukkhassa samudayo.

“Dependent on the ear and sounds, ear-consciousness arises… Dependent on the nose and smells… Dependent on the tongue and tastes… Dependent on the body and tactile objects… Dependent on the mind and mental phenomena, mind-consciousness arises. The meeting of the three is contact. With contact as condition, feeling arises; with feeling as condition, craving arises. This, bhikkhus, is the arising of suffering.

“Katamo ca, bhikkhave, dukkhassa atthaṅgamo? Cakkhuñca paṭicca rūpe ca uppajjati cakkhuviññāṇaṃ. Tiṇṇaṃ saṅgati phasso. Phassapaccayā vedanā; vedanāpaccayā taṇhā. Tassāyeva taṇhāya asesavirāganirodhā upādānanirodho; upādānanirodhā bhavanirodho; bhavanirodhā jātinirodho; jātinirodhā jarāmaraṇaṃ sokaparidevadukkhadomanassupāyāsā nirujjhanti. Evametassa kevalassa dukkhakkhandhassa nirodho hoti. Ayaṃ kho, bhikkhave, dukkhassa atthaṅgamo.

“And what, bhikkhus, is the cessation of suffering? Dependent on the eye and forms, eye-consciousness arises. The meeting of the three is contact. With contact as condition, feeling arises; with feeling as condition, craving arises. With the remainderless fading away and cessation of that very craving comes the cessation of clinging; with the cessation of clinging, the cessation of becoming; with the cessation of becoming, the cessation of birth; with the cessation of birth, aging and death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair cease. Such is the cessation of this whole mass of suffering. This, bhikkhus, is the cessation of suffering.

“Sotañca paṭicca sadde ca uppajjati sotaviññāṇaṃ…pe… ghānañca paṭicca gandhe ca…pe… jivhañca paṭicca rase ca…pe… kāyañca paṭicca phoṭṭhabbe ca…pe… manañca paṭicca dhamme ca uppajjati manoviññāṇaṃ. Tiṇṇaṃ saṅgati phasso. Phassapaccayā vedanā; vedanāpaccayā taṇhā. Tassāyeva taṇhāya asesavirāganirodhā upādānanirodho; upādānanirodhā bhavanirodho; bhavanirodhā jātinirodho; jātinirodhā jarāmaraṇaṃ sokaparidevadukkhadomanassupāyāsā [P 2.0073] nirujjhanti. Evametassa kevalassa dukkhakkhandhassa nirodho hoti. Ayaṃ kho, bhikkhave, dukkhassa atthaṅgamo”ti. Tatiyaṃ.

“Dependent on the ear and sounds, ear-consciousness arises… Dependent on the nose and smells… Dependent on the tongue and tastes… Dependent on the body and tactile objects… Dependent on the mind and mental phenomena, mind-consciousness arises. The meeting of the three is contact. With contact as condition, feeling arises; with feeling as condition, craving arises. With the remainderless fading away and cessation of that very craving comes the cessation of clinging; with the cessation of clinging, the cessation of becoming; with the cessation of becoming, the cessation of birth; with the cessation of birth, aging and death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair cease. Such is the cessation of this whole mass of suffering. This, bhikkhus, is the cessation of suffering.” The Third.

4. Lokasuttaṃ

4. 4. The Discourse on the World

44. Sāvatthiyaṃ [V 1.0065] viharati…pe… “lokassa, bhikkhave, samudayañca atthaṅgamañca desessāmi. Taṃ suṇātha, sādhukaṃ manasi karotha; bhāsissāmī”ti. “Evaṃ, bhante”ti kho te bhikkhū bhagavato paccassosuṃ. Bhagavā etadavoca –

44. At Sāvatthī... “Bhikkhus, I will teach the arising and the cessation of the world. Listen to that, attend carefully, and I will speak.” “Yes, Venerable Sir,” those bhikkhus replied to the Blessed One. The Blessed One said this:

“Katamo ca, bhikkhave, lokassa samudayo? Cakkhuñca paṭicca rūpe ca uppajjati cakkhuviññāṇaṃ. Tiṇṇaṃ [T 2.0088] saṅgati phasso. Phassapaccayā vedanā; vedanāpaccayā taṇhā; taṇhāpaccayā upādānaṃ; upādānapaccayā bhavo; bhavapaccayā jāti; jātipaccayā jarāmaraṇaṃ sokaparidevadukkhadomanassupāyāsā sambhavanti. Ayaṃ kho, bhikkhave, lokassa samudayo.

“And what, bhikkhus, is the arising of the world? Dependent on the eye and forms, eye-consciousness arises. The meeting of the three is contact. With contact as condition, feeling arises; with feeling as condition, craving arises; with craving as condition, clinging arises; with clinging as condition, becoming arises; with becoming as condition, birth arises; with birth as condition, aging-and-death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair come to be. This, bhikkhus, is the arising of the world.

“Sotañca [M 1.0302] paṭicca sadde ca…pe… ghānañca paṭicca gandhe ca… jivhañca paṭicca rase ca… kāyañca paṭicca phoṭṭhabbe ca… manañca paṭicca dhamme ca uppajjati manoviññāṇaṃ. Tiṇṇaṃ saṅgati phasso. Phassapaccayā vedanā…pe… jātipaccayā jarāmaraṇaṃ sokaparidevadukkhadomanassupāyāsā sambhavanti. Ayaṃ kho, bhikkhave, lokassa samudayo.

“Dependent on the ear and sounds... dependent on the nose and odors... dependent on the tongue and tastes... dependent on the body and tactile objects... dependent on the mind and mental objects, mind-consciousness arises. The meeting of the three is contact. With contact as condition, feeling arises... with birth as condition, aging-and-death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair come to be. This, bhikkhus, is the arising of the world.

“Katamo ca, bhikkhave, lokassa atthaṅgamo? Cakkhuñca paṭicca rūpe ca uppajjati cakkhuviññāṇaṃ. Tiṇṇaṃ saṅgati phasso. Phassapaccayā vedanā; vedanāpaccayā taṇhā. Tassāyeva taṇhāya asesavirāganirodhā upādānanirodho; upādānanirodhā bhavanirodho…pe… evametassa kevalassa dukkhakkhandhassa nirodho hoti. Ayaṃ kho, bhikkhave, lokassa atthaṅgamo.

“And what, bhikkhus, is the cessation of the world? Dependent on the eye and forms, eye-consciousness arises. The meeting of the three is contact. With contact as condition, feeling arises; with feeling as condition, craving arises. Through the remainderless fading away and cessation of that very craving comes the cessation of clinging; with the cessation of clinging comes the cessation of becoming... thus comes the cessation of this whole mass of suffering. This, bhikkhus, is the cessation of the world.

“Sotañca paṭicca sadde ca…pe… ghānañca [P 2.0074] paṭicca gandhe ca… jivhañca paṭicca rase ca… kāyañca paṭicca phoṭṭhabbe ca… manañca paṭicca dhamme ca uppajjati manoviññāṇaṃ. Tiṇṇaṃ saṅgati phasso. Phassapaccayā vedanā; vedanāpaccayā taṇhā. Tassāyeva taṇhāya asesavirāganirodhā upādānanirodho; upādānanirodhā bhavanirodho…pe… evametassa kevalassa [T 2.0089] dukkhakkhandhassa nirodho hoti. Ayaṃ kho, bhikkhave, lokassa atthaṅgamo”ti. Catutthaṃ.

“Dependent on the ear and sounds... dependent on the nose and odors... dependent on the tongue and tastes... dependent on the body and tactile objects... dependent on the mind and mental objects, mind-consciousness arises. The meeting of the three is contact. With contact as condition, feeling arises; with feeling as condition, craving arises. Through the remainderless fading away and cessation of that very craving, there is the cessation of clinging; with the cessation of clinging, there is the cessation of becoming... thus is the cessation of this entire mass of suffering. This, bhikkhus, is the cessation of the world.” The Fourth.

5. Ñātikasuttaṃ

5. The Discourse at Nātikā

45. Evaṃ [V 1.0066] me sutaṃ – ekaṃ samayaṃ bhagavā ñātike viharati giñjakāvasathe. Atha kho bhagavā rahogato paṭisallāno imaṃ dhammapariyāyaṃ abhāsi –

45. Thus have I heard. At one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Nātikā in the Brick Hall. Then, having gone to a secluded place and dwelling in solitude, the Blessed One spoke this discourse on the Dhamma:

“Cakkhuñca paṭicca rūpe ca uppajjati cakkhuviññāṇaṃ. Tiṇṇaṃ saṅgati phasso. Phassapaccayā vedanā, vedanāpaccayā taṇhā; taṇhāpaccayā upādānaṃ…pe… evametassa kevalassa dukkhakkhandhassa samudayo hoti.

“Dependent on the eye and forms, eye-consciousness arises. The meeting of the three is contact. With contact as condition, feeling; with feeling as condition, craving; with craving as condition, clinging… thus is the origin of this entire mass of suffering.

“Sotañca paṭicca sadde ca…pe… ghānañca paṭicca gandhe ca… jivhañca paṭicca rase ca… kāyañca paṭicca phoṭṭhabbe ca… manañca paṭicca dhamme ca uppajjati manoviññāṇaṃ. Tiṇṇaṃ saṅgati phasso. Phassapaccayā vedanā; vedanāpaccayā taṇhā; taṇhāpaccayā upādānaṃ…pe… evametassa kevalassa dukkhakkhandhassa samudayo hoti.

“Dependent on the ear and sounds… dependent on the nose and odors… dependent on the tongue and tastes… dependent on the body and tactile objects… dependent on the mind and mental phenomena, mind-consciousness arises. The meeting of the three is contact. With contact as condition, feeling; with feeling as condition, craving; with craving as condition, clinging… thus is the origin of this entire mass of suffering.

“Cakkhuñca [M 1.0303] paṭicca rūpe ca uppajjati cakkhuviññāṇaṃ. Tiṇṇaṃ saṅgati phasso. Phassapaccayā vedanā; vedanāpaccayā taṇhā. Tassāyeva taṇhāya asesavirāganirodhā upādānanirodho; upādānanirodhā bhavanirodho…pe… evametassa kevalassa dukkhakkhandhassa nirodho hoti.

“Dependent on the eye and forms, eye-consciousness arises. The meeting of the three is contact. With contact as condition, feeling; with feeling as condition, craving. Through the remainderless fading away and cessation of that very craving, there is the cessation of clinging; through the cessation of clinging, there is the cessation of becoming… thus is the cessation of this entire mass of suffering.

“Sotañca [P 2.0075] paṭicca sadde ca…pe… manañca paṭicca dhamme ca uppajjati manoviññāṇaṃ. Tiṇṇaṃ saṅgati phasso. Phassapaccayā vedanā; vedanāpaccayā taṇhā. Tassāyeva taṇhāya asesavirāganirodhā [T 2.0090] upādānanirodho; upādānanirodhā bhavanirodho…pe… evametassa kevalassa dukkhakkhandhassa nirodho hotī”ti.

“Dependent on the ear and sounds… dependent on the mind and mental phenomena, mind-consciousness arises. The meeting of the three is contact. With contact as condition, feeling; with feeling as condition, craving. Through the remainderless fading away and cessation of that very craving, there is the cessation of clinging; through the cessation of clinging, there is the cessation of becoming… thus is the cessation of this entire mass of suffering.”

Tena kho pana samayena aññataro bhikkhu bhagavato upassuti upassutiṃ (sī. pī.) ṭhito hoti. Addasā kho bhagavā taṃ bhikkhuṃ upassuti ṭhitaṃ. Disvāna taṃ bhikkhuṃ etadavoca – “assosi no tvaṃ, bhikkhu, imaṃ dhammapariyāya”nti? “Evaṃ, bhante”ti. “Uggaṇhāhi tvaṃ, bhikkhu, imaṃ dhammapariyāyaṃ; pariyāpuṇāhi tvaṃ, bhikkhu, imaṃ dhammapariyāyaṃ; dhārehi tvaṃ, bhikkhu, imaṃ dhammapariyāyaṃ. Atthasaṃhito ayaṃ atthasaṃhitoyaṃ (sī. syā. kaṃ.), atthasaṃhitāyaṃ (pī. ka.), bhikkhu, dhammapariyāyo ādibrahmacariyako”ti. Pañcamaṃ.

Now on that occasion a certain bhikkhu was standing within earshot of the Blessed One. The Blessed One saw that bhikkhu standing within earshot. Having seen him, he said to that bhikkhu: “Did you hear, bhikkhu, this discourse on the Dhamma?” “Yes, venerable sir.” “Learn this discourse on the Dhamma, bhikkhu; master this discourse on the Dhamma, bhikkhu; bear in mind this discourse on the Dhamma, bhikkhu. This discourse on the Dhamma, bhikkhu, is connected with the goal, it is fundamental to the holy life.” The Fifth.

6. Aññatarabrāhmaṇasuttaṃ

6. The Discourse with a Certain Brahmin

46. Sāvatthiyaṃ [V 1.0067] viharati. Atha kho aññataro brāhmaṇo yena bhagavā tenupasaṅkami; upasaṅkamitvā bhagavatā saddhiṃ sammodi. Sammodanīyaṃ kathaṃ sāraṇīyaṃ vītisāretvā ekamantaṃ nisīdi. Ekamantaṃ nisinno kho so brāhmaṇo bhagavantaṃ etadavoca –

46. The Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī. Then a certain brahmin approached the Blessed One. Having approached, he exchanged cordial greetings and memorable conversation with the Blessed One, and then sat down to one side. Seated to one side, that brahmin said this to the Blessed One:

“Kiṃ nu kho, bho gotama, so karoti so paṭisaṃvedayatī”ti? “‘So karoti so paṭisaṃvedayatī’ti kho, brāhmaṇa, ayameko anto”.

“Venerable Gotama, is it that the one who acts is the one who experiences?” “‘The one who acts is the one who experiences’—this, brahmin, is one extreme.”

“Kiṃ [P 2.0076] pana, bho gotama, añño karoti, añño paṭisaṃvedayatī”ti? “‘Añño karoti, añño paṭisaṃvedayatī’ti kho, brāhmaṇa, ayaṃ dutiyo anto. Ete te, brāhmaṇa, ubho ante anupagamma majjhena tathāgato dhammaṃ deseti – ‘avijjāpaccayā saṅkhārā; saṅkhārapaccayā viññāṇaṃ…pe… evametassa kevalassa dukkhakkhandhassa samudayo hoti. Avijjāya [M 1.0304] tveva asesavirāganirodhā saṅkhāranirodho; saṅkhāranirodhā viññāṇanirodho [T 2.0091] …pe… evametassa kevalassa dukkhakkhandhassa nirodho hotī’”ti.

“Then, Venerable Gotama, is it that one person acts and another experiences?” “‘One person acts and another experiences’—this, brahmin, is the second extreme. Without approaching either of these two extremes, the Tathāgata teaches the Dhamma by the middle way: ‘With ignorance as condition, formations arise; with formations as condition, consciousness arises… Thus is the arising of this entire mass of suffering. With the remainderless fading away and cessation of that very ignorance, there is the cessation of formations; with the cessation of formations, there is the cessation of consciousness… Thus is the cessation of this entire mass of suffering.’”

Evaṃ vutte, so brāhmaṇo bhagavantaṃ etadavoca – “abhikkantaṃ, bho gotama, abhikkantaṃ, bho gotama,…pe… upāsakaṃ maṃ bhavaṃ gotamo dhāretu ajjatagge pāṇupetaṃ saraṇaṃ gata”nti. Chaṭṭhaṃ.

When this was said, that brahmin said this to the Blessed One: “Excellent, Venerable Gotama! Excellent, Venerable Gotama! … May the Venerable Gotama remember me as a lay follower who has gone for refuge for life, beginning from today.” The Sixth.

7. Jāṇussoṇisuttaṃ

7. The Discourse with Jāṇussoṇi

47. Sāvatthiyaṃ viharati. Atha kho jāṇussoṇi brāhmaṇo yena bhagavā tenupasaṅkami; upasaṅkamitvā bhagavatā saddhiṃ…pe… ekamantaṃ nisinno kho jāṇussoṇi brāhmaṇo bhagavantaṃ etadavoca –

47. The Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī. Then the brahmin Jāṇussoṇi approached the Blessed One. Having approached, he exchanged cordial greetings and memorable conversation with the Blessed One, and then sat down to one side. Seated to one side, the brahmin Jāṇussoṇi said this to the Blessed One:

“Kiṃ [V 1.0068] nu kho, bho, gotama, sabbamatthī”ti? “‘Sabbamatthī’ti kho, brāhmaṇa, ayameko anto”.

“Venerable Gotama, does everything exist?” “‘Everything exists’—this, brahmin, is one extreme.”

“Kiṃ pana, bho gotama, sabbaṃ natthī”ti? “‘Sabbaṃ natthī’ti kho, brāhmaṇa, ayaṃ dutiyo anto. Ete te, brāhmaṇa, ubho ante anupagamma majjhena tathāgato dhammaṃ deseti – ‘avijjāpaccayā saṅkhārā; saṅkhārapaccayā viññāṇaṃ…pe… evametassa kevalassa dukkhakkhandhassa samudayo hoti. Avijjāya tveva asesavirāganirodhā saṅkhāranirodho; saṅkhāranirodhā viññāṇanirodho…pe… evametassa kevalassa dukkhakkhandhassa nirodho hotī’”ti.

“Then, Venerable Gotama, does everything not exist?” “‘Everything does not exist’—this, brahmin, is the second extreme. Without approaching either of these two extremes, the Tathāgata teaches the Dhamma by the middle way: ‘With ignorance as condition, formations arise; with formations as condition, consciousness arises… Thus is the arising of this entire mass of suffering. With the remainderless fading away and cessation of that very ignorance, there is the cessation of formations; with the cessation of formations, there is the cessation of consciousness… Thus is the cessation of this entire mass of suffering.’”

Evaṃ vutte, jāṇussoṇi brāhmaṇo bhagavantaṃ etadavoca [P 2.0077] – “abhikkantaṃ bho gotama…pe… pāṇupetaṃ saraṇaṃ gata”nti. Sattamaṃ.

When this was said, the brahmin Jāṇussoṇi said this to the Blessed One: “Excellent, Venerable Gotama! … May the Venerable Gotama remember me as a lay follower who has gone for refuge for life, beginning from today.” The Seventh.

8. Lokāyatikasuttaṃ

8. The Lokāyatika Sutta

48. Sāvatthiyaṃ viharati. Atha kho lokāyatiko brāhmaṇo yena [T 2.0092] bhagavā…pe… ekamantaṃ nisinno kho lokāyatiko brāhmaṇo bhagavantaṃ etadavoca –

48. At Sāvatthī. Then a Lokāyatika brahmin went to the Blessed One... Seated to one side, the Lokāyatika brahmin said this to the Blessed One:

“Kiṃ nu kho, bho gotama, sabbamatthī”ti? “‘Sabbamatthī’ti kho, brāhmaṇa, jeṭṭhametaṃ lokāyataṃ”.

“Master Gotama, does everything exist?” “Brahmin, the view ‘Everything exists’ is the foremost worldly doctrine.”

“Kiṃ [M 1.0305] pana, bho gotama, sabbaṃ natthī”ti? “‘Sabbaṃ natthī’ti kho, brāhmaṇa, dutiyametaṃ lokāyataṃ”.

“Then, Master Gotama, does everything not exist?” “Brahmin, the view ‘Everything does not exist’ is the second worldly doctrine.”

“Kiṃ nu kho, bho gotama, sabbamekatta”nti? “‘Sabbamekatta’nti kho, brāhmaṇa, tatiyametaṃ lokāyataṃ”.

“Master Gotama, is everything a unity?” “Brahmin, the view ‘Everything is a unity’ is the third worldly doctrine.”

“Kiṃ [V 1.0069] pana, bho gotama, sabbaṃ puthutta”nti? “‘Sabbaṃ puthutta’nti kho, brāhmaṇa, catutthametaṃ lokāyataṃ”.

“Then, Master Gotama, is everything a plurality?” “Brahmin, the view ‘Everything is a plurality’ is the fourth worldly doctrine.”

“Ete te, brāhmaṇa, ubho ante anupagamma majjhena tathāgato dhammaṃ deseti – ‘avijjāpaccayā saṅkhārā; saṅkhārapaccayā viññāṇaṃ…pe… evametassa kevalassa dukkhakkhandhassa samudayo hoti. Avijjāya tveva asesavirāganirodhā saṅkhāranirodho; saṅkhāranirodhā viññāṇanirodho…pe… evametassa kevalassa dukkhakkhandhassa nirodho hotī’”ti.

“Brahmin, not approaching either of these two extremes, the Tathāgata teaches the Dhamma by the middle: ‘With ignorance as condition, volitional formations come to be; with volitional formations as condition, consciousness comes to be… Thus is the origin of this whole mass of suffering. With the remainderless fading away and cessation of that very ignorance, comes the cessation of volitional formations; with the cessation of volitional formations, the cessation of consciousness… Thus is the cessation of this whole mass of suffering.’”

Evaṃ vutte, lokāyatiko brāhmaṇo bhagavantaṃ etadavoca – “abhikkantaṃ, bho gotama…pe… ajjatagge pāṇupetaṃ saraṇaṃ gata”nti. Aṭṭhamaṃ.

When this was said, the Lokāyatika brahmin said to the Blessed One: “Excellent, Master Gotama! ... From this day forth, may you remember me as a lay follower who has gone for refuge for life.” Eighth.

9. Ariyasāvakasuttaṃ

9. Discourse on the Noble Disciple

49. Sāvatthiyaṃ viharati…pe… “na[P 2.0078], bhikkhave, sutavato ariyasāvakassa evaṃ hoti – ‘kiṃ nu kho kismiṃ sati kiṃ hoti, kissuppādā kiṃ uppajjati? (Kismiṃ sati saṅkhārā honti, kismiṃ sati viññāṇaṃ hoti,) ( ) etthantare pāṭhā kesuci potthakesu na dissantīti sī. pī. potthakesu dassitā. tathā sati anantarasuttaṭīkāya sameti kismiṃ sati nāmarūpaṃ hoti, kismiṃ sati saḷāyatanaṃ hoti, kismiṃ sati phasso hoti, kismiṃ sati vedanā [T 2.0093] hoti, kismiṃ sati taṇhā hoti, kismiṃ sati upādānaṃ hoti, kismiṃ sati bhavo hoti, kismiṃ sati jāti hoti, kismiṃ sati jarāmaraṇaṃ hotī’”ti?

49. At Sāvatthī... “Bhikkhus, it does not occur to a learned noble disciple: ‘When what exists, what comes to be? With the arising of what, what arises? When what exists, do volitional formations come to be? When what exists, does consciousness come to be? When what exists, does name-and-form come to be? When what exists, do the six sense bases come to be? When what exists, does contact come to be? When what exists, does feeling come to be? When what exists, does craving come to be? When what exists, does clinging come to be? When what exists, does becoming come to be? When what exists, does birth come to be? When what exists, does aging-and-death come to be?’”

“Atha kho, bhikkhave, sutavato ariyasāvakassa aparappaccayā ñāṇamevettha hoti – ‘imasmiṃ sati idaṃ hoti, imassuppādā idaṃ uppajjati. (Avijjāya sati saṅkhārā honti; saṅkhāresu sati viññāṇaṃ hoti;) ( ) etthakesu pāṭhā kesuci potthakesu na dissantīti sī. pī. potthakesu dassitā. tathā sati anantarasuttaṭīkāya sameti viññāṇe sati nāmarūpaṃ hoti; nāmarūpe sati saḷāyatanaṃ hoti[M 1.0306]; saḷāyatane sati phasso hoti; phasse sati vedanā hoti; vedanāya sati taṇhā hoti; taṇhāya sati upādānaṃ hoti; upādāne sati bhavo hoti; bhave sati jāti hoti; jātiyā sati jarāmaraṇaṃ hotī’ti. So evaṃ pajānāti – ‘evamayaṃ loko samudayatī’”ti.

“Rather, bhikkhus, a learned noble disciple has knowledge in this matter that is not dependent on another: ‘When this exists, that comes to be; with the arising of this, that arises. When ignorance exists, volitional formations come to be; when volitional formations exist, consciousness comes to be; when consciousness exists, name-and-form comes to be; when name-and-form exists, the six sense bases come to be; when the six sense bases exist, contact comes to be; when contact exists, feeling comes to be; when feeling exists, craving comes to be; when craving exists, clinging comes to be; when clinging exists, becoming comes to be; when becoming exists, birth comes to be; when birth exists, aging-and-death comes to be.’ He understands thus: ‘This is how this world originates.’”

“Na[V 1.0070], bhikkhave, sutavato ariyasāvakassa evaṃ hoti – ‘kiṃ nu kho kismiṃ asati kiṃ na hoti, kissa nirodhā kiṃ nirujjhati? (Kismiṃ asati saṅkhārā na honti, kismiṃ asati viññāṇaṃ na hoti,) ( ) etthantare pāṭhāpi tattha tatheva dassitā kismiṃ asati nāmarūpaṃ na hoti, kismiṃ asati saḷāyatanaṃ na hoti, kismiṃ asati phasso na hoti, kismiṃ asati vedanā na hoti, kismiṃ asati taṇhā na hoti, kismiṃ asati upādānaṃ na hoti, kismiṃ asati bhavo na hoti, kismiṃ asati jāti na hoti, kismiṃ asati jarāmaraṇaṃ na hotī’”ti?

“Bhikkhus, it does not occur to a learned noble disciple: ‘When what does not exist, what does not come to be? With the cessation of what, what ceases? When what does not exist, do volitional formations not come to be? When what does not exist, does consciousness not come to be? When what does not exist, does name-and-form not come to be? When what does not exist, do the six sense bases not come to be? When what does not exist, does contact not come to be? When what does not exist, does feeling not come to be? When what does not exist, does craving not come to be? When what does not exist, does clinging not come to be? When what does not exist, does becoming not come to be? When what does not exist, does birth not come to be? When what does not exist, does aging-and-death not come to be?’”

“Atha kho, bhikkhave, sutavato ariyasāvakassa aparappaccayā ñāṇamevettha hoti – ‘imasmiṃ asati idaṃ na hoti, imassa nirodhā idaṃ nirujjhati. (Avijjāya asati saṅkhārā na honti; saṅkhāresu asati viññāṇaṃ na hoti;) ( ) etthantare pāṭhāpi tattha tatheva dassitā viññāṇe asati nāmarūpaṃ na hoti; nāmarūpe asati saḷāyatanaṃ [T 2.0094] na hoti…pe… bhavo na hoti… jāti na hoti… jātiyā asati jarāmaraṇaṃ na hotī’ti. So evaṃ pajānāti – ‘evamayaṃ loko nirujjhatī’”ti.

“Rather, bhikkhus, a learned noble disciple has knowledge in this matter that is not dependent on another: ‘When this does not exist, that does not come to be; with the cessation of this, that ceases. When ignorance does not exist, volitional formations do not come to be; when volitional formations do not exist, consciousness does not come to be; when consciousness does not exist, name-and-form does not come to be; when name-and-form does not exist, the six sense bases do not come to be… when becoming does not exist, birth does not come to be… when birth does not exist, aging-and-death does not come to be.’ He understands thus: ‘This is how this world ceases.’”

“Yato [P 2.0079] kho, bhikkhave, ariyasāvako evaṃ lokassa samudayañca atthaṅgamañca yathābhūtaṃ pajānāti, ayaṃ vuccati, bhikkhave, ariyasāvako diṭṭhisampanno itipi…pe… amatadvāraṃ āhacca tiṭṭhati itipī”ti. Navamaṃ.

“When, Bhikkhus, a noble disciple thus understands the origin and cessation of the world as it really is, this noble disciple, Bhikkhus, is called one accomplished in view... one who stands having reached the door to the Deathless.” Ninth.

10. Dutiyaariyasāvakasuttaṃ

10. The Second Discourse on the Noble Disciple

50. Sāvatthiyaṃ viharati…pe… “na, bhikkhave, sutavato ariyasāvakassa evaṃ hoti – ‘kiṃ nu kho kismiṃ sati kiṃ hoti, kissuppādā kiṃ uppajjati? Kismiṃ sati saṅkhārā honti, kismiṃ sati viññāṇaṃ hoti, kismiṃ sati nāmarūpaṃ hoti, kismiṃ sati saḷāyatanaṃ hoti, kismiṃ sati [M 1.0307] phasso hoti, kismiṃ sati vedanā hoti, kismiṃ sati taṇhā hoti, kismiṃ sati upādānaṃ hoti, kismiṃ sati bhavo hoti, kismiṃ sati jāti hoti, kismiṃ sati jarāmaraṇaṃ hotī’”ti?

50. At Sāvatthī... “Bhikkhus, it does not occur to an instructed noble disciple: ‘When what exists, what comes to be? With the arising of what, what arises? When what exists, do volitional formations come to be? When what exists, does consciousness come to be? When what exists, does name-and-form come to be? When what exists, do the six sense bases come to be? When what exists, does contact come to be? When what exists, does feeling come to be? When what exists, does craving come to be? When what exists, does clinging come to be? When what exists, does becoming come to be? When what exists, does birth come to be? When what exists, does aging-and-death come to be?’”

“Atha kho, bhikkhave, sutavato ariyasāvakassa aparappaccayā ñāṇamevettha hoti – ‘imasmiṃ [V 1.0071] sati idaṃ hoti, imassuppādā idaṃ uppajjati. Avijjāya sati saṅkhārā honti; saṅkhāresu sati viññāṇaṃ hoti; viññāṇe sati nāmarūpaṃ hoti; nāmarūpe sati saḷāyatanaṃ hoti; saḷāyatane sati phasso hoti; phasse sati vedanā hoti[T 2.0095]; vedanāya sati taṇhā hoti; taṇhāya sati upādānaṃ hoti; upādāne sati bhavo hoti; bhave sati jāti hoti; jātiyā sati jarāmaraṇaṃ hotī’ti. So evaṃ pajānāti – ‘evamayaṃ loko samudayatī’”ti.

“Rather, bhikkhus, the instructed noble disciple has knowledge in this matter that is not dependent on another: ‘When this exists, that comes to be; with the arising of this, that arises. When ignorance exists, volitional formations come to be; when volitional formations exist, consciousness comes to be; when consciousness exists, name-and-form comes to be; when name-and-form exists, the six sense bases come to be; when the six sense bases exist, contact comes to be; when contact exists, feeling comes to be; when feeling exists, craving comes to be; when craving exists, clinging comes to be; when clinging exists, becoming comes to be; when becoming exists, birth comes to be; when birth exists, aging-and-death comes to be.’ He understands thus: ‘This is how this world originates.’”

“Na, bhikkhave, sutavato ariyasāvakassa evaṃ hoti – ‘kiṃ nu kho kismiṃ asati kiṃ na hoti, kissa nirodhā kiṃ nirujjhati? Kismiṃ asati saṅkhārā na honti, kismiṃ asati viññāṇaṃ na hoti, kismiṃ asati nāmarūpaṃ na hoti, kismiṃ asati saḷāyatanaṃ na hoti, kismiṃ asati phasso na hoti, kismiṃ asati vedanā na hoti, kismiṃ asati taṇhā na hoti…pe… upādānaṃ… bhavo… jāti… kismiṃ asati jarāmaraṇaṃ na hotī’”ti?

“Bhikkhus, it does not occur to an instructed noble disciple thus: ‘When what does not exist, what does not come to be? With the cessation of what, what ceases? When what does not exist, do volitional formations not come to be? When what does not exist, does consciousness not come to be? When what does not exist, does name-and-form not come to be? When what does not exist, do the six sense bases not come to be? When what does not exist, does contact not come to be? When what does not exist, does feeling not come to be? When what does not exist, does craving not come to be?…clinging…becoming…birth…When what does not exist, does aging and death not come to be?’”

“Atha kho, bhikkhave, sutavato ariyasāvakassa aparappaccayā ñāṇamevettha hoti – ‘imasmiṃ asati idaṃ na hoti, imassa nirodhā idaṃ nirujjhati. Avijjāya asati saṅkhārā [P 2.0080] na honti; saṅkhāresu asati viññāṇaṃ na hoti; viññāṇe asati nāmarūpaṃ na hoti; nāmarūpe asati saḷāyatanaṃ na hoti…pe… jātiyā asati jarāmaraṇaṃ na hotī’ti. So evaṃ pajānāti – ‘evamayaṃ loko nirujjhatī’”ti.

“But then, bhikkhus, the instructed noble disciple has knowledge here that is not dependent on another: ‘When this does not exist, that does not come to be; with the cessation of this, that ceases. When ignorance does not exist, volitional formations do not come to be; when volitional formations do not exist, consciousness does not come to be; when consciousness does not exist, name-and-form does not come to be; when name-and-form does not exist, the six sense bases do not come to be… when birth does not exist, aging and death do not come to be.’ He understands thus: ‘This is how this world ceases.’”

“Yato kho, bhikkhave, ariyasāvako evaṃ lokassa samudayañca atthaṅgamañca yathābhūtaṃ pajānāti, ayaṃ vuccati, bhikkhave, ariyasāvako diṭṭhisampanno itipi, dassanasampanno itipi, āgato imaṃ saddhammaṃ itipi, passati imaṃ saddhammaṃ itipi, sekkhena ñāṇena samannāgato itipi[T 2.0096], sekkhāya [M 1.0308] vijjāya samannāgato itipi, dhammasotaṃ samāpanno itipi, ariyo nibbedhikapañño itipi, amatadvāraṃ āhacca tiṭṭhati itipī”ti. Dasamaṃ.

“When, bhikkhus, a noble disciple thus understands as it really is the origination and the passing away of the world, he is called, bhikkhus, a noble disciple accomplished in view, accomplished in vision, one who has arrived at this true Dhamma, one who sees this true Dhamma, one endowed with the knowledge of a learner, endowed with the true knowledge of a learner, one who has entered the stream of the Dhamma, a noble one with penetrating wisdom, one who stands having reached the door of the Deathless.”

Gahapativaggo pañcamo.

The Chapter on Householders, the Fifth.

Tassuddānaṃ –

The summary of its contents:

Dve [V 1.0072] pañcaverabhayā vuttā, dukkhaṃ loko ca ñātikaṃ;

Aññataraṃ jāṇussoṇi ca, lokāyatikena aṭṭhamaṃ;

Dve ariyasāvakā vuttā, vaggo tena pavuccatīti.

Two discourses on the five fears and dangers are taught, suffering, the world, and relatives; the Aññatara and Jāṇussoṇi, and the eighth with the cosmologist; two discourses on the noble disciples are taught, therefore it is called a chapter.

6. Dukkhavaggo

6. The Chapter on Suffering

1. Parivīmaṃsanasuttaṃ

1. The Discourse on Investigation

51. Evaṃ [T 2.0097] me sutaṃ – ekaṃ samayaṃ bhagavā sāvatthiyaṃ viharati jetavane anāthapiṇḍikassa ārāme. Tatra kho bhagavā bhikkhū āmantesi – “bhikkhavo”ti. “Bhadante”ti te bhikkhū bhagavato paccassosuṃ. Bhagavā etadavoca –

51. Thus have I heard. At one time the Blessed One was dwelling in Sāvatthī, in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika's Park. There, the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus: 'Bhikkhus.' 'Venerable sir,' those bhikkhus replied to the Blessed One. The Blessed One said this:

“Kittāvatā nu kho, bhikkhave, bhikkhū parivīmaṃsamāno parivīmaṃseyya sabbaso sammā dukkhakkhayāyā”ti? “Bhagavaṃmūlakā no, bhante, dhammā bhagavaṃnettikā bhagavaṃpaṭisaraṇā[P 2.0081]. Sādhu vata, bhante, bhagavantaṃyeva paṭibhātu etassa bhāsitassa attho. Bhagavato sutvā bhikkhū dhāressantī”ti. “Tena hi, bhikkhave, suṇātha, sādhukaṃ manasi karotha, bhāsissāmī”ti. “Evaṃ, bhante”ti kho te bhikkhū bhagavato paccassosuṃ. Bhagavā etadavoca –

“Bhikkhus, to what extent should a bhikkhu, when investigating, investigate in every way and rightly for the destruction of suffering?” “Venerable sir, for us, the teachings have the Blessed One as their root, the Blessed One as their guide, and the Blessed One as their refuge. It would be good, venerable sir, if the meaning of this statement would become clear to the Blessed One himself. Having heard it from the Blessed One, the bhikkhus will bear it in mind.” “In that case, bhikkhus, listen and attend closely; I will speak.” “Yes, venerable sir,” those bhikkhus replied to the Blessed One. The Blessed One said this:

“Idha, bhikkhave, bhikkhu parivīmaṃsamāno parivīmaṃsati – ‘yaṃ kho idaṃ anekavidhaṃ nānappakārakaṃ dukkhaṃ loke uppajjati jarāmaraṇaṃ; idaṃ nu kho dukkhaṃ kiṃnidānaṃ kiṃsamudayaṃ kiṃjātikaṃ kiṃpabhavaṃ? Kismiṃ sati jarāmaraṇaṃ hoti, kismiṃ asati jarāmaraṇaṃ na hotī’ti? So parivīmaṃsamāno evaṃ pajānāti – ‘yaṃ kho idaṃ anekavidhaṃ nānappakārakaṃ dukkhaṃ loke uppajjati [M 1.0309] jarāmaraṇaṃ, idaṃ kho dukkhaṃ jātinidānaṃ jātisamudayaṃ jātijātikaṃ jātippabhavaṃ. Jātiyā sati jarāmaraṇaṃ hoti, jātiyā asati jarāmaraṇaṃ na hotī’”ti.

“Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu, when investigating, investigates thus: ‘Whatever suffering of many kinds and various sorts arises in the world, that is, aging and death—what is the source of this suffering, what is its origin, what is its genesis, what is its provenance? When what exists does aging and death come to be? When what does not exist does aging and death not come to be?’ When investigating, he understands thus: ‘Whatever suffering of many kinds and various sorts arises in the world, that is, aging and death—this suffering has birth as its source, birth as its origin, birth as its genesis, and birth as its provenance. When birth exists, aging and death come to be; when birth does not exist, aging and death do not come to be.’”

“So [V 1.0073] jarāmaraṇañca pajānāti, jarāmaraṇasamudayañca pajānāti, jarāmaraṇanirodhañca [T 2.0098] pajānāti, yā ca jarāmaraṇanirodhasāruppagāminī paṭipadā tañca pajānāti, tathā paṭipanno ca hoti anudhammacārī; ayaṃ vuccati, bhikkhave, bhikkhu sabbaso sammā dukkhakkhayāya paṭipanno jarāmaraṇanirodhāya.

“He understands aging and death, he understands the origin of aging and death, he understands the cessation of aging and death, and he understands the practice that is suitable for and leads to the cessation of aging and death. He is one who practices accordingly, practicing in conformity with the Dhamma. This, bhikkhus, is called a bhikkhu who is practicing in every way and rightly for the destruction of suffering, for the cessation of aging and death.”

“Athāparaṃ parivīmaṃsamāno parivīmaṃsati – ‘jāti panāyaṃ kiṃnidānā kiṃsamudayā kiṃjātikā kiṃpabhavā, kismiṃ sati jāti hoti, kismiṃ asati jāti na hotī’ti? So parivīmaṃsamāno evaṃ pajānāti – ‘jāti bhavanidānā bhavasamudayā bhavajātikā bhavappabhavā; bhave sati jāti hoti, bhave asati jāti na hotī’”ti.

“Furthermore, when investigating, he investigates thus: ‘Now, this birth—what is its source, what is its origin, what is its genesis, what is its provenance? When what exists does birth come to be? When what does not exist does birth not come to be?’ When investigating, he understands thus: ‘Birth has becoming as its source, becoming as its origin, becoming as its genesis, and becoming as its provenance. When becoming exists, birth comes to be; when becoming does not exist, birth does not come to be.’”

“So jātiñca pajānāti, jātisamudayañca pajānāti, jātinirodhañca pajānāti, yā ca jātinirodhasāruppagāminī paṭipadā tañca pajānāti, tathā paṭipanno ca hoti anudhammacārī; ayaṃ vuccati, bhikkhave, bhikkhu sabbaso sammā dukkhakkhayāya paṭipanno jātinirodhāya.

“He understands birth, he understands the origin of birth, he understands the cessation of birth, and he understands the practice that is suitable for and leads to the cessation of birth. He is one who practices accordingly, practicing in conformity with the Dhamma. This, bhikkhus, is called a bhikkhu who is practicing in every way and rightly for the destruction of suffering, for the cessation of birth.”

“Athāparaṃ parivīmaṃsamāno parivīmaṃsati – ‘bhavo panāyaṃ kiṃnidāno…pe… upādānaṃ panidaṃ kiṃnidānaṃ… taṇhā panāyaṃ kiṃnidānā… vedanā… phasso… saḷāyatanaṃ panidaṃ kiṃnidānaṃ… nāmarūpaṃ panidaṃ… viññāṇaṃ panidaṃ… saṅkhārā panime kiṃnidānā kiṃsamudayā kiṃjātikā kiṃpabhavā; kismiṃ sati saṅkhārā honti, kismiṃ asati saṅkhārā na hontī’ti? So parivīmaṃsamāno evaṃ pajānāti – ‘saṅkhārā avijjānidānā [T 2.0099] avijjāsamudayā avijjājātikā avijjāpabhavā; avijjāya [P 2.0082] sati saṅkhārā honti, avijjāya asati saṅkhārā na hontī’”ti.

“Furthermore, when investigating, he investigates thus: ‘Now, this becoming—what is its source? … Now, this clinging—what is its source? … Now, this craving—what is its source? … feeling… contact… Now, these six sense bases—what is their source? … Now, this name-and-form… Now, this consciousness… Now, these formations—what is their source, what is their origin, what is their genesis, what is their provenance? When what exists do formations come to be? When what does not exist do formations not come to be?’ When investigating, he understands thus: ‘Formations have ignorance as their source, ignorance as their origin, ignorance as their genesis, and ignorance as their provenance. When ignorance exists, formations come to be; when ignorance does not exist, formations do not come to be.’”

“So saṅkhāre ca pajānāti, saṅkhārasamudayañca pajānāti, saṅkhāranirodhañca pajānāti, yā ca saṅkhāranirodhasāruppagāminī paṭipadā tañca pajānāti, tathā paṭipanno ca hoti anudhammacārī[V 1.0074]; ayaṃ vuccati, bhikkhave, bhikkhu sabbaso sammā dukkhakkhayāya paṭipanno saṅkhāranirodhāya.

He understands formations, he understands the origin of formations, he understands the cessation of formations, and he understands the practice that is suitable for and leads to the cessation of formations. He is one who practices accordingly, practicing in conformity with the Dhamma. This, monks, is called a monk who is practicing rightly and in every way for the destruction of suffering, for the cessation of formations.

“Avijjāgato [M 1.0310] yaṃ, bhikkhave, purisapuggalo puññaṃ ce saṅkhāraṃ abhisaṅkharoti, puññūpagaṃ hoti viññāṇaṃ. Apuññaṃ ce saṅkhāraṃ abhisaṅkharoti, apuññūpagaṃ hoti viññāṇaṃ. Āneñjaṃ ce saṅkhāraṃ abhisaṅkharoti āneñjūpagaṃ hoti viññāṇaṃ. Yato kho, bhikkhave, bhikkhuno avijjā pahīnā hoti vijjā uppannā, so avijjāvirāgā vijjuppādā neva puññābhisaṅkhāraṃ abhisaṅkharoti na apuññābhisaṅkhāraṃ abhisaṅkharoti na āneñjābhisaṅkhāraṃ abhisaṅkharoti. Anabhisaṅkharonto anabhisañcetayanto na kiñci loke upādiyati; anupādiyaṃ na paritassati, aparitassaṃ paccattaññeva parinibbāyati. ‘Khīṇā jāti, vusitaṃ brahmacariyaṃ, kataṃ karaṇīyaṃ, nāparaṃ itthattāyā’ti pajānāti.

Monks, when a person is overcome by ignorance, if he fabricates a meritorious formation, consciousness resorts to merit. If he fabricates a demeritorious formation, consciousness resorts to demerit. If he fabricates an imperturbable formation, consciousness resorts to the imperturbable. But when, monks, a monk's ignorance is abandoned and knowledge has arisen, then through dispassion for ignorance and the arising of knowledge, he no longer fabricates a meritorious formation, nor a demeritorious formation, nor an imperturbable formation. Not fabricating and not forming intentions, he does not cling to anything in the world. Not clinging, he is not agitated. Being unagitated, he personally attains Parinibbāna. He understands: ‘Birth is destroyed, the holy life has been lived, what had to be done has been done, there is nothing further for this state of being.’

“So sukhaṃ ce vedanaṃ vedayati, sā aniccāti pajānāti, anajjhositāti pajānāti, anabhinanditāti pajānāti. Dukkhaṃ ce vedanaṃ vedayati, sā aniccāti pajānāti, anajjhositāti pajānāti, anabhinanditāti pajānāti. Adukkhamasukhaṃ ce vedanaṃ vedayati, sā aniccāti [T 2.0100] pajānāti, anajjhositāti pajānāti, anabhinanditāti pajānāti. So sukhaṃ ce vedanaṃ vedayati, visaṃyutto naṃ vedayati. Dukkhaṃ ce vedanaṃ vedayati, visaṃyutto naṃ taṃ vedanaṃ (sī. pī.), vedanaṃ (ka.) vedayati. Adukkhamasukhaṃ ce vedanaṃ vedayati, visaṃyutto naṃ vedayati.

If he feels a pleasant feeling, he understands: ‘It is impermanent.’ He understands: ‘It is not clung to.’ He understands: ‘It is not delighted in.’ If he feels a painful feeling, he understands: ‘It is impermanent.’ He understands: ‘It is not clung to.’ He understands: ‘It is not delighted in.’ If he feels a neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling, he understands: ‘It is impermanent.’ He understands: ‘It is not clung to.’ He understands: ‘It is not delighted in.’ If he feels a pleasant feeling, he feels it detachedly. If he feels a painful feeling, he feels it detachedly. If he feels a neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling, he feels it detachedly.

“So [P 2.0083] kāyapariyantikaṃ vedanaṃ vedayamāno kāyapariyantikaṃ vedanaṃ vedayāmīti pajānāti, jīvitapariyantikaṃ vedanaṃ vedayamāno jīvitapariyantikaṃ vedanaṃ vedayāmīti pajānāti. Kāyassa bhedā uddhaṃ jīvitapariyādānā idheva sabbavedayitāni anabhinanditāni sītībhavissanti, sarīrāni avasissantīti pajānāti.

Feeling a feeling limited by the body, he knows: 'I feel a feeling limited by the body.' Feeling a feeling limited by life, he knows: 'I feel a feeling limited by life.' He knows: 'After the breaking up of the body, beyond the exhaustion of life, all that is felt, not being delighted in, will become cool right here. Only the bodily remains will be left.'

“Seyyathāpi, bhikkhave, puriso kumbhakārapākā uṇhaṃ kumbhaṃ uddharitvā same bhūmibhāge paṭisisseyya paṭiviseyya (sī.), patiṭṭhapeyya (syā. kaṃ. pī.), paṭiseveyya (ṭīkā). Tatra yāyaṃ usmā sā tattheva vūpasameyya, kapallāni avasisseyyuṃ. Evameva kho, bhikkhave, bhikkhu kāyapariyantikaṃ vedanaṃ vedayamāno kāyapariyantikaṃ vedanaṃ vedayāmīti pajānāti, jīvitapariyantikaṃ vedanaṃ vedayamāno jīvitapariyantikaṃ [M 1.0311] vedanaṃ vedayāmīti pajānāti. Kāyassa [V 1.0075] bhedā uddhaṃ jīvitapariyādānā idheva sabbavedayitāni anabhinanditāni sītībhavissanti, sarīrāni avasissantīti pajānāti.

Just as, monks, a man might take a hot pot from a potter's kiln and set it down on level ground. The heat in it would then subside right there, and the pot-sherds would remain. In the same way, monks, a monk feeling a feeling limited by the body knows: 'I feel a feeling limited by the body.' Feeling a feeling limited by life, he knows: 'I feel a feeling limited by life.' He knows: 'After the breaking up of the body, beyond the exhaustion of life, all that is felt, not being delighted in, will become cool right here. Only the bodily remains will be left.'

“Taṃ kiṃ maññatha, bhikkhave, api nu kho khīṇāsavo bhikkhu puññābhisaṅkhāraṃ vā abhisaṅkhareyya apuññābhisaṅkhāraṃ vā abhisaṅkhareyya āneñjābhisaṅkhāraṃ vā abhisaṅkhareyyā”ti? “No hetaṃ, bhante”. “Sabbaso vā [T 2.0101] pana saṅkhāresu asati, saṅkhāranirodhā api nu kho viññāṇaṃ paññāyethā”ti? “No hetaṃ, bhante”. “Sabbaso vā pana viññāṇe asati, viññāṇanirodhā api nu kho nāmarūpaṃ paññāyethā”ti? “No hetaṃ, bhante”. “Sabbaso vā pana nāmarūpe asati, nāmarūpanirodhā api nu kho saḷāyatanaṃ paññāyethā”ti? “No hetaṃ, bhante”. “Sabbaso vā pana saḷāyatane asati, saḷāyatananirodhā api nu kho phasso paññāyethā”ti? “No hetaṃ, bhante”. “Sabbaso [P 2.0084] vā pana phasse asati, phassanirodhā api nu kho vedanā paññāyethā”ti? “No hetaṃ, bhante”. “Sabbaso vā pana vedanāya asati, vedanānirodhā api nu kho taṇhā paññāyethā”ti? “No hetaṃ, bhante”. “Sabbaso vā pana taṇhāya asati, taṇhānirodhā api nu kho upādānaṃ paññāyethā”ti? “No hetaṃ, bhante”. “Sabbaso vā pana upādāne asati, upādānanirodhā api nu kho bhavo paññāyethā”ti. “No hetaṃ, bhante”. “Sabbaso vā pana bhave asati, bhavanirodhā api nu kho jāti paññāyethā”ti? “No hetaṃ, bhante”. “Sabbaso vā pana jātiyā asati, jātinirodhā api nu kho jarāmaraṇaṃ paññāyethā”ti? “No hetaṃ, bhante”.

“What do you think, monks? Would a monk whose taints are destroyed still generate meritorious volitional formations, unmeritorious volitional formations, or imperturbable volitional formations?” “No, venerable sir.” “But with the complete absence of formations, with the cessation of formations, would consciousness be discerned?” “No, venerable sir.” “But with the complete absence of consciousness, with the cessation of consciousness, would name-and-form be discerned?” “No, venerable sir.” “But with the complete absence of name-and-form, with the cessation of name-and-form, would the six sense bases be discerned?” “No, venerable sir.” “But with the complete absence of the six sense bases, with the cessation of the six sense bases, would contact be discerned?” “No, venerable sir.” “But with the complete absence of contact, with the cessation of contact, would feeling be discerned?” “No, venerable sir.” “But with the complete absence of feeling, with the cessation of feeling, would craving be discerned?” “No, venerable sir.” “But with the complete absence of craving, with the cessation of craving, would clinging be discerned?” “No, venerable sir.” “But with the complete absence of clinging, with the cessation of clinging, would existence be discerned?” “No, venerable sir.” “But with the complete absence of existence, with the cessation of existence, would birth be discerned?” “No, venerable sir.” “But with the complete absence of birth, with the cessation of birth, would aging and death be discerned?” “No, venerable sir.”

“Sādhu sādhu, bhikkhave, evametaṃ, bhikkhave, netaṃ aññathā. Saddahatha me taṃ, bhikkhave, adhimuccatha, nikkaṅkhā ettha hotha nibbicikicchā. Esevanto dukkhassā”ti. Paṭhamaṃ.

“Good, good, monks! That is so, monks, it is not otherwise. Trust me in this, monks. Be resolved, be without doubt, be without uncertainty in this matter. This indeed is the end of suffering.” The First.

2. Upādānasuttaṃ

2. The Discourse on Clinging

52. Sāvatthiyaṃ [T 2.0102] viharati…pe… “upādāniyesu, bhikkhave, dhammesu assādānupassino viharato taṇhā pavaḍḍhati. Taṇhāpaccayā upādānaṃ; upādānapaccayā bhavo; bhavapaccayā jāti; jātipaccayā jarāmaraṇaṃ sokaparidevadukkhadomanassupāyāsā sambhavanti. Evametassa kevalassa dukkhakkhandhassa samudayo hoti”.

52. At Sāvatthī... “Monks, for one who dwells contemplating gratification in things that are the basis for clinging, craving increases. With craving as a condition, clinging comes to be; with clinging as a condition, becoming comes to be; with becoming as a condition, birth comes to be; with birth as a condition, aging and death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, displeasure, and despair come to be. Thus is the origin of this entire mass of suffering.”

“Seyyathāpi[M 1.0312][V 1.0076], bhikkhave, dasannaṃ vā kaṭṭhavāhānaṃ vīsāya [P 2.0085] vā kaṭṭhavāhānaṃ tiṃsāya vā kaṭṭhavāhānaṃ cattārīsāya vā kaṭṭhavāhānaṃ mahāaggikkhandho jaleyya. Tatra puriso kālena kālaṃ sukkhāni ceva tiṇāni pakkhipeyya, sukkhāni ca gomayāni pakkhipeyya, sukkhāni ca kaṭṭhāni pakkhipeyya. Evañhi so, bhikkhave, mahāaggikkhandho tadāhāro tadupādāno ciraṃ dīghamaddhānaṃ jaleyya. Evameva kho, bhikkhave, upādāniyesu dhammesu assādānupassino viharato taṇhā pavaḍḍhati. Taṇhāpaccayā upādānaṃ…pe… evametassa kevalassa dukkhakkhandhassa samudayo hoti.

“Bhikkhus, just as a great mass of fire from ten, twenty, thirty, or forty cartloads of firewood might burn. There, a person would from time to time throw in dry grass, dry cow dung, and dry firewood. In this way, bhikkhus, that great mass of fire, with that as its nutriment and that as its fuel, would burn for a very long time. So too, for one who dwells contemplating gratification in things that are the basis for clinging, craving increases. With craving as a condition, clinging comes to be… and so on… Thus is the origin of this entire mass of suffering.”

“Upādāniyesu, bhikkhave, dhammesu ādīnavānupassino viharato taṇhā nirujjhati. Taṇhānirodhā upādānanirodho; upādānanirodhā bhavanirodho; bhavanirodhā jātinirodho; jātinirodhā jarāmaraṇaṃ sokaparidevadukkhadomanassupāyāsā nirujjhanti. Evametassa kevalassa dukkhakkhandhassa nirodho hoti.

“Bhikkhus, for one who dwells contemplating the danger in things that are the basis for clinging, craving ceases. With the cessation of craving, there is the cessation of clinging; with the cessation of clinging, there is the cessation of becoming; with the cessation of becoming, there is the cessation of birth; with the cessation of birth, aging and death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, displeasure, and despair cease. Thus is the cessation of this entire mass of suffering.”

“Seyyathāpi, bhikkhave, dasannaṃ vā kaṭṭhavāhānaṃ vīsāya vā tiṃsāya [T 2.0103] vā cattārīsāya vā kaṭṭhavāhānaṃ mahāaggikkhandho jaleyya; tatra puriso na kālena kālaṃ sukkhāni ceva tiṇāni pakkhipeyya, na sukkhāni ca gomayāni pakkhipeyya, na sukkhāni ca kaṭṭhāni pakkhipeyya. Evañhi so, bhikkhave, mahāaggikkhandho purimassa ca upādānassa pariyādānā aññassa ca anupahārā anupāhārā (pī.) anāhāro nibbāyeyya. Evameva kho, bhikkhave, upādāniyesu dhammesu ādīnavānupassino viharato taṇhā nirujjhati, taṇhānirodhā upādānanirodho…pe… evametassa kevalassa dukkhakkhandhassa nirodho hotī”ti. Dutiyaṃ.

“Bhikkhus, just as a great mass of fire from ten, twenty, thirty, or forty cartloads of firewood might burn; but a person would not from time to time throw in dry grass, dry cow dung, or dry firewood. In this way, bhikkhus, that great mass of fire, by the exhaustion of its former fuel and through the non-provision of other fuel, would be extinguished for lack of nutriment. So too, for one who dwells contemplating the danger in things that are the basis for clinging, craving ceases. With the cessation of craving, there is the cessation of clinging… and so on… Thus is the cessation of this entire mass of suffering.” The Second.

3. Saṃyojanasuttaṃ

3. The Discourse on Fetters

53. Sāvatthiyaṃ viharati [P 2.0086] …pe… “saṃyojaniyesu, bhikkhave, dhammesu assādānupassino viharato taṇhā pavaḍḍhati. Taṇhāpaccayā upādānaṃ; upādānapaccayā bhavo; bhavapaccayā jāti; jātipaccayā jarāmaraṇaṃ sokaparidevadukkhadomanassupāyāsā sambhavanti. Evametassa kevalassa dukkhakkhandhassa samudayo hoti”.

53. At Sāvatthī… “Bhikkhus, for one who dwells contemplating gratification in things that are a cause for fetters, craving increases. With craving as a condition, clinging comes to be; with clinging as a condition, becoming comes to be; with becoming as a condition, birth comes to be; with birth as a condition, aging and death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, displeasure, and despair come to be. Thus is the arising of this entire mass of suffering.”

“Seyyathāpi[M 1.0313][V 1.0077], bhikkhave, telañca paṭicca vaṭṭiñca paṭicca telappadīpo jhāyeyya. Tatra puriso kālena kālaṃ telaṃ āsiñceyya vaṭṭiṃ upasaṃhareyya. Evañhi so, bhikkhave, telappadīpo tadāhāro tadupādāno ciraṃ dīghamaddhānaṃ jaleyya. Evameva kho, bhikkhave, saṃyojaniyesu dhammesu assādānupassino viharato taṇhā pavaḍḍhati. Taṇhāpaccayā upādānaṃ; upādānapaccayā bhavo; bhavapaccayā jāti[T 2.0104]; jātipaccayā jarāmaraṇaṃ sokaparidevadukkhadomanassupāyāsā sambhavanti. Evametassa kevalassa dukkhakkhandhassa samudayo hoti.

“Bhikkhus, just as an oil lamp would burn in dependence on oil and a wick. There, a person might from time to time pour in oil and tend to the wick. In this way, bhikkhus, that oil lamp, with that as its nutriment and that as its fuel, would burn for a very long time. So too, for one who dwells contemplating gratification in things that are a cause for fetters, craving increases. With craving as a condition, clinging comes to be; with clinging as a condition, becoming comes to be; with becoming as a condition, birth comes to be; with birth as a condition, aging and death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, displeasure, and despair come to be. Thus is the arising of this entire mass of suffering.”

“Saṃyojaniyesu, bhikkhave, dhammesu ādīnavānupassino viharato taṇhā nirujjhati. Taṇhānirodhā upādānanirodho; upādānanirodhā bhavanirodho; bhavanirodhā jātinirodho; jātinirodhā jarāmaraṇaṃ sokaparidevadukkhadomanassupāyāsā nirujjhanti. Evametassa kevalassa dukkhakkhandhassa nirodho hoti.

“Bhikkhus, for one who dwells contemplating the danger in things that are a cause for fetters, craving ceases. With the cessation of craving, there is the cessation of clinging; with the cessation of clinging, there is the cessation of becoming; with the cessation of becoming, there is the cessation of birth; with the cessation of birth, aging and death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, displeasure, and despair cease. Thus is the cessation of this entire mass of suffering.”

“Seyyathāpi, bhikkhave, telañca paṭicca vaṭṭiñca paṭicca telappadīpo jhāyeyya. Tatra puriso na kālena kālaṃ telaṃ āsiñceyya na vaṭṭiṃ upasaṃhareyya. Evañhi so, bhikkhave, telappadīpo purimassa ca upādānassa pariyādānā aññassa ca anupahārā anāhāro nibbāyeyya. Evameva kho, bhikkhave, saṃyojaniyesu dhammesu ādīnavānupassino viharato taṇhā nirujjhati. Taṇhānirodhā upādānanirodho…pe… evametassa kevalassa dukkhakkhandhassa nirodho hotī”ti. Tatiyaṃ.

“Bhikkhus, just as an oil lamp would burn in dependence on oil and a wick, but a person would not from time to time pour in oil or tend to the wick. In this way, bhikkhus, that oil lamp, through the exhaustion of its former fuel and the non-provision of other fuel, would be extinguished for lack of nutriment. So too, for one who dwells contemplating the danger in things that are a cause for fetters, craving ceases. With the cessation of craving, there is the cessation of clinging… and so on… Thus is the cessation of this entire mass of suffering.” The Third.

4. Dutiyasaṃyojanasuttaṃ

4. The Second Discourse on Fetters

54. Sāvatthiyaṃ viharati [P 2.0087] …pe… “seyyathāpi, bhikkhave, telañca paṭicca vaṭṭiñca paṭicca telappadīpo jhāyeyya. Tatra puriso kālena kālaṃ telaṃ āsiñceyya vaṭṭiṃ upasaṃhareyya. Evañhi so, bhikkhave, telappadīpo tadāhāro tadupādāno ciraṃ dīghamaddhānaṃ jaleyya. Evameva kho, bhikkhave, saṃyojaniyesu dhammesu assādānupassino [T 2.0105] viharato taṇhā pavaḍḍhati. Taṇhāpaccayā upādānaṃ…pe… evametassa kevalassa dukkhakkhandhassa samudayo hoti”.

54. At Sāvatthī... “Bhikkhus, just as an oil lamp would burn in dependence on oil and a wick. There, a person might from time to time pour in oil and tend to the wick. In this way, bhikkhus, that oil lamp, with that as its nutriment and that as its fuel, would burn for a very long time. So too, for one who dwells contemplating gratification in things that are a cause for fetters, craving increases. With craving as a condition, clinging comes to be... and so on... Thus is the arising of this entire mass of suffering.”

“Seyyathāpi[M 1.0314], bhikkhave, telañca paṭicca vaṭṭiñca paṭicca telappadīpo jhāyeyya. Tatra puriso na kālena kālaṃ telaṃ āsiñceyya na vaṭṭiṃ upasaṃhareyya[V 1.0078]. Evañhi so, bhikkhave, telappadīpo purimassa ca upādānassa pariyādānā aññassa ca anupahārā anāhāro nibbāyeyya. Evameva kho, bhikkhave, saṃyojaniyesu dhammesu ādīnavānupassino viharato taṇhā nirujjhati. Taṇhānirodhā upādānanirodho…pe… evametassa kevalassa dukkhakkhandhassa nirodho hotī”ti. Catutthaṃ.

“Bhikkhus, just as an oil lamp would burn in dependence on oil and a wick, but a person would not from time to time pour in oil or tend to the wick. In this way, bhikkhus, that oil lamp, through the exhaustion of its former fuel and the non-provision of other fuel, would be extinguished for lack of nutriment. So too, for one who dwells contemplating the danger in things that are a cause for fetters, craving ceases. With the cessation of craving, there is the cessation of clinging... and so on... Thus is the cessation of this entire mass of suffering.” The Fourth.

5. Mahārukkhasuttaṃ

5. The Discourse on the Great Tree

55. Sāvatthiyaṃ viharati…pe… “upādāniyesu, bhikkhave, dhammesu assādānupassino viharato taṇhā pavaḍḍhati. Taṇhāpaccayā upādānaṃ; upādānapaccayā bhavo…pe… evametassa kevalassa dukkhakkhandhassa samudayo hoti”.

55. At Sāvatthī... “Bhikkhus, for one who dwells contemplating gratification in things that are a basis for clinging, craving increases. With craving as a condition, clinging arises; with clinging as a condition, becoming arises... Thus is the arising of this entire mass of suffering.”

“Seyyathāpi, bhikkhave, mahārukkho. Tassa yāni ceva mūlāni adhogamāni, yāni ca tiriyaṅgamāni, sabbāni tāni uddhaṃ ojaṃ abhiharanti. Evañhi so, bhikkhave, mahārukkho tadāhāro tadupādāno ciraṃ dīghamaddhānaṃ tiṭṭheyya. Evameva kho, bhikkhave, upādāniyesu dhammesu assādānupassino viharato taṇhā pavaḍḍhati. Taṇhāpaccayā upādānaṃ…pe… evametassa [T 2.0106] kevalassa dukkhakkhandhassa samudayo hoti.

“Just as, Bhikkhus, there is a great tree. Whatever of its roots go downwards and whatever go across, all of them draw sap upwards. Thus, Bhikkhus, that great tree, having that as its nutriment and that as its sustenance, would stand for a long, long time. In the very same way, Bhikkhus, for one who dwells contemplating gratification in things that are a basis for clinging, craving increases. With craving as a condition, clinging arises... Thus is the arising of this entire mass of suffering.”

“Upādāniyesu[P 2.0088], bhikkhave, dhammesu ādīnavānupassino viharato taṇhā nirujjhati. Taṇhānirodhā upādānanirodho; upādānanirodhā bhavanirodho…pe… evametassa kevalassa dukkhakkhandhassa nirodho hoti.

“Bhikkhus, for one who dwells contemplating the danger in things that are a basis for clinging, craving ceases. With the cessation of craving, clinging ceases; with the cessation of clinging, becoming ceases... Thus is the cessation of this entire mass of suffering.”

“Seyyathāpi, bhikkhave, mahārukkho. Atha puriso āgaccheyya kuddālapiṭakaṃ kudālapiṭakaṃ (aññattha) ādāya. So taṃ rukkhaṃ mūle chindeyya, mūlaṃ chinditvā palikhaṇeyya paliṃkhaṇeyya (pī. ka.), palikhaṇitvā mūlāni uddhareyya antamaso usīranāḷimattānipi. So taṃ rukkhaṃ khaṇḍākhaṇḍikaṃ chindeyya, khaṇḍākhaṇḍikaṃ chinditvā phāleyya, phāletvā sakalikaṃ sakalikaṃ kareyya, sakalikaṃ sakalikaṃ karitvā vātātape visoseyya; vātātape visosetvā agginā ḍaheyya, agginā ḍahetvā masiṃ kareyya, masiṃ [V 1.0079] karitvā mahāvāte vā ophuṇeyya opuneyya (sī. pī.), ophuneyya (syā. kaṃ. ka.) nadiyā vā sīghasotāya pavāheyya. Evañhi so, bhikkhave, mahārukkho ucchinnamūlo [M 1.0315] assa tālāvatthukato anabhāvaṃkato anabhāvakato (sī.), anabhāvaṅgato (syā. kaṃ.) āyatiṃ anuppādadhammo. Evameva kho, bhikkhave, upādāniyesu dhammesu ādīnavānupassino viharato taṇhā nirujjhati. Taṇhānirodhā upādānanirodho; upādānanirodhā bhavanirodho…pe… evametassa kevalassa dukkhakkhandhassa nirodho hotī”ti. Pañcamaṃ.

“Just as, Bhikkhus, there is a great tree. Then a man would come, taking a spade and a basket. He would cut that tree at the root; having cut it at the root, he would dig; having dug, he would pull out the roots, even down to the fibrous rootlets. He would cut that tree into pieces; having cut it into pieces, he would split it; having split it, he would make it into splinters; having made it into splinters, he would dry it in the wind and sun; having dried it in the wind and sun, he would burn it with fire; having burned it with fire, he would make it into ash; having made it into ash, he would winnow it in a strong wind or let it be carried away by a river with a swift current. Thus, Bhikkhus, that great tree would be cut off at the root, made like a palm stump, brought to a state of non-existence, and of a nature not to arise again in the future. In the very same way, Bhikkhus, for one who dwells contemplating the danger in things that are a basis for clinging, craving ceases. With the cessation of craving, clinging ceases; with the cessation of clinging, becoming ceases... Thus is the cessation of this entire mass of suffering.” Fifth.

6. Dutiyamahārukkhasuttaṃ

6. The Second Discourse on the Great Tree

56. Sāvatthiyaṃ viharati…pe… “seyyathāpi, bhikkhave, mahārukkho. Tassa yāni ceva mūlāni adhogamāni, yāni ca tiriyaṅgamāni[T 2.0107], sabbāni tāni uddhaṃ ojaṃ abhiharanti. Evañhi so, bhikkhave, mahārukkho tadāhāro tadupādāno ciraṃ dīghamaddhānaṃ tiṭṭheyya. Evameva kho, bhikkhave, upādāniyesu dhammesu assādānupassino viharato taṇhā pavaḍḍhati. Taṇhāpaccayā upādānaṃ [P 2.0089]…pe… evametassa kevalassa dukkhakkhandhassa samudayo hoti”.

56. At Sāvatthī... “Just as, Bhikkhus, there is a great tree. Whatever of its roots go downwards and whatever go across, all of them draw sap upwards. Thus, Bhikkhus, that great tree, having that as its nutriment and that as its sustenance, would stand for a long, long time. In the very same way, Bhikkhus, for one who dwells contemplating gratification in things that are a basis for clinging, craving increases. With craving as a condition, clinging arises... Thus is the arising of this entire mass of suffering.”

“Seyyathāpi, bhikkhave, mahārukkho. Atha puriso āgaccheyya kuddālapiṭakaṃ ādāya. So taṃ rukkhaṃ mūle chindeyya, mūle chetvā palikhaṇeyya, palikhaṇitvā mūlāni uddhareyya…pe… nadiyā vā sīghasotāya pavāheyya. Evañhi so, bhikkhave, mahārukkho ucchinnamūlo assa tālāvatthukato anabhāvaṅkato āyatiṃ anuppādadhammo. Evameva kho, bhikkhave, upādāniyesu dhammesu ādīnavānupassino viharato taṇhā nirujjhati. Taṇhānirodhā upādānanirodho…pe… evametassa kevalassa dukkhakkhandhassa nirodho hotī”ti. Chaṭṭhaṃ.

“Just as, Bhikkhus, there is a great tree. Then a man would come, taking a spade and a basket. He would cut that tree at the root; having cut it at the root, he would dig; having dug, he would pull out the roots... or let it be carried away by a river with a swift current. Thus, Bhikkhus, that great tree would be cut off at the root, made like a palm stump, brought to a state of non-existence, and of a nature not to arise again in the future. In the very same way, Bhikkhus, for one who dwells contemplating the danger in things that are a basis for clinging, craving ceases. With the cessation of craving, clinging ceases... Thus is the cessation of this entire mass of suffering.” Sixth.

7. Taruṇarukkhasuttaṃ

7. The Discourse on the Young Tree

57. Sāvatthiyaṃ viharati…pe… “saṃyojaniyesu, bhikkhave, dhammesu assādānupassino viharato taṇhā pavaḍḍhati. Taṇhāpaccayā upādānaṃ…pe… evametassa kevalassa dukkhakkhandhassa samudayo hoti”.

57. At Sāvatthī... “Bhikkhus, for one who dwells contemplating gratification in things that are a basis for fetters, craving increases. With craving as a condition, clinging arises... Thus is the arising of this entire mass of suffering.”

“Seyyathāpi, bhikkhave, taruṇo rukkho. Tassa puriso kālena kālaṃ mūlāni palimajjeyya palisanneyya (sī.), palisajjeyya (syā. kaṃ. pī.), palipaṭṭheyya (ka.), palisandeyya, palibandheyya (ṭīkānurūpaṃ) kālena kālaṃ paṃsuṃ dadeyya, kālena [T 2.0108] kālaṃ [M 1.0316][V 1.0080] udakaṃ dadeyya. Evañhi so, bhikkhave, taruṇo rukkho tadāhāro tadupādāno vuddhiṃ virūḷhiṃ vepullaṃ āpajjeyya. Evameva kho, bhikkhave, saṃyojaniyesu dhammesu assādānupassino viharato taṇhā pavaḍḍhati. Taṇhāpaccayā upādānaṃ…pe… evametassa kevalassa dukkhakkhandhassa samudayo hoti.

“Just as, Bhikkhus, there is a young tree. A man might, from time to time, clear its roots, from time to time give it soil, and from time to time give it water. Thus, Bhikkhus, that young tree, having that as its nutriment and that as its sustenance, would attain growth, flourishing, and expansion. In the very same way, Bhikkhus, for one who dwells contemplating gratification in things that are a basis for fetters, craving increases. With craving as a condition, clinging arises... Thus is the arising of this entire mass of suffering.”

“Saṃyojaniyesu, bhikkhave, dhammesu ādīnavānupassino viharato taṇhā nirujjhati. Taṇhānirodhā upādānanirodho…pe… evametassa kevalassa dukkhakkhandhassa nirodho hoti.

“Bhikkhus, for one who dwells contemplating the danger in things that are a basis for fetters, craving ceases. With the cessation of craving, clinging ceases... Thus is the cessation of this entire mass of suffering.”

“Seyyathāpi[P 2.0090], bhikkhave, taruṇo rukkho. Atha puriso āgaccheyya kuddālapiṭakaṃ ādāya…pe… nadiyā vā sīghasotāya pavāheyya. Evañhi so, bhikkhave, taruṇo rukkho ucchinnamūlo assa tālāvatthukato anabhāvaṅkato āyatiṃ anuppādadhammo. Evameva kho, bhikkhave, saṃyojaniyesu dhammesu ādīnavānupassino viharato taṇhā nirujjhati. Taṇhānirodhā upādānanirodho…pe… evametassa kevalassa dukkhakkhandhassa nirodho hotī”ti. Sattamaṃ.

“Just as, Bhikkhus, there is a young tree. Then a man would come, taking a spade and a basket... and let it be carried away by a river with a swift current. Thus, Bhikkhus, that young tree would be cut off at the root, made like a palm stump, brought to a state of non-existence, and of a nature not to arise again in the future. In the very same way, Bhikkhus, for one who dwells contemplating the danger in things that are a basis for fetters, craving ceases. With the cessation of craving, clinging ceases... Thus is the cessation of this entire mass of suffering.” Seventh.

8. Nāmarūpasuttaṃ

8. The Discourse on Name-and-Form

58. Sāvatthiyaṃ viharati…pe… “saṃyojaniyesu, bhikkhave, dhammesu assādānupassino viharato nāmarūpassa avakkanti hoti. Nāmarūpapaccayā saḷāyatanaṃ…pe… evametassa kevalassa dukkhakkhandhassa samudayo hoti”.

58. At Sāvatthī... “Bhikkhus, for one who dwells contemplating gratification in things that are a basis for fetters, the descent of name-and-form occurs. With name-and-form as a condition, the six sense bases arise... Thus is the arising of this entire mass of suffering.”

“Seyyathāpi, bhikkhave, mahārukkho. Tassa yāni ceva mūlāni [T 2.0109] adhogamāni, yāni ca tiriyaṅgamāni, sabbāni tāni uddhaṃ ojaṃ abhiharanti. Evañhi so, bhikkhave, mahārukkho tadāhāro tadupādāno ciraṃ dīghamaddhānaṃ tiṭṭheyya. Evameva kho, bhikkhave, saṃyojaniyesu dhammesu assādānupassino viharato nāmarūpassa avakkanti hoti…pe….

“Suppose, Bhikkhus, there is a great tree. Whatever roots it has going downwards and whatever roots it has going sideways, all of them convey sap upwards. In this way, Bhikkhus, that great tree, with that as its nutriment and that as its sustenance, would stand for a long, long time. So too, Bhikkhus, for one who dwells contemplating gratification in phenomena that are causes for fetters, the descent of name-and-form occurs… and so on….”

“Saṃyojaniyesu, bhikkhave, dhammesu ādīnavānupassino viharato nāmarūpassa avakkanti na hoti. Nāmarūpanirodhā [P 2.0091] saḷāyatananirodho…pe… evametassa kevalassa dukkhakkhandhassa nirodho hoti.

“Bhikkhus, for one who dwells contemplating the danger in phenomena that are causes for fetters, the descent of name-and-form does not occur. With the cessation of name-and-form, there is the cessation of the six sense bases… and so on… Thus is the cessation of this whole mass of suffering.”

“Seyyathāpi[M 1.0317][V 1.0081], bhikkhave, mahārukkho. Atha puriso āgaccheyya kuddālapiṭakaṃ ādāya…pe… āyatiṃ anuppādadhammo. Evameva kho, bhikkhave, saṃyojaniyesu dhammesu ādīnavānupassino viharato nāmarūpassa avakkanti na hoti. Nāmarūpanirodhā saḷāyatananirodho…pe… evametassa kevalassa dukkhakkhandhassa nirodho hotī”ti. Aṭṭhamaṃ.

“Suppose, Bhikkhus, there is a great tree. Then a man might come, having taken a hoe and a basket… and so on… making it incapable of future arising. So too, Bhikkhus, for one who dwells contemplating the danger in phenomena that are causes for fetters, the descent of name-and-form does not occur. With the cessation of name-and-form, there is the cessation of the six sense bases… and so on… Thus is the cessation of this whole mass of suffering.” Eighth.

9. Viññāṇasuttaṃ

9. The Discourse on Consciousness

59. Sāvatthiyaṃ viharati…pe… “saṃyojaniyesu, bhikkhave, dhammesu assādānupassino viharato viññāṇassa avakkanti hoti. Viññāṇapaccayā nāmarūpaṃ…pe… evametassa kevalassa dukkhakkhandhassa samudayo hoti”.

59. At Sāvatthī… and so on… “Bhikkhus, for one who dwells contemplating gratification in phenomena that are causes for fetters, the descent of consciousness occurs. With consciousness as condition, name-and-form comes to be… and so on… Thus is the origin of this whole mass of suffering.”

“Seyyathāpi, bhikkhave, mahārukkho. Tassa yāni ceva mūlāni [T 2.0110] …pe… evameva kho, bhikkhave, saṃyojaniyesu dhammesu assādānupassino viharato viññāṇassa avakkanti hoti…pe….

“Suppose, Bhikkhus, there is a great tree. Whatever roots it has… and so on… So too, Bhikkhus, for one who dwells contemplating gratification in phenomena that are causes for fetters, the descent of consciousness occurs… and so on….”
