Idañca pana mayaṃ āyasmato sāriputtassa bhāsitaṃ imehi chattiṃsāya vatthūhi anumodāma – ‘jarāmaraṇassa ce, āvuso, bhikkhu nibbidāya virāgāya nirodhāya dhammaṃ deseti, dhammakathiko bhikkhūti alaṃ [P 2.0115] vacanāya. Jarāmaraṇassa ce, āvuso, bhikkhu nibbidāya virāgāya nirodhāya paṭipanno hoti, dhammānudhammappaṭipanno bhikkhūti alaṃ vacanāya. Jarāmaraṇassa ce, āvuso, bhikkhu nibbidā virāgā nirodhā anupādā vimutto hoti, diṭṭhadhammanibbānappatto bhikkhūti alaṃ vacanāya. Jātiyā ce… bhavassa ce… upādānassa ce… taṇhāya ce… vedanāya ce… phassassa ce… saḷāyatanassa ce… nāmarūpassa ce… viññāṇassa ce… saṅkhārānaṃ ce… avijjāya ce, āvuso, bhikkhu nibbidāya virāgāya nirodhāya dhammaṃ deseti, dhammakathiko bhikkhūti alaṃ vacanāya. Avijjāya ce, āvuso, bhikkhu nibbidāya virāgāya nirodhāya paṭipanno hoti, dhammānudhammappaṭipanno bhikkhūti alaṃ vacanāya[T 2.0140]. Avijjāya ce, āvuso, bhikkhu nibbidā virāgā nirodhā anupādā vimutto hoti, diṭṭhadhammanibbānappatto bhikkhūti alaṃ vacanāyā’”ti. Sattamaṃ.

“But how, friend Sāriputta, is the meaning of this statement to be understood?” “In that case, friend, I will make a simile for you. For by means of a simile, some wise persons here understand the meaning of what is said. Suppose, friend, two sheaves of reeds were to stand leaning against one another. In this very way, friend, from name-and-form as a condition, consciousness comes to be; from consciousness as a condition, name-and-form comes to be; from name-and-form as a condition, the six sense bases come to be; from the six sense bases as a condition, contact comes to be… thus is the origin of this entire mass of suffering. If, friend, one of those sheaves of reeds were to be pulled away, the one would fall; and if the other were to be pulled away, the other would fall. In this very way, friend, from the cessation of name-and-form, there is the cessation of consciousness; from the cessation of consciousness, there is the cessation of name-and-form; from the cessation of name-and-form, there is the cessation of the six sense bases; from the cessation of the six sense bases, there is the cessation of contact… thus is the cessation of this entire mass of suffering.” “It is wonderful, friend Sāriputta! It is marvelous, friend Sāriputta! How exceedingly well this has been spoken by the Venerable Sāriputta. And we rejoice in this statement of the Venerable Sāriputta on these thirty-six grounds: ‘If, friend, a bhikkhu teaches the Dhamma for disenchantment, for dispassion, and for cessation regarding aging and death, it is fitting to call him a bhikkhu who is a speaker of the Dhamma. If, friend, a bhikkhu is practicing for disenchantment, for dispassion, and for cessation regarding aging and death, it is fitting to call him a bhikkhu who is practicing in accordance with the Dhamma. If, friend, a bhikkhu, through disenchantment, dispassion, and cessation, is liberated without clinging regarding aging and death, it is fitting to call him a bhikkhu who has attained Nibbāna in this very life. If, regarding birth… existence… clinging… craving… feeling… contact… the six sense bases… name-and-form… consciousness… formations… If, friend, a bhikkhu teaches the Dhamma for disenchantment, for dispassion, and for cessation regarding ignorance, it is fitting to call him a bhikkhu who is a speaker of the Dhamma. If, friend, a bhikkhu is practicing for disenchantment, for dispassion, and for cessation regarding ignorance, it is fitting to call him a bhikkhu who is practicing in accordance with the Dhamma. If, friend, a bhikkhu, through disenchantment, dispassion, and cessation, is liberated without clinging regarding ignorance, it is fitting to call him a bhikkhu who has attained Nibbāna in this very life.’” The seventh.

8. Kosambisuttaṃ

8. The Discourse at Kosambī

68. Ekaṃ [V 1.0101] samayaṃ āyasmā ca musilo mūsilo (sī.), musīlo (pī.) āyasmā ca paviṭṭho saviṭṭho (sī. pī.) āyasmā ca nārado āyasmā ca ānando kosambiyaṃ viharanti ghositārāme. Atha kho āyasmā paviṭṭho āyasmantaṃ musilaṃ etadavoca – “aññatreva, āvuso musila, saddhāya aññatra ruciyā aññatra anussavā aññatra ākāraparivitakkā aññatra diṭṭhinijjhānakkhantiyā atthāyasmato musilassa paccattameva ñāṇaṃ – ‘jātipaccayā jarāmaraṇa’”nti? “Aññatreva, āvuso paviṭṭha, saddhāya aññatra ruciyā aññatra anussavā aññatra ākāraparivitakkā aññatra diṭṭhinijjhānakkhantiyā ahametaṃ jānāmi ahametaṃ passāmi – ‘jātipaccayā jarāmaraṇa’”nti.

68. At one time the Venerable Musila, the Venerable Paviṭṭha, the Venerable Nārada, and the Venerable Ānanda were dwelling at Kosambī in Ghosita’s Park. Then the Venerable Paviṭṭha said this to the Venerable Musila: “Friend Musila, apart from faith, apart from preference, apart from oral tradition, apart from reflection on reasons, apart from acceptance of a view upon reflection, does the Venerable Musila have his own direct knowledge that: ‘From birth as a condition, aging and death come to be’?” “Friend Paviṭṭha, apart from faith, apart from preference, apart from oral tradition, apart from reflection on reasons, apart from acceptance of a view upon reflection, I know this, I see this: ‘From birth as a condition, aging and death come to be.’”

“Aññatreva[P 2.0116], āvuso musila, saddhāya aññatra ruciyā aññatra anussavā aññatra ākāraparivitakkā aññatra diṭṭhinijjhānakkhantiyā atthāyasmato musilassa [M 1.0337] paccattameva ñāṇaṃ – ‘bhavapaccayā jātīti…pe… upādānapaccayā bhavoti… taṇhāpaccayā upādānanti… vedanāpaccayā taṇhāti… phassapaccayā vedanāti… saḷāyatanapaccayā phassoti… nāmarūpapaccayā saḷāyatananti… viññāṇapaccayā nāmarūpanti… saṅkhārapaccayā viññāṇanti… avijjāpaccayā [T 2.0141] saṅkhārā’”ti? “Aññatreva, āvuso paviṭṭha, saddhāya aññatra ruciyā aññatra anussavā aññatra ākāraparivitakkā aññatra diṭṭhinijjhānakkhantiyā ahametaṃ jānāmi ahametaṃ passāmi – ‘avijjāpaccayā saṅkhārā’”ti.

“Friend Musila, apart from faith, apart from preference, apart from oral tradition, apart from reflection on reasons, apart from acceptance of a view upon reflection, does the Venerable Musila have his own direct knowledge that: ‘From existence as a condition, birth comes to be’… ‘From clinging as a condition, existence comes to be’… ‘From craving as a condition, clinging comes to be’… ‘From feeling as a condition, craving comes to be’… ‘From contact as a condition, feeling comes to be’… ‘From the six sense bases as a condition, contact comes to be’… ‘From name-and-form as a condition, the six sense bases come to be’… ‘From consciousness as a condition, name-and-form comes to be’… ‘From formations as a condition, consciousness comes to be’… ‘From ignorance as a condition, formations come to be’?” “Friend Paviṭṭha, apart from faith, apart from preference, apart from oral tradition, apart from reflection on reasons, apart from acceptance of a view upon reflection, I know this, I see this: ‘From ignorance as a condition, formations come to be.’”

“Aññatreva, āvuso musila, saddhāya aññatra ruciyā aññatra anussavā aññatra ākāraparivitakkā aññatra diṭṭhinijjhānakkhantiyā atthāyasmato musilassa paccattameva ñāṇaṃ – ‘jātinirodhā jarāmaraṇanirodho’”ti? “Aññatreva, āvuso paviṭṭha, saddhāya aññatra ruciyā aññatra anussavā aññatra ākāraparivitakkā aññatra diṭṭhinijjhānakkhantiyā ahametaṃ jānāmi ahametaṃ passāmi – ‘jātinirodhā jarāmaraṇanirodho’”ti.

“Friend Musila, apart from faith, apart from preference, apart from oral tradition, apart from reflection on reasons, apart from acceptance of a view upon reflection, does the Venerable Musila have his own direct knowledge that: ‘From the cessation of birth, there is the cessation of aging and death’?” “Friend Paviṭṭha, apart from faith, apart from preference, apart from oral tradition, apart from reflection on reasons, apart from acceptance of a view upon reflection, I know this, I see this: ‘From the cessation of birth, there is the cessation of aging and death.’”

“Aññatreva[V 1.0102], āvuso musila, saddhāya aññatra ruciyā aññatra anussavā aññatra ākāraparivitakkā aññatra diṭṭhinijjhānakkhantiyā atthāyasmato musilassa paccattameva ñāṇaṃ – ‘bhavanirodhā jātinirodhoti…pe… upādānanirodhā bhavanirodhoti… taṇhānirodhā upādānanirodhoti… vedanānirodhā taṇhānirodhoti… phassanirodhā vedanānirodhoti… saḷāyatananirodhā phassanirodhoti… nāmarūpanirodhā saḷāyatananirodhoti… viññāṇanirodhā nāmarūpanirodhoti [P 2.0117]… saṅkhāranirodhā viññāṇanirodhoti… avijjānirodhā saṅkhāranirodho’”ti? “Aññatreva, āvuso paviṭṭha, saddhāya aññatra ruciyā aññatra anussavā aññatra ākāraparivitakkā aññatra diṭṭhinijjhānakkhantiyā [T 2.0142] ahametaṃ jānāmi ahametaṃ passāmi – ‘avijjānirodhā saṅkhāranirodho’”ti.

“Friend Musīla, apart from faith, apart from inclination, apart from oral tradition, apart from reflection on reasons, apart from acceptance of a view after consideration, does the Venerable Musīla have personal knowledge thus: ‘With the cessation of becoming, there is the cessation of birth… with the cessation of clinging, there is the cessation of becoming… with the cessation of craving, there is the cessation of clinging… with the cessation of feeling, there is the cessation of craving… with the cessation of contact, there is the cessation of feeling… with the cessation of the six sense bases, there is the cessation of contact… with the cessation of name-and-form, there is the cessation of the six sense bases… with the cessation of consciousness, there is the cessation of name-and-form… with the cessation of formations, there is the cessation of consciousness… with the cessation of ignorance, there is the cessation of formations’?” “Friend Paviṭṭha, apart from faith, apart from inclination, apart from oral tradition, apart from reflection on reasons, apart from acceptance of a view after consideration, I know this, I see this: ‘With the cessation of ignorance, there is the cessation of formations.’”

“Aññatreva, āvuso musila, saddhāya aññatra ruciyā aññatra anussavā aññatra ākāraparivitakkā aññatra diṭṭhinijjhānakkhantiyā atthāyasmato musilassa paccattameva ñāṇaṃ – ‘bhavanirodho nibbāna’”nti? “Aññatreva, āvuso paviṭṭha, saddhāya aññatra ruciyā aññatra anussavā aññatra [M 1.0338] ākāraparivitakkā aññatra diṭṭhinijjhānakkhantiyā ahametaṃ jānāmi ahametaṃ passāmi – ‘bhavanirodho nibbāna’”nti.

“Friend Musīla, apart from faith, apart from inclination, apart from oral tradition, apart from reflection on reasons, apart from acceptance of a view after consideration, does the Venerable Musīla have personal knowledge thus: ‘The cessation of becoming is Nibbāna’?” “Friend Paviṭṭha, apart from faith, apart from inclination, apart from oral tradition, apart from reflection on reasons, apart from acceptance of a view after consideration, I know this, I see this: ‘The cessation of becoming is Nibbāna.’”

“Tenahāyasmā musilo arahaṃ khīṇāsavo”ti? Evaṃ vutte, āyasmā musilo tuṇhī ahosi. Atha kho āyasmā nārado āyasmantaṃ paviṭṭhaṃ etadavoca – “sādhāvuso paviṭṭha, ahaṃ etaṃ pañhaṃ labheyyaṃ. Maṃ etaṃ pañhaṃ puccha. Ahaṃ te etaṃ pañhaṃ byākarissāmī”ti. “Labhatāyasmā nārado etaṃ pañhaṃ. Pucchāmahaṃ āyasmantaṃ nāradaṃ etaṃ pañhaṃ. Byākarotu ca me āyasmā nārado etaṃ pañhaṃ”.

“Then the Venerable Musīla is an Arahant, one with taints destroyed.” When this was said, the Venerable Musīla became silent. Then the Venerable Nārada said this to the Venerable Paviṭṭha: “Friend Paviṭṭha, please, may I receive this question. Ask me this question. I will answer this question for you.” “Let the Venerable Nārada receive this question. I will ask the Venerable Nārada this question. And may the Venerable Nārada answer this question for me.”

“Aññatreva, āvuso nārada, saddhāya aññatra ruciyā aññatra anussavā aññatra ākāraparivitakkā aññatra diṭṭhinijjhānakkhantiyā atthāyasmato nāradassa paccattameva ñāṇaṃ – ‘jātipaccayā jarāmaraṇa’”nti? “Aññatreva, āvuso paviṭṭha, saddhāya aññatra ruciyā aññatra anussavā aññatra ākāraparivitakkā aññatra diṭṭhinijjhānakkhantiyā ahametaṃ [T 2.0143] jānāmi ahametaṃ passāmi – ‘jātipaccayā jarāmaraṇa’”nti.

“Friend Nārada, apart from faith, apart from inclination, apart from oral tradition, apart from reflection on reasons, apart from acceptance of a view after consideration, does the Venerable Nārada have personal knowledge thus: ‘With birth as condition, aging and death come to be’?” “Friend Paviṭṭha, apart from faith, apart from inclination, apart from oral tradition, apart from reflection on reasons, apart from acceptance of a view after consideration, I know this, I see this: ‘With birth as condition, aging and death come to be.’”

“Aññatreva[V 1.0103], āvuso nārada, saddhāya aññatra ruciyā aññatra anussavā aññatra ākāraparivitakkā aññatra diṭṭhinijjhānakkhantiyā atthāyasmato nāradassa paccattameva ñāṇaṃ – bhavapaccayā jāti…pe… avijjāpaccayā saṅkhārā”ti? “Aññatreva, āvuso paviṭṭha, saddhāya aññatra ruciyā aññatra anussavā aññatra ākāraparivitakkā aññatra diṭṭhinijjhānakkhantiyā ahametaṃ jānāmi ahametaṃ passāmi – ‘avijjāpaccayā saṅkhārā’”ti.

“Friend Nārada, apart from faith, apart from inclination, apart from oral tradition, apart from reflection on reasons, apart from acceptance of a view after consideration, does the Venerable Nārada have personal knowledge thus: ‘With becoming as condition, birth comes to be… with ignorance as condition, formations come to be’?” “Friend Paviṭṭha, apart from faith, apart from inclination, apart from oral tradition, apart from reflection on reasons, apart from acceptance of a view after consideration, I know this, I see this: ‘With ignorance as condition, formations come to be.’”

“Aññatreva, āvuso nārada, saddhāya aññatra ruciyā aññatra anussavā aññatra ākāraparivitakkā aññatra diṭṭhinijjhānakkhantiyā atthāyasmato nāradassa paccattameva ñāṇaṃ – ‘jātinirodhā jarāmaraṇanirodho’”ti? “Aññatreva, āvuso paviṭṭha, saddhāya aññatra ruciyā aññatra anussavā aññatra ākāraparivitakkā aññatra diṭṭhinijjhānakkhantiyā ahametaṃ jānāmi ahametaṃ passāmi – ‘jātinirodhā jarāmaraṇanirodho’”ti.

“Friend Nārada, apart from faith, apart from inclination, apart from oral tradition, apart from reflection on reasons, apart from acceptance of a view after consideration, does the Venerable Nārada have personal knowledge thus: ‘With the cessation of birth, there is the cessation of aging and death’?” “Friend Paviṭṭha, apart from faith, apart from inclination, apart from oral tradition, apart from reflection on reasons, apart from acceptance of a view after consideration, I know this, I see this: ‘With the cessation of birth, there is the cessation of aging and death.’”

“Aññatreva, āvuso nārada, saddhāya aññatra ruciyā aññatra anussavā aññatra ākāraparivitakkā aññatra diṭṭhinijjhānakkhantiyā atthāyasmato nāradassa [M 1.0339] paccattameva ñāṇaṃ – ‘bhavanirodhā jātinirodhoti…pe… avijjānirodhā saṅkhāranirodho’”ti? “Aññatreva, āvuso paviṭṭha, saddhāya aññatra [T 2.0144] ruciyā aññatra anussavā aññatra ākāraparivitakkā aññatra diṭṭhinijjhānakkhantiyā ahametaṃ jānāmi ahametaṃ passāmi – ‘avijjānirodhā saṅkhāranirodho’”ti.

“Friend Nārada, apart from faith, apart from inclination, apart from oral tradition, apart from reflection on reasons, apart from acceptance of a view after consideration, does the Venerable Nārada have personal knowledge thus: ‘With the cessation of becoming, there is the cessation of birth… with the cessation of ignorance, there is the cessation of formations’?” “Friend Paviṭṭha, apart from faith, apart from inclination, apart from oral tradition, apart from reflection on reasons, apart from acceptance of a view after consideration, I know this, I see this: ‘With the cessation of ignorance, there is the cessation of formations.’”

“Aññatreva, āvuso nārada, saddhāya aññatra ruciyā aññatra anussavā aññatra ākāraparivitakkā aññatra diṭṭhinijjhānakkhantiyā atthāyasmato nāradassa paccattameva ñāṇaṃ – ‘bhavanirodho nibbāna’”nti? “Aññatreva, āvuso paviṭṭha, saddhāya aññatra ruciyā aññatra anussavā aññatra ākāraparivitakkā aññatra diṭṭhinijjhānakkhantiyā ahametaṃ jānāmi ahametaṃ passāmi – ‘bhavanirodho nibbāna’”nti.

“Friend Nārada, apart from faith, apart from inclination, apart from oral tradition, apart from reflection on reasons, apart from acceptance of a view after consideration, does the Venerable Nārada have personal knowledge thus: ‘The cessation of becoming is Nibbāna’?” “Friend Paviṭṭha, apart from faith, apart from inclination, apart from oral tradition, apart from reflection on reasons, apart from acceptance of a view after consideration, I know this, I see this: ‘The cessation of becoming is Nibbāna.’”

“Tenahāyasmā nārado arahaṃ khīṇāsavo”ti? “‘Bhavanirodho [P 2.0118] nibbāna’nti kho me, āvuso, yathābhūtaṃ sammappaññāya sudiṭṭhaṃ, na camhi arahaṃ khīṇāsavo. Seyyathāpi, āvuso, kantāramagge [V 1.0104] udapāno. Tatra nevassa rajju na udakavārako. Atha puriso āgaccheyya ghammābhitatto ghammapareto kilanto tasito pipāsito, so taṃ udapānaṃ olokeyya. Tassa ‘udaka’nti hi kho ñāṇaṃ assa, na ca kāyena phusitvā vihareyya. Evameva kho, āvuso, ‘bhavanirodho nibbāna’nti yathābhūtaṃ sammappaññāya sudiṭṭhaṃ, na camhi arahaṃ khīṇāsavo”ti.

“If that is so, Venerable Nārada, are you an Arahant, one whose taints are destroyed?” “Friend, ‘The cessation of becoming is Nibbāna’—this indeed has been well seen by me with right wisdom as it truly is, yet I am not an Arahant, one whose taints are destroyed. Suppose, friend, on a difficult path there were a well, but it had neither a rope nor a water pot. Then a man would come along, afflicted by heat, overcome by heat, weary, thirsty, and parched. He would look into that well. The knowledge ‘there is water’ would indeed arise for him, yet he would remain without having touched it with his body. In this very same way, friend, ‘The cessation of becoming is Nibbāna’—this has been well seen with right wisdom as it truly is, yet I am not an Arahant, one whose taints are destroyed.”

Evaṃ vutte, āyasmā ānando āyasmantaṃ paviṭṭhaṃ etadavoca – “evaṃvādī evaṃvādiṃ (?) tvaṃ, āvuso paviṭṭha, āyasmantaṃ nāradaṃ kiṃ vadesī”ti? “Evaṃvādāhaṃ, āvuso ānanda, āyasmantaṃ nāradaṃ na kiñci vadāmi aññatra kalyāṇā aññatra kusalā”ti. Aṭṭhamaṃ.

When this was said, the Venerable Ānanda said this to the Venerable Paviṭṭha: “Friend Paviṭṭha, you who hold such a view, what do you say to the Venerable Nārada?” “Friend Ānanda, holding such a view, I say nothing to the Venerable Nārada apart from what is good, apart from what is wholesome.” The eighth.

9. Upayantisuttaṃ

9. The Discourse on Increasing

69. Evaṃ me sutaṃ – ekaṃ samayaṃ bhagavā sāvatthiyaṃ viharati jetavane anāthapiṇḍikassa ārāme. Tatra kho…pe… “mahāsamuddo, bhikkhave, upayanto mahānadiyo upayāpeti, mahānadiyo upayantiyo kunnadiyo [M 1.0340] upayāpenti, kunnadiyo upayantiyo mahāsobbhe upayāpenti, mahāsobbhā [T 2.0145] upayantā kusobbhe upayāpenti. Evameva kho, bhikkhave, avijjā upayantī saṅkhāre upayāpeti, saṅkhārā upayantā viññāṇaṃ upayāpenti, viññāṇaṃ upayantaṃ nāmarūpaṃ upayāpeti, nāmarūpaṃ upayantaṃ saḷāyatanaṃ upayāpeti, saḷāyatanaṃ upayantaṃ phassaṃ upayāpeti, phasso upayanto vedanaṃ upayāpeti, vedanā upayantī taṇhaṃ upayāpeti, taṇhā upayantī upādānaṃ upayāpeti, upādānaṃ upayantaṃ bhavaṃ [P 2.0119] upayāpeti, bhavo upayanto jātiṃ upayāpeti, jāti upayantī jarāmaraṇaṃ upayāpeti.

69. Thus have I heard. On one occasion, the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s Park. There... “Bhikkhus, when the great ocean increases, it causes the great rivers to increase. When the great rivers increase, they cause the small rivers to increase. When the small rivers increase, they cause the great pools to increase. When the great pools increase, they cause the small pools to increase. In this very same way, bhikkhus, when ignorance increases, it causes formations to increase. When formations increase, they cause consciousness to increase. When consciousness increases, it causes name-and-form to increase. When name-and-form increases, it causes the six sense bases to increase. When the six sense bases increase, they cause contact to increase. When contact increases, it causes feeling to increase. When feeling increases, it causes craving to increase. When craving increases, it causes clinging to increase. When clinging increases, it causes becoming to increase. When becoming increases, it causes birth to increase. When birth increases, it causes aging-and-death to increase.

“Mahāsamuddo, bhikkhave, apayanto mahānadiyo apayāpeti, mahānadiyo apayantiyo kunnadiyo apayāpenti, kunnadiyo apayantiyo mahāsobbhe apayāpenti, mahāsobbhā apayantā kusobbhe apayāpenti. Evameva kho, bhikkhave, avijjā apayantī saṅkhāre apayāpeti, saṅkhārā apayantā viññāṇaṃ apayāpenti, viññāṇaṃ apayantaṃ nāmarūpaṃ apayāpeti, nāmarūpaṃ apayantaṃ saḷāyatanaṃ apayāpeti, saḷāyatanaṃ apayantaṃ phassaṃ apayāpeti, phasso apayanto vedanaṃ apayāpeti, vedanā apayantī taṇhaṃ apayāpeti, taṇhā apayantī upādānaṃ apayāpeti, upādānaṃ [V 1.0105] apayantaṃ bhavaṃ apayāpeti, bhavo apayanto jātiṃ apayāpeti, jāti apayantī jarāmaraṇaṃ apayāpetī”ti. Navamaṃ.

“Bhikkhus, when the great ocean declines, it causes the great rivers to decline. When the great rivers decline, they cause the small rivers to decline. When the small rivers decline, they cause the great pools to decline. When the great pools decline, they cause the small pools to decline. In this very same way, bhikkhus, when ignorance declines, it causes formations to decline. When formations decline, they cause consciousness to decline. When consciousness declines, it causes name-and-form to decline. When name-and-form declines, it causes the six sense bases to decline. When the six sense bases decline, they cause contact to decline. When contact declines, it causes feeling to decline. When feeling declines, it causes craving to decline. When craving declines, it causes clinging to decline. When clinging declines, it causes becoming to decline. When becoming declines, it causes birth to decline. When birth declines, it causes aging-and-death to decline.” The ninth.

10. Susimasuttaṃ

10. The Discourse on Susima

70. Evaṃ me sutaṃ – ekaṃ samayaṃ bhagavā rājagahe viharati veḷuvane [T 2.0146] kalandakanivāpe. Tena kho pana samayena bhagavā sakkato hoti garukato mānito pūjito apacito lābhī cīvara-piṇḍapāta-senāsana-gilānappaccaya-bhesajjaparikkhārānaṃ. Bhikkhusaṅghopi sakkato hoti garukato mānito pūjito apacito lābhī cīvara-piṇḍapāta-senāsanagilānappaccaya-bhesajjaparikkhārānaṃ. Aññatitthiyā pana paribbājakā asakkatā honti agarukatā amānitā apūjitā anapacitā, na lābhino cīvara-piṇḍapāta-senāsanagilānappaccaya-bhesajjaparikkhārānaṃ.

70. Thus have I heard. At one time the Blessed One was dwelling in Rājagaha, in the Veḷuvana, the Kalandakanivāpa. At that time, the Blessed One was respected, revered, esteemed, worshipped, and attended upon; he was a recipient of robes, alms-food, lodgings, and medicinal requisites for the sick. The community of monks was also respected, revered, esteemed, worshipped, and attended upon; it was a recipient of robes, alms-food, lodgings, and medicinal requisites for the sick. But the wanderers of other sects were not respected, not revered, not esteemed, not worshipped, and not attended upon; they were not recipients of robes, alms-food, lodgings, and medicinal requisites for the sick.

Tena [M 1.0341] kho pana samayena susimo susīmo (sī. ka.) paribbājako rājagahe paṭivasati mahatiyā paribbājakaparisāya saddhiṃ. Atha [P 2.0120] kho susimassa paribbājakassa parisā susimaṃ paribbājakaṃ etadavocuṃ – “ehi tvaṃ, āvuso susima, samaṇe gotame brahmacariyaṃ cara. Tvaṃ dhammaṃ pariyāpuṇitvā amhe vāceyyāsi vācessasi (pī. ka.). Taṃ mayaṃ dhammaṃ pariyāpuṇitvā gihīnaṃ bhāsissāma. Evaṃ mayampi sakkatā bhavissāma garukatā mānitā pūjitā apacitā lābhino cīvara-piṇḍapātasenāsana-gilānappaccaya-bhesajjaparikkhārāna”nti. “Evamāvuso”ti kho susimo paribbājako sakāya parisāya paṭissuṇitvā yenāyasmā ānando tenupasaṅkami; upasaṅkamitvā āyasmatā ānandena saddhiṃ sammodi. Sammodanīyaṃ kathaṃ sāraṇīyaṃ vītisāretvā ekamantaṃ nisīdi. Ekamantaṃ nisinno kho susimo paribbājako āyasmantaṃ ānandaṃ etadavoca – “icchāmahaṃ, āvuso ānanda, imasmiṃ dhammavinaye brahmacariyaṃ caritu”nti.

At that time, the wanderer Susīma was dwelling in Rājagaha together with a large assembly of wanderers. Then the assembly of the wanderer Susīma said this to the wanderer Susīma: 'Come, friend Susīma, practice the holy life under the ascetic Gotama. Having learned the Dhamma, you should teach it to us. We, having learned that Dhamma, will preach it to the householders. Thus, we too will be respected, revered, esteemed, worshipped, and attended upon; we will be recipients of robes, alms-food, lodgings, and medicinal requisites for the sick.' 'So be it, friends,' the wanderer Susīma replied, having agreed to his assembly. He then approached the Venerable Ānanda. Having approached, he exchanged courteous and memorable greetings with the Venerable Ānanda. Having concluded this talk, he sat down to one side. Seated to one side, the wanderer Susīma said this to the Venerable Ānanda: 'Friend Ānanda, I wish to practice the holy life in this Dhamma and Discipline.'

Atha [T 2.0147] kho āyasmā ānando susimaṃ paribbājakaṃ ādāya yena bhagavā tenupasaṅkami; upasaṅkamitvā bhagavantaṃ abhivādetvā ekamantaṃ nisīdi. Ekamantaṃ nisinno kho āyasmā ānando bhagavantaṃ etadavoca – “ayaṃ, bhante, susimo paribbājako evamāha – ‘icchāmahaṃ, āvuso ānanda, imasmiṃ dhammavinaye brahmacariyaṃ caritu”nti. “Tenahānanda, susimaṃ pabbājethā”ti[V 1.0106]. Alattha kho susimo paribbājako bhagavato santike pabbajjaṃ, alattha upasampadaṃ.

Then the Venerable Ānanda, taking the wanderer Susīma, approached the Blessed One. Having approached and paid homage to the Blessed One, he sat down to one side. Seated to one side, the Venerable Ānanda said this to the Blessed One: 'Venerable Sir, this wanderer Susīma says thus: “Friend Ānanda, I wish to practice the holy life in this Dhamma and Discipline.”' 'Then, Ānanda, give the going forth to Susīma.' The wanderer Susīma received the going forth in the presence of the Blessed One; he received the higher ordination.

Tena kho pana samayena sambahulehi bhikkhūhi bhagavato santike aññā byākatā hoti – “khīṇā jāti, vusitaṃ brahmacariyaṃ, kataṃ karaṇīyaṃ, nāparaṃ itthattāyāti pajānāmā”ti. Assosi kho āyasmā susimo – “sambahulehi kira bhikkhūhi [P 2.0121] bhagavato santike aññā byākatā – ‘khīṇā jāti, vusitaṃ brahmacariyaṃ, kataṃ karaṇīyaṃ, nāparaṃ itthattāyā’ti pajānāmā”ti. Atha kho āyasmā susimo yena te bhikkhū tenupasaṅkami; upasaṅkamitvā tehi bhikkhūhi saddhiṃ sammodi. Sammodanīyaṃ kathaṃ sāraṇīyaṃ vītisāretvā ekamantaṃ nisīdi. Ekamantaṃ nisinno kho āyasmā susimo te bhikkhū etadavoca – “saccaṃ kirāyasmantehi [M 1.0342] bhagavato santike aññā byākatā – ‘khīṇā jāti, vusitaṃ brahmacariyaṃ, kataṃ karaṇīyaṃ, nāparaṃ itthattāyā’ti pajānāmā”ti? “Evamāvuso”ti.

At that time, a number of monks had declared final knowledge in the presence of the Blessed One, saying: 'Birth is destroyed, the holy life has been lived, what was to be done has been done, there is nothing further for this state of being, we understand.' The Venerable Susīma heard: 'It is said that a number of monks have declared final knowledge in the presence of the Blessed One, saying: “Birth is destroyed, the holy life has been lived, what was to be done has been done, there is nothing further for this state of being, we understand.”' Then the Venerable Susīma approached those monks. Having approached, he exchanged courteous and memorable greetings with those monks. Having concluded this talk, he sat down to one side. Seated to one side, the Venerable Susīma said to those monks: 'Is it true, Venerable ones, as has been said, that you have declared final knowledge in the presence of the Blessed One, saying: “Birth is destroyed, the holy life has been lived, what was to be done has been done, there is nothing further for this state of being, we understand”?' 'So it is, friend.'

“Api pana api nu (sī. syā. kaṃ.) evamuparipi tumhe āyasmanto evaṃ jānantā evaṃ passantā [T 2.0148] anekavihitaṃ iddhividhaṃ paccanubhotha – ekopi hutvā bahudhā hotha, bahudhāpi hutvā eko hotha; āvibhāvaṃ, tirobhāvaṃ, tirokuṭṭaṃ tiropākāraṃ tiropabbataṃ asajjamānā gacchatha, seyyathāpi ākāse; pathaviyāpi ummujjanimujjaṃ karotha, seyyathāpi udake; udakepi abhijjamāne gacchatha, seyyathāpi pathaviyaṃ; ākāsepi pallaṅkena kamatha, seyyathāpi pakkhī sakuṇo; imepi candimasūriye evaṃmahiddhike evaṃmahānubhāve pāṇinā parimasatha parimajjatha, yāva brahmalokāpi kāyena vasaṃ vattethā”ti? “No hetaṃ, āvuso”.

“But, Venerable ones, knowing thus and seeing thus, do you experience the various kinds of psychic power: being one, do you become many; being many, do you become one; do you experience appearance and disappearance; do you go unhindered through a wall, a rampart, or a mountain as if through space; do you dive in and out of the earth as if in water; do you walk on water without it breaking as if on earth; do you travel cross-legged in the sky like a winged bird; do you touch and stroke with your hand these sun and moon, so mighty and powerful; do you exercise mastery with the body even as far as the Brahmā world?” “Not so, friend.”

“Api pana tumhe āyasmanto evaṃ jānantā evaṃ passantā dibbāya sotadhātuyā visuddhāya atikkantamānusikāya ubho sadde suṇātha dibbe ca mānuse ca ye dūre santike cā”ti? “No hetaṃ, āvuso”.

“But, Venerable ones, knowing thus and seeing thus, do you, with the divine ear-element, which is purified and surpasses the human, hear both kinds of sounds, divine and human, those that are far and near?” “Not so, friend.”

“Api pana tumhe āyasmanto evaṃ jānantā evaṃ passantā parasattānaṃ parapuggalānaṃ cetasā ceto paricca pajānātha – sarāgaṃ vā cittaṃ sarāgaṃ cittanti pajānātha; vītarāgaṃ vā cittaṃ vītarāgaṃ cittanti pajānātha; sadosaṃ vā cittaṃ sadosaṃ cittanti pajānātha; vītadosaṃ vā [V 1.0107] cittaṃ vītadosaṃ cittanti pajānātha; samohaṃ vā cittaṃ samohaṃ [P 2.0122] cittanti pajānātha; vītamohaṃ vā cittaṃ vītamohaṃ cittanti pajānātha; saṃkhittaṃ vā cittaṃ saṃkhittaṃ cittanti pajānātha; vikkhittaṃ vā cittaṃ vikkhittaṃ cittanti pajānātha; mahaggataṃ vā cittaṃ mahaggataṃ cittanti pajānātha; amahaggataṃ vā cittaṃ amahaggataṃ cittanti pajānātha[T 2.0149]; sauttaraṃ vā cittaṃ sauttaraṃ cittanti pajānātha; anuttaraṃ vā cittaṃ anuttaraṃ cittanti pajānātha; samāhitaṃ vā cittaṃ samāhitaṃ cittanti pajānātha; asamāhitaṃ vā cittaṃ asamāhitaṃ cittanti pajānātha; vimuttaṃ vā cittaṃ vimuttaṃ cittanti pajānātha[M 1.0343]; avimuttaṃ vā cittaṃ avimuttaṃ cittanti pajānāthā”ti? “No hetaṃ, āvuso”.

“But, Venerable ones, knowing thus and seeing thus, do you understand the minds of other beings and other individuals by encompassing mind with mind—knowing a mind with lust as a mind with lust; a mind without lust as a mind without lust; a mind with hatred as a mind with hatred; a mind without hatred as a mind without hatred; a mind with delusion as a mind with delusion; a mind without delusion as a mind without delusion; a constricted mind as a constricted mind; a scattered mind as a scattered mind; an exalted mind as an exalted mind; an unexalted mind as an unexalted mind; a surpassable mind as a surpassable mind; an unsurpassed mind as an unsurpassed mind; a concentrated mind as a concentrated mind; an unconcentrated mind as an unconcentrated mind; a liberated mind as a liberated mind; an unliberated mind as an unliberated mind?” “Not so, friend.”

“Api pana tumhe āyasmanto evaṃ jānantā evaṃ passantā anekavihitaṃ pubbenivāsaṃ anussaratha, seyyathidaṃ – ekampi jātiṃ dvepi jātiyo tissopi jātiyo catassopi jātiyo pañcapi jātiyo dasapi jātiyo vīsampi jātiyo tiṃsampi jātiyo cattārīsampi jātiyo paññāsampi jātiyo jātisatampi jātisahassampi jātisatasahassampi, anekepi saṃvaṭṭakappe anekepi vivaṭṭakappe anekepi saṃvaṭṭavivaṭṭakappe – ‘amutrāsiṃ evaṃnāmo evaṃgotto evaṃvaṇṇo evamāhāro evaṃsukhadukkhapaṭisaṃvedī evamāyupariyanto, so tato cuto amutra udapādiṃ; tatrāpāsiṃ evaṃnāmo evaṃgotto evaṃvaṇṇo evamāhāro evaṃsukhadukkhapaṭisaṃvedī evamāyupariyanto, so tato cuto idhūpapanno’ti. Iti sākāraṃ sauddesaṃ anekavihitaṃ pubbenivāsaṃ anussarathā”ti? “No hetaṃ, āvuso”.

“But, Venerable ones, knowing thus and seeing thus, do you recall your manifold past lives, such as one birth, two births, three births, four births, five births, ten births, twenty births, thirty births, forty births, fifty births, a hundred births, a thousand births, a hundred thousand births; many eons of contraction, many eons of expansion, many eons of contraction and expansion, thinking, ‘There, I was of such a name, such a clan, such an appearance, such food, such an experience of pleasure and pain, with such a lifespan. Passing away from there, I arose elsewhere. There too, I was of such a name, such a clan, such an appearance, such food, such an experience of pleasure and pain, with such a lifespan. Passing away from there, I have arisen here.’ Thus, with its aspects and details, do you recall your manifold past lives?” “Not so, friend.”

“Api pana tumhe āyasmanto evaṃ jānantā evaṃ passantā dibbena cakkhunā visuddhena atikkantamānusakena satte passatha cavamāne upapajjamāne [T 2.0150] hīne paṇīte suvaṇṇe dubbaṇṇe, sugate duggate yathākammūpage satte pajānātha – ‘ime vata bhonto sattā kāyaduccaritena samannāgatā [P 2.0123] vacīduccaritena samannāgatā manoduccaritena samannāgatā, ariyānaṃ upavādakā micchādiṭṭhikā micchādiṭṭhikammasamādānā, te kāyassa bhedā paraṃ maraṇā apāyaṃ duggatiṃ vinipātaṃ nirayaṃ upapannā; ime vā pana bhonto sattā kāyasucaritena samannāgatā vacīsucaritena samannāgatā manosucaritena samannāgatā, ariyānaṃ anupavādakā sammādiṭṭhikā sammādiṭṭhikammasamādānā te kāyassa bhedā paraṃ maraṇā sugatiṃ saggaṃ lokaṃ upapannā’ti, iti dibbena cakkhunā visuddhena atikkantamānusakena satte passatha cavamāne upapajjamāne hīne paṇīte [V 1.0108] suvaṇṇe dubbaṇṇe, sugate duggate yathākammūpage satte pajānāthā”ti? “No hetaṃ, āvuso”.

“Furthermore, venerables, knowing thus and seeing thus, do you, with the divine eye which is purified and surpasses the human, see beings passing away and being reborn—inferior and superior, beautiful and ugly, fortunate and unfortunate—and do you understand beings faring according to their kamma thus: ‘Indeed, sirs, these beings were endowed with misconduct of body, speech, and mind, were revilers of the noble ones, held wrong view, and undertook actions based on wrong view. They, with the breakup of the body, after death, have been reborn in a state of loss, a bad destination, the abyss, in hell. Or indeed, sirs, these beings were endowed with good conduct of body, speech, and mind, were not revilers of the noble ones, held right view, and undertook actions based on right view. They, with the breakup of the body, after death, have been reborn in a good destination, in the heavenly world’? Thus, with the divine eye which is purified and surpasses the human, do you see beings passing away and being reborn—inferior and superior, beautiful and ugly, fortunate and unfortunate—and do you understand beings faring according to their kamma?” “Not so, friend.”

“Api pana tumhe āyasmanto evaṃ jānantā evaṃ passantā ye te santā vimokkhā atikkamma rūpe āruppā, te kāyena phusitvā viharathā”ti? “No hetaṃ, āvuso”.

“Furthermore, venerables, knowing thus and seeing thus, do you dwell having touched with the body those peaceful, formless liberations that transcend form?” “Not so, friend.”

“Ettha [M 1.0344] dāni āyasmanto idañca veyyākaraṇaṃ imesañca dhammānaṃ asamāpatti; idaṃ no, āvuso, katha”nti? “Paññāvimuttā kho mayaṃ, āvuso susimā”ti.

“Now, venerables, there is this explanation on the one hand, and the non-attainment of these states on the other. How can this be, friend?” “We are liberated by wisdom, friend Susīma.”

“Na khvāhaṃ imassa āyasmantānaṃ saṃkhittena bhāsitassa vitthārena atthaṃ ājānāmi. Sādhu me āyasmanto tathā bhāsantu yathāhaṃ imassa āyasmantānaṃ saṃkhittena bhāsitassa [T 2.0151] vitthārena atthaṃ ājāneyya”nti. “Ājāneyyāsi [P 2.0124] vā tvaṃ, āvuso susima, na vā tvaṃ ājāneyyāsi atha kho paññāvimuttā maya”nti.

“I do not understand in detail the meaning of what the venerables have said in brief. It would be good if the venerables would speak in such a way that I might understand in detail the meaning of what they have said in brief.” “Whether you understand it, friend Susīma, or whether you do not, we are nevertheless liberated by wisdom.”

Atha kho āyasmā susimo uṭṭhāyāsanā yena bhagavā tenupasaṅkami; upasaṅkamitvā bhagavantaṃ abhivādetvā ekamantaṃ nisīdi. Ekamantaṃ nisinno kho āyasmā susimo yāvatako tehi bhikkhūhi saddhiṃ ahosi kathāsallāpo taṃ sabbaṃ bhagavato ārocesi. “Pubbe kho, susima, dhammaṭṭhitiñāṇaṃ, pacchā nibbāne ñāṇa”nti.

Then the Venerable Susīma rose from his seat, approached the Blessed One, paid homage to him, and sat down to one side. Having sat down to one side, the Venerable Susīma reported to the Blessed One the entire conversation he had with those monks. The Blessed One said: “First, Susīma, comes the knowledge of the stability of phenomena, and afterwards, the knowledge of Nibbāna.”

“Na khvāhaṃ, bhante, imassa bhagavatā bhagavato (pī.) saṃkhittena bhāsitassa vitthārena atthaṃ ājānāmi. Sādhu me, bhante, bhagavā tathā bhāsatu yathāhaṃ imassa bhagavatā saṃkhittena bhāsitassa vitthārena atthaṃ ājāneyya”nti. “Ājāneyyāsi vā tvaṃ, susima, na vā tvaṃ ājāneyyāsi, atha kho dhammaṭṭhitiñāṇaṃ pubbe, pacchā nibbāne ñāṇaṃ”.

“Venerable sir, I do not understand in detail the meaning of this brief statement spoken by the Blessed One. It would be good if the Blessed One would speak in such a way that I might understand in detail the meaning of this brief statement spoken by the Blessed One.” “Whether you understand it, Susīma, or whether you do not, first comes the knowledge of the stability of phenomena, and afterwards, the knowledge of Nibbāna.”

“Taṃ kiṃ maññasi, susima, rūpaṃ niccaṃ vā aniccaṃ vā”ti? “Aniccaṃ, bhante”. “Yaṃ panāniccaṃ dukkhaṃ vā taṃ sukhaṃ vā”ti? “Dukkhaṃ, bhante”. “Yaṃ panāniccaṃ dukkhaṃ vipariṇāmadhammaṃ, kallaṃ nu taṃ samanupassituṃ – ‘etaṃ mama, esohamasmi, eso me attā’”ti? “No hetaṃ, bhante”. “Vedanā niccā vā aniccā vā”ti? “Aniccā, bhante”[V 1.0109]. “Yaṃ panāniccaṃ, dukkhaṃ vā taṃ sukhaṃ vā”ti? “Dukkhaṃ, bhante”. “Yaṃ panāniccaṃ dukkhaṃ vipariṇāmadhammaṃ, kallaṃ nu taṃ samanupassituṃ – ‘etaṃ mama, esohamasmi, eso [T 2.0152] me attā’”ti? “No hetaṃ, bhante”. “Saññā niccā vā aniccā vā”ti? “Aniccā, bhante”…pe… “saṅkhārā niccā vā aniccā vā”ti? “Aniccā, bhante”. “Yaṃ panāniccaṃ dukkhaṃ vā taṃ sukhaṃ vā”ti? “Dukkhaṃ, bhante”. “Yaṃ panāniccaṃ dukkhaṃ vipariṇāmadhammaṃ, kallaṃ nu taṃ samanupassituṃ – ‘etaṃ mama, esohamasmi, eso me attā’”ti? “No hetaṃ, bhante”. “Viññāṇaṃ niccaṃ vā aniccaṃ vā”ti? “Aniccaṃ[P 2.0125], bhante”. “Yaṃ panāniccaṃ [M 1.0345] dukkhaṃ vā taṃ sukhaṃ vā”ti? “Dukkhaṃ, bhante”. “Yaṃ panāniccaṃ dukkhaṃ vipariṇāmadhammaṃ, kallaṃ nu taṃ samanupassituṃ – ‘etaṃ mama, esohamasmi, eso me attā’”ti? “No hetaṃ, bhante”.

“What do you think, Susīma, is form permanent or impermanent?” “Impermanent, venerable sir.” “And that which is impermanent, is it suffering or happiness?” “Suffering, venerable sir.” “And that which is impermanent, suffering, and subject to change, is it fitting to regard it thus: ‘This is mine, this I am, this is my self’?” “Certainly not, venerable sir.” “Is feeling permanent or impermanent?” “Impermanent, venerable sir.” “And that which is impermanent, is it suffering or happiness?” “Suffering, venerable sir.” “And that which is impermanent, suffering, and subject to change, is it fitting to regard it thus: ‘This is mine, this I am, this is my self’?” “Certainly not, venerable sir.” “Is perception permanent or impermanent?” “Impermanent, venerable sir.” … “Are formations permanent or impermanent?” “Impermanent, venerable sir.” “And that which is impermanent, is it suffering or happiness?” “Suffering, venerable sir.” “And that which is impermanent, suffering, and subject to change, is it fitting to regard it thus: ‘This is mine, this I am, this is my self’?” “Certainly not, venerable sir.” “Is consciousness permanent or impermanent?” “Impermanent, venerable sir.” “And that which is impermanent, is it suffering or happiness?” “Suffering, venerable sir.” “And that which is impermanent, suffering, and subject to change, is it fitting to regard it thus: ‘This is mine, this I am, this is my self’?” “Certainly not, venerable sir.”

“Tasmātiha, susima, yaṃ kiñci rūpaṃ atītānāgatapaccuppannaṃ ajjhattaṃ vā bahiddhā vā oḷārikaṃ vā sukhumaṃ vā hīnaṃ vā paṇītaṃ vā yaṃ dūre santike vā, sabbaṃ rūpaṃ netaṃ mama nesohamasmi na meso attāti; evametaṃ yathābhūtaṃ sammappaññāya daṭṭhabbaṃ. Yā kāci vedanā atītānāgatapaccuppannā ajjhattaṃ vā bahiddhā vā oḷārikā vā sukhumā vā hīnā vā paṇītā vā yā dūre santike vā, sabbā vedanā netaṃ mama nesohamasmi na meso attāti; evametaṃ yathābhūtaṃ sammappaññāya daṭṭhabbaṃ. Yā kāci saññā…pe… ye keci saṅkhārā atītānāgatapaccuppannā ajjhattaṃ vā bahiddhā vā oḷārikā vā sukhumā vā hīnā vā paṇītā vā ye dūre santike vā, sabbe saṅkhārā netaṃ mama nesohamasmi na [T 2.0153] meso attāti; evametaṃ yathābhūtaṃ sammappaññāya daṭṭhabbaṃ. Yaṃ kiñci viññāṇaṃ atītānāgatapaccuppannaṃ ajjhattaṃ vā bahiddhā vā oḷārikaṃ vā sukhumaṃ vā hīnaṃ vā paṇītaṃ vā yaṃ dūre santike vā, sabbaṃ viññāṇaṃ netaṃ mama nesohamasmi na meso attāti; evametaṃ yathābhūtaṃ sammappaññāya daṭṭhabbaṃ.

“Therefore, Susima, whatever form there is, whether past, future, or present; internal or external; gross or subtle; inferior or superior; far or near—all form should be seen as it really is with right wisdom thus: ‘This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self.’ Whatever feeling there is, whether past, future, or present; internal or external; gross or subtle; inferior or superior; far or near—all feeling should be seen as it really is with right wisdom thus: ‘This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self.’ Whatever perception there is… Whatever formations there are, whether past, future, or present; internal or external; gross or subtle; inferior or superior; far or near—all formations should be seen as they really are with right wisdom thus: ‘This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self.’ Whatever consciousness there is, whether past, future, or present; internal or external; gross or subtle; inferior or superior; far or near—all consciousness should be seen as it really is with right wisdom thus: ‘This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self.’”

“Evaṃ passaṃ, susima, sutavā ariyasāvako rūpasmimpi nibbindati, vedanāyapi nibbindati, saññāyapi nibbindati, saṅkhāresupi nibbindati, viññāṇasmimpi nibbindati. Nibbindaṃ virajjati, virāgā vimuccati, vimuttasmiṃ vimuttamiti ñāṇaṃ hoti. ‘Khīṇā jāti, vusitaṃ brahmacariyaṃ, kataṃ karaṇīyaṃ, nāparaṃ itthattāyā’ti pajānāti.

“Seeing thus, Susima, the learned noble disciple becomes disenchanted with form, disenchanted with feeling, disenchanted with perception, disenchanted with formations, and disenchanted with consciousness. Being disenchanted, he becomes dispassionate. Through dispassion, he is liberated. When liberated, the knowledge arises: ‘I am liberated.’ He understands: ‘Birth is destroyed, the holy life has been lived, what had to be done has been done, there is nothing further for this state of being.’”

“‘Jātipaccayā [V 1.0110] jarāmaraṇa’nti, susima, passasī”ti? “Evaṃ, bhante”. “‘Bhavapaccayā jātī’ti, susima, passasī”ti? “Evaṃ, bhante”. “‘Upādānapaccayā bhavo’ti, susima, passasī”ti? “Evaṃ, bhante”. “‘Taṇhāpaccayā [P 2.0126] upādāna’nti, susima, passasī”ti? “Evaṃ, bhante”. “Vedanāpaccayā taṇhāti… phassapaccayā vedanāti… saḷāyatanapaccayā phassoti… nāmarūpapaccayā saḷāyatananti… viññāṇapaccayā nāmarūpanti… saṅkhārapaccayā viññāṇanti… avijjāpaccayā saṅkhārāti, susima, passasī”ti? “Evaṃ, bhante”.

“Susima, do you see that ‘aging and death are conditioned by birth’?” “Yes, venerable sir.” “Susima, do you see that ‘birth is conditioned by becoming’?” “Yes, venerable sir.” “Susima, do you see that ‘becoming is conditioned by clinging’?” “Yes, venerable sir.” “Susima, do you see that ‘clinging is conditioned by craving’?” “Yes, venerable sir.” “That ‘craving is conditioned by feeling’… that ‘feeling is conditioned by contact’… that ‘contact is conditioned by the six sense bases’… that ‘the six sense bases are conditioned by name-and-form’… that ‘name-and-form is conditioned by consciousness’… that ‘consciousness is conditioned by formations’… Susima, do you see that ‘formations are conditioned by ignorance’?” “Yes, venerable sir.”

“‘Jātinirodhā [M 1.0346] jarāmaraṇanirodho’ti, susima, passasī”ti? “Evaṃ, bhante”[T 2.0154]. “‘Bhavanirodhā jātinirodho’ti susima, passasī”ti? “Evaṃ, bhante”. “Upādānanirodhā bhavanirodhoti… taṇhānirodhā upādānanirodhoti… vedanānirodhā taṇhānirodhoti… phassanirodhā vedanānirodhoti… saḷāyatananirodhā phassanirodhoti… nāmarūpanirodhā saḷāyatananirodhoti… viññāṇanirodhā nāmarūpanirodhoti… saṅkhāranirodhā viññāṇanirodhoti… avijjānirodhā saṅkhāranirodhoti, susima, passasī”ti? “Evaṃ, bhante”.

“Susima, do you see that ‘with the cessation of birth, there is the cessation of aging and death’?” “Yes, venerable sir.” “Susima, do you see that ‘with the cessation of becoming, there is the cessation of birth’?” “Yes, venerable sir.” “That ‘with the cessation of clinging, there is the cessation of becoming’… that ‘with the cessation of craving, there is the cessation of clinging’… that ‘with the cessation of feeling, there is the cessation of craving’… that ‘with the cessation of contact, there is the cessation of feeling’… that ‘with the cessation of the six sense bases, there is the cessation of contact’… that ‘with the cessation of name-and-form, there is the cessation of the six sense bases’… that ‘with the cessation of consciousness, there is the cessation of name-and-form’… that ‘with the cessation of formations, there is the cessation of consciousness’… Susima, do you see that ‘with the cessation of ignorance, there is the cessation of formations’?” “Yes, venerable sir.”

“Api pana tvaṃ, susima, evaṃ jānanto evaṃ passanto anekavihitaṃ iddhividhaṃ paccanubhosi – ekopi hutvā bahudhā hosi, bahudhāpi hutvā eko hosi; āvibhāvaṃ, tirobhāvaṃ, tirokuṭṭaṃ tiropākāraṃ tiropabbataṃ asajjamāno gacchasi, seyyathāpi ākāse; pathaviyāpi ummujjanimujjaṃ karosi, seyyathāpi udake; udakepi abhijjamāno gacchasi, seyyathāpi pathaviyaṃ; ākāsepi pallaṅkena kamasi, seyyathāpi pakkhī sakuṇo; imepi candimasūriye evaṃmahiddhike evaṃmahānubhāve pāṇinā parimasasi parimajjasi, yāva brahmalokāpi kāyena vasaṃ vattesī”ti? “No hetaṃ, bhante”.

“But, Susima, knowing thus and seeing thus, do you experience the various kinds of psychic power: having been one, you become many; having been many, you become one; you appear and disappear; you go unhindered through a wall, a rampart, or a mountain as if through space; you dive in and out of the earth as if in water; you walk on water without it breaking apart as if on earth; you travel cross-legged in the sky like a winged bird; you touch and stroke with your hand these sun and moon, so mighty and powerful; and you wield mastery with your body even up to the Brahmā world?” “That is not so, venerable sir.”

“Api pana tvaṃ, susima, evaṃ jānanto evaṃ passanto dibbāya sotadhātuyā visuddhāya atikkantamānusikāya ubho sadde suṇasi dibbe ca mānuse ca ye dūre santike cā”ti? “No [P 2.0127] hetaṃ, bhante”.

“But Susima, knowing thus and seeing thus, do you hear with the divine ear element, purified and surpassing the human, both kinds of sounds, divine and human, whether far or near?” “That is not so, venerable sir.”

“Api [T 2.0155] pana tvaṃ, susima, evaṃ jānanto evaṃ passanto parasattānaṃ parapuggalānaṃ cetasā ceto [V 1.0111] paricca pajānāsi – sarāgaṃ vā cittaṃ sarāgaṃ cittanti pajānāsi…pe… vimuttaṃ vā cittaṃ vimuttaṃ cittanti pajānāsī”ti? “No hetaṃ, bhante”.

“But, Susima, knowing thus and seeing thus, do you, having encompassed with your own mind the minds of other beings, other persons, know them? Do you know a mind with lust as ‘a mind with lust’… a liberated mind as ‘a liberated mind’?” “That is not so, venerable sir.”

“Api pana tvaṃ, susima, evaṃ jānanto evaṃ passanto anekavihitaṃ pubbenivāsaṃ anussarasi, seyyathidaṃ – ekampi jātiṃ…pe… iti sākāraṃ sauddesaṃ anekavihitaṃ pubbenivāsaṃ anussarasī”ti? “No hetaṃ, bhante”.

“But, Susima, knowing thus and seeing thus, do you recollect your manifold past abodes, that is to say, one birth… thus, do you recollect your manifold past abodes with their aspects and details?” “That is not so, venerable sir.”

“Api pana tvaṃ, susima, evaṃ jānanto evaṃ passanto dibbena cakkhunā visuddhena atikkantamānusakena satte passasi cavamāne…pe… yathākammūpage satte pajānāsī”ti? “No hetaṃ, bhante”.

“But, Susima, knowing thus and seeing thus, with the divine eye, purified and surpassing the human, do you see beings passing away… do you know beings faring on according to their kamma?” “That is not so, venerable sir.”

“Api [M 1.0347] pana tvaṃ, susima, evaṃ jānanto evaṃ passanto ye te santā vimokkhā atikkamma rūpe, āruppā te kāyena phusitvā viharasī”ti? “No hetaṃ, bhante”.

“But, Susima, knowing thus and seeing thus, do you dwell having touched with the body those peaceful liberations which, transcending form, are the formless attainments?” “That is not so, venerable sir.”

“Ettha dāni, susima, idañca veyyākaraṇaṃ imesañca dhammānaṃ asamāpatti, idaṃ no, susima, katha”nti?

“Now, Susima, there is this declaration, and also the non-attainment of these states. How can this be, Susima?”

Atha kho āyasmā susimo bhagavato pādesu sirasā nipatitvā bhagavantaṃ etadavoca – “accayo maṃ, bhante, accagamā yathābālaṃ yathāmūḷhaṃ yathāakusalaṃ, yvāhaṃ evaṃ svākkhāte dhammavinaye dhammatthenako pabbajito. Tassa me, bhante, bhagavā accayaṃ accayato paṭiggaṇhātu āyatiṃ saṃvarāyā”ti.

Then the Venerable Susima, falling with his head at the feet of the Blessed One, said this to the Blessed One: “A transgression overcame me, venerable sir, according to my foolishness, my bewilderment, and my unskillfulness, in that I went forth as a thief of the Dhamma in this well-proclaimed Dhamma and Discipline. May the Blessed One accept my transgression as a transgression, for the sake of restraint in the future.”

“Taggha [T 2.0156] tvaṃ, susima, accayo accagamā yathābālaṃ yathāmūḷhaṃ yathāakusalaṃ, yo tvaṃ evaṃ svākkhāte dhammavinaye dhammatthenako pabbajito. Seyyathāpi[P 2.0128], susima, coraṃ āgucāriṃ gahetvā rañño dasseyyuṃ – ‘ayaṃ te, deva, coro āgucārī, imassa yaṃ icchasi taṃ daṇḍaṃ paṇehī’ti. Tamenaṃ rājā evaṃ vadeyya – ‘gacchatha, bho, imaṃ purisaṃ daḷhāya rajjuyā pacchābāhaṃ gāḷhabandhanaṃ bandhitvā khuramuṇḍaṃ karitvā kharassarena paṇavena rathiyāya rathiyaṃ siṅghāṭakena siṅghāṭakaṃ parinetvā dakkhiṇena dvārena nikkhāmetvā dakkhiṇato nagarassa sīsaṃ chindathā’ti[V 1.0112]. Tamenaṃ rañño purisā daḷhāya rajjuyā pacchābāhaṃ gāḷhabandhanaṃ bandhitvā khuramuṇḍaṃ karitvā kharassarena paṇavena rathiyāya rathiyaṃ siṅghāṭakena siṅghāṭakaṃ parinetvā dakkhiṇena dvārena nikkhāmetvā dakkhiṇato nagarassa sīsaṃ chindeyyuṃ. Taṃ kiṃ maññasi, susima, api nu so puriso tatonidānaṃ dukkhaṃ domanassaṃ paṭisaṃvediyethā”ti? “Evaṃ, bhante”.

“Indeed, Susima, a transgression overcame you, according to your foolishness, your bewilderment, and your unskillfulness, in that you went forth as a thief of the Dhamma in this well-proclaimed Dhamma and Discipline. Suppose, Susima, they were to seize a thief, a wrongdoer, and bring him before the king, saying: ‘Your majesty, this is a thief, a wrongdoer. Impose upon him whatever punishment you wish.’ The king would say: ‘Go, sirs, and bind this man’s arms tightly behind his back with a strong rope, shave his head with a razor, and lead him around from street to street, from crossroads to crossroads, with a harsh-sounding drum. Then take him out through the southern gate and cut off his head south of the city.’ The king’s men would then bind his arms tightly behind his back with a strong rope, shave his head with a razor, and lead him around from street to street, from crossroads to crossroads, with a harsh-sounding drum. Then they would take him out through the southern gate and cut off his head south of the city. What do you think, Susima, would that man experience pain and displeasure on account of that?” “Yes, venerable sir.”

“Yaṃ kho so, susima, puriso tatonidānaṃ dukkhaṃ domanassaṃ paṭisaṃvediyetha paṭisaṃvediyetha vā, na vā paṭisaṃvediyetha (ka.). Yā evaṃ svākkhāte dhammavinaye dhammatthenakassa pabbajjā, ayaṃ tato dukkhavipākatarā ca kaṭukavipākatarā ca, api ca vinipātāya saṃvattati. Yato ca kho tvaṃ, susima, accayaṃ accayato disvā yathādhammaṃ paṭikarosi taṃ te mayaṃ paṭiggaṇhāma. Vuddhi hesā, susima, ariyassa vinaye [M 1.0348] yo accayaṃ accayato disvā yathādhammaṃ [T 2.0157] paṭikaroti, āyatiñca āyatiṃ (syā. kaṃ.) saṃvaraṃ āpajjatī”ti. Dasamaṃ.

“Susima, whatever pain and displeasure that man would experience on account of that, the going forth as a thief of the Dhamma in this well-proclaimed Dhamma and Discipline has a result that is more painful and more bitter than that, and indeed, it leads to ruin. But because, Susima, you have seen your transgression as a transgression and make amends according to the Dhamma, we accept that of you. For this is growth in the Noble One’s Discipline: that one sees a transgression as a transgression, makes amends according to the Dhamma, and undertakes restraint for the future.”

Mahāvaggo sattamo.

The Great Chapter, the seventh.

Tassuddānaṃ –

The summary of it:

Dve assutavatā vuttā, puttamaṃsena cāparaṃ;

Atthirāgo ca nagaraṃ, sammasaṃ naḷakalāpiyaṃ;

Kosambī upayanti ca, dasamo susimena cāti dasamo vutto susīmenāti (sī.).

Two on the uninstructed were spoken, and another on a son's flesh; With-lust and the city, pondering, the bundle of reeds; Kosambī and approaching, and the tenth with Susīma.

8. Samaṇabrāhmaṇavaggo

8. The Chapter on Ascetics and Brahmins

1. Jarāmaraṇasuttaṃ

1. The Discourse on Aging and Death

71. Evaṃ [T 2.0158][P 2.0129] me sutaṃ – ekaṃ samayaṃ bhagavā sāvatthiyaṃ viharati jetavane anāthapiṇḍikassa ārāme. Tatra kho bhagavā…pe… “ye hi keci, bhikkhave[V 1.0113], samaṇā vā brāhmaṇā vā jarāmaraṇaṃ nappajānanti, jarāmaraṇasamudayaṃ nappajānanti, jarāmaraṇanirodhaṃ nappajānanti, jarāmaraṇanirodhagāminiṃ paṭipadaṃ nappajānanti, na me te, bhikkhave, samaṇā vā brāhmaṇā vā samaṇesu vā samaṇasammatā brāhmaṇesu vā brāhmaṇasammatā, na ca pana te āyasmanto sāmaññatthaṃ vā brahmaññatthaṃ vā diṭṭheva dhamme sayaṃ abhiññā sacchikatvā upasampajja viharanti.

71. Thus have I heard. At one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s Park. There the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus thus: “Bhikkhus, whatever ascetics or brahmins do not understand aging and death, do not understand the origin of aging and death, do not understand the cessation of aging and death, do not understand the path leading to the cessation of aging and death—these, bhikkhus, are not considered by me as ascetics among ascetics or brahmins among brahmins. Nor do those venerable ones, having realized it for themselves with direct knowledge, in this very life, enter upon and dwell in the state of asceticism or the state of brahminhood.

“Ye ca kho keci, bhikkhave, samaṇā vā brāhmaṇā vā jarāmaraṇaṃ pajānanti…pe… paṭipadaṃ pajānanti, te kho me, bhikkhave, samaṇā vā brāhmaṇā vā samaṇesu ceva samaṇasammatā brāhmaṇesu ca brāhmaṇasammatā, te ca panāyasmanto sāmaññatthañca brahmaññatthañca diṭṭheva dhamme sayaṃ abhiññā sacchikatvā upasampajja viharantī”ti. (Suttanto eko). Paṭhamaṃ.

“But, bhikkhus, whatever ascetics or brahmins understand aging and death… understand the path leading to the cessation of aging and death—these, bhikkhus, are considered by me as ascetics among ascetics and brahmins among brahmins. And those venerable ones, having realized it for themselves with direct knowledge, in this very life, enter upon and dwell in the state of asceticism and the state of brahminhood.” (This is one discourse.) The first.

2-11. Jātisuttādidasakaṃ

2–11. The Decade Beginning with the Discourse on Birth

72. Sāvatthiyaṃ [M 1.0349] viharati…pe… jātiṃ nappajānanti…pe….

72. At Sāvatthī… They do not understand birth…

(3) Bhavaṃ nappajānanti…pe….

(3) They do not understand existence…

(4) Upādānaṃ nappajānanti…pe….

(4) They do not understand clinging…

(5) Taṇhaṃ nappajānanti…pe….

(5) They do not understand craving…

(6) Vedanaṃ nappajānanti…pe….

(6) They do not understand feeling…

(7) Phassaṃ [V 1.0114] nappajānanti…pe….

(7) They do not understand contact…

(8) Saḷāyatanaṃ nappajānanti…pe….

(8) They do not understand the six sense bases…

(9) Nāmarūpaṃ [T 2.0159] nappajānanti…pe….

(9) They do not understand name-and-form…

(10) Viññāṇaṃ nappajānanti…pe….

(10) They do not understand consciousness…

(11) “Saṅkhāre [P 2.0130] nappajānanti, saṅkhārasamudayaṃ nappajānanti, saṅkhāranirodhaṃ nappajānanti, saṅkhāranirodhagāminiṃ paṭipadaṃ nappajānanti…pe… saṅkhāre pajānanti…pe… sayaṃ abhiññā sacchikatvā upasampajja viharantī”ti. Ekādasamaṃ.

(11) “They do not understand formations, they do not understand the origin of formations, they do not understand the cessation of formations, they do not understand the path leading to the cessation of formations… …they understand formations… …having realized it for themselves with direct knowledge, in this very life, enter upon and dwell in the state of asceticism and the state of brahminhood.” The eleventh.

Samaṇabrāhmaṇavaggo aṭṭhamo.

The Chapter on Ascetics and Brahmins is the eighth.

Tassuddānaṃ –

The summary of this chapter:

Paccayekādasa vuttā, catusaccavibhajjanā;

Samaṇabrāhmaṇavaggo, nidāne bhavati aṭṭhamo.

Eleven suttas on the conditions were taught, an analysis of the Four Truths; the Chapter on Ascetics and Brahmins is the eighth in the Nidāna Vagga.

Vagguddānaṃ –

The summary of the chapters:

Buddho āhāro dasabalo, kaḷāro gahapatipañcamo;

Dukkhavaggo mahāvaggo, aṭṭhamo samaṇabrāhmaṇoti.

The Buddha, Āhāra, Dasabala, Kaḷāra, and Gahapati as the fifth; the Dukkha Vagga, the Mahā Vagga, and the eighth is the Samaṇabrāhmaṇa.

1. The Discourse on the Teacher

73. Sāvatthiyaṃ [T 2.0160][V 1.0115] viharati…pe… “jarāmaraṇaṃ, bhikkhave, ajānatā apassatā yathābhūtaṃ jarāmaraṇe yathābhūtaṃ ñāṇāya satthā pariyesitabbo; jarāmaraṇasamudayaṃ ajānatā apassatā yathābhūtaṃ jarāmaraṇasamudaye yathābhūtaṃ [M 1.0350] ñāṇāya satthā pariyesitabbo; jarāmaraṇanirodhaṃ ajānatā apassatā yathābhūtaṃ jarāmaraṇanirodhe yathābhūtaṃ ñāṇāya satthā pariyesitabbo; jarāmaraṇanirodhagāminiṃ paṭipadaṃ ajānatā apassatā yathābhūtaṃ jarāmaraṇanirodhagāminiyā paṭipadāya yathābhūtaṃ ñāṇāya satthā pariyesitabbo”ti. (Suttanto eko). Paṭhamaṃ.

73. At Sāvatthī... “Bhikkhus, for one who does not know and see aging and death as it really is, a teacher should be sought for true knowledge of aging and death as it really is. For one who does not know and see the origin of aging and death as it really is, a teacher should be sought for true knowledge of the origin of aging and death as it really is. For one who does not know and see the cessation of aging and death as it really is, a teacher should be sought for true knowledge of the cessation of aging and death as it really is. For one who does not know and see the path leading to the cessation of aging and death as it really is, a teacher should be sought for true knowledge of the path leading to the cessation of aging and death as it really is.” (One discourse.) The first.

(Sabbesaṃ peyyālo evaṃ vitthāretabbo)

The elision section for all should be elaborated in this way.

Antarapeyyālo navamo.

The ninth intermediate repetition section.

Tassuddānaṃ –

The summary verse for that:

Satthā sikkhā ca yogo ca, chando ussoḷhipañcamī;

Appaṭivāni ātappaṃ, vīriyaṃ [P 2.0133] sātaccamuccati;

Sati ca sampajaññañca, appamādena dvādasāti.

The Teacher, Training, and Effort, Zeal, with Exertion as the fifth; Non-retreat, Ardor, Energy, and Persistence are spoken of; Mindfulness and Clear Comprehension, and with Heedfulness make twelve.

Suttantā antarapeyyālā niṭṭhitā.

The suttas of the intermediate repetition section are concluded.

Pare [V 1.0118] te dvādasa honti, suttā dvattiṃsa satāni;

Catusaccena te vuttā, peyyālaantaramhi yeti peyyālā antaramhi yeti (sī. syā. kaṃ.).

There are those other twelve, and one hundred and thirty-two suttas. Those which are within the repetition section are spoken in terms of the Four Truths.

Antarapeyyālesu uddānaṃ samattaṃ.

The summary verse for the intermediate repetitions is complete.

Nidānasaṃyuttaṃ samattaṃ.

The Connected Discourses on Causation is complete.

2. Abhisamayasaṃyuttaṃ

2. 2. The Connected Discourses on Realization

1. Nakhasikhāsuttaṃ

1. 1. The Fingernail Sutta

74. Evaṃ [T 2.0162][V 1.0119][M 1.0352] me sutaṃ – ekaṃ samayaṃ bhagavā sāvatthiyaṃ viharati jetavane anāthapiṇḍikassa ārāme. Atha kho bhagavā parittaṃ nakhasikhāyaṃ paṃsuṃ āropetvā bhikkhū āmantesi – “taṃ kiṃ maññatha, bhikkhave, katamaṃ nu kho bahutaraṃ, yo vāyaṃ yo cāyaṃ (sabbattha) dutiyasuttādīsu pana vāsaddoyeva dissati mayā paritto nakhasikhāyaṃ paṃsu āropito, ayaṃ vā mahāpathavī”ti?

74. Thus have I heard. At one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s Park. Then the Blessed One, having placed a little bit of dust on the tip of his fingernail, addressed the bhikkhus: “What do you think, bhikkhus? Which is more: this little bit of dust placed by me on the tip of my fingernail, or this great earth?”

“Etadeva, bhante, bahutaraṃ, yadidaṃ mahāpathavī. Appamattako bhagavatā paritto nakhasikhāyaṃ paṃsu āropito. Neva satimaṃ kalaṃ upeti na sahassimaṃ kalaṃ upeti na satasahassimaṃ kalaṃ upeti mahāpathaviṃ upanidhāya bhagavatā paritto nakhasikhāyaṃ paṃsu āropito”ti. “Evameva kho, bhikkhave, ariyasāvakassa diṭṭhisampannassa puggalassa abhisametāvino etadeva bahutaraṃ dukkhaṃ yadidaṃ parikkhīṇaṃ pariyādiṇṇaṃ; appamattakaṃ avasiṭṭhaṃ. Neva satimaṃ kalaṃ upeti na sahassimaṃ [P 2.0134] kalaṃ upeti na satasahassimaṃ kalaṃ upeti purimaṃ dukkhakkhandhaṃ parikkhīṇaṃ pariyādiṇṇaṃ upanidhāya yadidaṃ sattakkhattuṃparamatā. Evaṃ mahatthiyo kho, bhikkhave, dhammābhisamayo; evaṃ mahatthiyo dhammacakkhupaṭilābho”ti. Paṭhamaṃ.

“Venerable sir, the great earth is indeed far more. The little bit of dust placed by the Blessed One on the tip of his fingernail is insignificant. Compared to the great earth, the little bit of dust placed by the Blessed One on the tip of his fingernail does not amount to a hundredth part, nor a thousandth part, nor a hundred-thousandth part.” “Just so, bhikkhus, for a noble disciple accomplished in view, a person who has penetrated the truths, this suffering that has been utterly destroyed and brought to an end is far more; what remains is insignificant. Compared to the former mass of suffering that has been utterly destroyed and brought to an end, it does not amount to a hundredth part, nor a thousandth part, nor a hundred-thousandth part—that is, for one who is at most a seven-more-times-returner. So great in benefit, bhikkhus, is the realization of the Dhamma; so great in benefit is the attainment of the eye of the Dhamma.”

2. Pokkharaṇīsuttaṃ

2. The Sutta on the Pond

75. Sāvatthiyaṃ viharati…pe… “seyyathāpi, bhikkhave, pokkharaṇī paññāsayojanāni āyāmena paññāsayojanāni vitthārena paññāsayojanāni [T 2.0163] ubbedhena, puṇṇā udakassa samatittikā kākapeyyā. Tato puriso kusaggena udakaṃ uddhareyya. Taṃ kiṃ maññatha, bhikkhave[V 1.0120], katamaṃ nu kho bahutaraṃ, yaṃ vā kusaggena udakaṃ ubbhataṃ yaṃ vā pokkharaṇiyā udaka”nti?

75. He was dwelling at Sāvatthī... "Suppose, bhikkhus, there was a pond fifty leagues in length, fifty leagues in width, and fifty leagues in depth, full of water, level with the bank, from which a crow could drink. From there, a man were to draw out water with the tip of a blade of kusa grass. What do you think of this, bhikkhus? Which is more: the water drawn out with the tip of a blade of kusa grass, or the water in the pond?"

“Etadeva, bhante, bahutaraṃ, yadidaṃ pokkharaṇiyā udakaṃ. Appamattakaṃ kusaggena udakaṃ ubbhataṃ. Neva satimaṃ kalaṃ upeti [M 1.0353] na sahassimaṃ kalaṃ upeti na satasahassimaṃ kalaṃ upeti pokkharaṇiyā udakaṃ upanidhāya kusaggena udakaṃ ubbhata”nti. “Evameva kho, bhikkhave, ariyasāvakassa diṭṭhisampannassa puggalassa abhisametāvino etadeva bahutaraṃ dukkhaṃ yadidaṃ parikkhīṇaṃ pariyādiṇṇaṃ; appamattakaṃ avasiṭṭhaṃ. Neva satimaṃ kalaṃ upeti na sahassimaṃ kalaṃ upeti na satasahassimaṃ kalaṃ upeti purimaṃ dukkhakkhandhaṃ parikkhīṇaṃ pariyādiṇṇaṃ upanidhāya, yadidaṃ sattakkhattuṃparamatā. Evaṃ mahatthiyo kho, bhikkhave, dhammābhisamayo; evaṃ mahatthiyo dhammacakkhupaṭilābho”ti. Dutiyaṃ.

"Venerable Sir, this is indeed much more: the water in the pond. Insignificant is the water drawn out with the tip of a blade of kusa grass. When compared with the water in the pond, the water drawn out with the tip of a blade of kusa grass does not amount to a hundredth part, nor a thousandth part, nor a hundred-thousandth part." "Even so, bhikkhus, for a noble disciple, a person accomplished in view who has penetrated the truths, this suffering is much more, that is, what has been utterly destroyed and exhausted; insignificant is what remains. When compared with the former mass of suffering that has been utterly destroyed and exhausted, that which is at most seven more existences does not amount to a hundredth part, nor a thousandth part, nor a hundred-thousandth part. So greatly beneficial, bhikkhus, is the penetration of the Dhamma; so greatly beneficial is the attainment of the Dhamma-eye." Second.

3. Sambhejjaudakasuttaṃ

3. The Sutta on the Confluence of Waters

76. Sāvatthiyaṃ viharati…pe… “seyyathāpi[P 2.0135], bhikkhave, yatthimā mahānadiyo saṃsandanti samenti, seyyathidaṃ – gaṅgā yamunā aciravatī sarabhū mahī, tato puriso dve vā tīṇi vā udakaphusitāni uddhareyya. Taṃ kiṃ maññatha, bhikkhave, katamaṃ nu kho bahutaraṃ, yāni vā dve vā tīṇi vā udakaphusitāni ubbhatāni yaṃ vā sambhejjaudaka”nti?

76. He was dwelling at Sāvatthī... "Suppose, bhikkhus, where these great rivers flow together and meet—that is to say, the Gaṅgā, the Yamunā, the Aciravatī, the Sarabhū, and the Mahī—a man were to draw out two or three drops of water from there. What do you think of this, bhikkhus? Which is more: the two or three drops of water that were drawn out, or the water of the confluence?"

“Etadeva, bhante, bahutaraṃ yadidaṃ sambhejjaudakaṃ; appamattakāni [T 2.0164] dve vā tīṇi vā udakaphusitāni ubbhatāni. Neva satimaṃ kalaṃ upenti na sahassimaṃ kalaṃ upenti na satasahassimaṃ kalaṃ upenti sambhejjaudakaṃ upanidhāya dve vā tīṇi vā udakaphusitāni ubbhatānī”ti. “Evameva kho, bhikkhave…pe… dhammacakkhupaṭilābho”ti. Tatiyaṃ.

"Venerable Sir, this is indeed much more: the water of the confluence. Insignificant are the two or three drops of water drawn out. When compared with the water of the confluence, the two or three drops of water drawn out do not amount to a hundredth part, nor a thousandth part, nor a hundred-thousandth part." "Even so, bhikkhus... the attainment of the Dhamma-eye." Third.

4. Dutiyasambhejjaudakasuttaṃ

4. The Second Sutta on the Confluence of Waters

77. Sāvatthiyaṃ viharati…pe… “seyyathāpi, bhikkhave, yatthimā mahānadiyo saṃsandanti samenti, seyyathidaṃ – gaṅgā yamunā aciravatī sarabhū mahī, taṃ udakaṃ parikkhayaṃ pariyādānaṃ gaccheyya [V 1.0121] ṭhapetvā dve vā tīṇi vā udakaphusitāni. Taṃ kiṃ maññatha, bhikkhave, katamaṃ nu kho bahutaraṃ, yaṃ vā sambhejjaudakaṃ parikkhīṇaṃ pariyādiṇṇaṃ yāni vā dve vā tīṇi vā udakaphusitāni avasiṭṭhānī”ti?

77. He was dwelling at Sāvatthī... "Suppose, bhikkhus, where these great rivers flow together and meet—namely, the Gaṅgā, the Yamunā, the Aciravatī, the Sarabhū, and the Mahī—that water were to come to depletion and exhaustion, setting aside two or three drops of water. What do you think of this, bhikkhus? Which is more: the water of the confluence that is depleted and exhausted, or the two or three drops of water that remain?"

“Etadeva, bhante, bahutaraṃ sambhejjaudakaṃ yadidaṃ parikkhīṇaṃ pariyādiṇṇaṃ; appamattakāni dve vā tīṇi vā udakaphusitāni avasiṭṭhāni. Neva satimaṃ kalaṃ [M 1.0354] upenti na sahassimaṃ kalaṃ upenti na satasahassimaṃ kalaṃ upenti sambhejjaudakaṃ parikkhīṇaṃ pariyādiṇṇaṃ upanidhāya dve vā tīṇi vā udakaphusitāni avasiṭṭhānī”ti. “Evameva kho, bhikkhave…pe… dhammacakkhupaṭilābho”ti. Catutthaṃ.

"Venerable sir, this indeed is much more: the water of the confluence that is depleted and exhausted. The two or three drops of water that remain are of little measure. In comparison with the depleted and exhausted water of the confluence, the two or three remaining drops of water do not amount to a hundredth part, nor a thousandth part, nor a hundred-thousandth part." "In the same way, bhikkhus... the attainment of the Dhamma-eye." Fourth.

5. Pathavīsuttaṃ

5. The Sutta on the Earth

78. Sāvatthiyaṃ viharati…pe… “seyyathāpi[P 2.0136], bhikkhave, puriso [T 2.0165] mahāpathaviyā satta kolaṭṭhimattiyo guḷikā upanikkhipeyya. Taṃ kiṃ maññatha, bhikkhave, katamaṃ nu kho bahutaraṃ, yā vā satta kolaṭṭhimattiyo guḷikā upanikkhittā ayaṃ yā (syā. ka.) vā mahāpathavī”ti?

78. He was dwelling at Sāvatthī... "Suppose, bhikkhus, a man were to place seven pellets of clay the size of jujube seeds on the great earth. What do you think of this, bhikkhus? Which is more: the seven pellets of clay the size of jujube seeds that have been placed, or this great earth?"

“Etadeva, bhante, bahutaraṃ, yadidaṃ mahāpathavī; appamattikā satta kolaṭṭhimattiyo guḷikā upanikkhittā. Neva satimaṃ kalaṃ upenti na sahassimaṃ kalaṃ upenti na satasahassimaṃ kalaṃ upenti mahāpathaviṃ upanidhāya satta kolaṭṭhimattiyo guḷikā upanikkhittā”ti. “Evameva kho, bhikkhave…pe… dhammacakkhupaṭilābho”ti. Pañcamaṃ.

"Venerable sir, this indeed is much more: namely, the great earth. The seven placed pellets of clay the size of jujube seeds are of little measure. In comparison with the great earth, the seven placed pellets of clay the size of jujube seeds do not amount to a hundredth part, nor a thousandth part, nor a hundred-thousandth part." "In the same way, bhikkhus... the attainment of the Dhamma-eye." Fifth.

6. Dutiyapathavīsuttaṃ

6. The Second Sutta on the Earth

79. Sāvatthiyaṃ viharati…pe… “seyyathāpi, bhikkhave, mahāpathavī parikkhayaṃ pariyādānaṃ gaccheyya, ṭhapetvā satta kolaṭṭhimattiyo guḷikā. Taṃ kiṃ maññatha, bhikkhave, katamaṃ nu kho bahutaraṃ, yaṃ vā mahāpathaviyā parikkhīṇaṃ pariyādiṇṇaṃ yā vā satta kolaṭṭhimattiyo guḷikā avasiṭṭhā”ti?

79. He was dwelling at Sāvatthī... "Suppose, bhikkhus, the great earth were to come to depletion and exhaustion, setting aside seven pellets of clay the size of jujube seeds. What do you think of this, bhikkhus? Which is more: that of the great earth which is depleted and exhausted, or the seven pellets of clay the size of jujube seeds that remain?"

“Etadeva [V 1.0122] bhante, bahutaraṃ, mahāpathaviyā, yadidaṃ parikkhīṇaṃ pariyādiṇṇaṃ; appamattikā satta kolaṭṭhimattiyo guḷikā avasiṭṭhā. Neva satimaṃ kalaṃ upenti na sahassimaṃ kalaṃ upenti na satasahassimaṃ kalaṃ upenti mahāpathaviyā parikkhīṇaṃ pariyādiṇṇaṃ upanidhāya satta kolaṭṭhimattiyo guḷikā avasiṭṭhā”ti. “Evameva kho, bhikkhave…pe… dhammacakkhupaṭilābho”ti. Chaṭṭhaṃ.

"Venerable sir, this indeed is much more: of the great earth, that which is depleted and exhausted. The seven remaining pellets of clay the size of jujube seeds are of little measure. In comparison with the depletion and exhaustion of the great earth, the seven remaining pellets of clay the size of jujube seeds do not amount to a hundredth part, nor a thousandth part, nor a hundred-thousandth part." "In the same way, bhikkhus... the attainment of the Dhamma-eye." Sixth.

7. Samuddasuttaṃ

7. The Sutta on the Ocean

80. Sāvatthiyaṃ [T 2.0166] viharati…pe… “seyyathāpi, bhikkhave, puriso mahāsamuddato dve vā tīṇi vā udakaphusitāni uddhareyya. Taṃ kiṃ maññatha, bhikkhave[M 1.0355], katamaṃ nu kho bahutaraṃ, yāni vā dve vā tīṇi vā udakaphusitāni ubbhatāni yaṃ vā mahāsamudde udaka”nti?

80. At Sāvatthī… “Suppose, bhikkhus, a man were to draw up two or three drops of water from the great ocean. What do you think, bhikkhus, which is more: the two or three drops of water drawn up, or the water in the great ocean?”

“Etadeva[P 2.0137], bhante, bahutaraṃ, yadidaṃ mahāsamudde udakaṃ; appamattakāni dve vā tīṇi vā udakaphusitāni ubbhatāni. Neva satimaṃ kalaṃ upenti na sahassimaṃ kalaṃ upenti na satasahassimaṃ kalaṃ upenti mahāsamudde udakaṃ upanidhāya dve vā tīṇi vā udakaphusitāni ubbhatānī”ti. “Evameva kho, bhikkhave…pe… dhammacakkhupaṭilābho”ti. Sattamaṃ.

“Venerable sir, the water in the great ocean is far greater. The two or three drops of water drawn up are insignificant. Compared to the water in the great ocean, the two or three drops of water drawn up do not amount to a hundredth part, nor a thousandth part, nor a hundred-thousandth part.” “In the same way, bhikkhus… the attainment of the Dhamma-eye.” Seventh.

8. Dutiyasamuddasuttaṃ

8. The Second Discourse on the Ocean

81. Sāvatthiyaṃ viharati…pe… “seyyathāpi, bhikkhave, mahāsamuddo parikkhayaṃ pariyādānaṃ gaccheyya, ṭhapetvā dve vā tīṇi vā udakaphusitāni. Taṃ kiṃ maññatha, bhikkhave, katamaṃ nu kho bahutaraṃ, yaṃ vā mahāsamudde udakaṃ parikkhīṇaṃ pariyādinnaṃ yāni vā dve vā tīṇi vā udakaphusitāni avasiṭṭhānī”ti?

81. At Sāvatthī… “Suppose, bhikkhus, the great ocean were to be depleted and exhausted, leaving behind just two or three drops of water. What do you think, bhikkhus, which is more: the water in the great ocean that has been depleted and exhausted, or the two or three drops of water that remain?”

“Etadeva, bhante, bahutaraṃ mahāsamudde udakaṃ, yadidaṃ parikkhīṇaṃ pariyādiṇṇaṃ; appamattakāni dve vā tīṇi vā udakaphusitāni avasiṭṭhāni. Neva satimaṃ kalaṃ upenti na sahassimaṃ kalaṃ upenti na satasahassimaṃ kalaṃ upenti mahāsamudde udakaṃ parikkhīṇaṃ pariyādiṇṇaṃ [V 1.0123] upanidhāya dve vā tīṇi vā udakaphusitāni avasiṭṭhānī”ti. “Evameva [T 2.0167] kho bhikkhave…pe… dhammacakkhupaṭilābho”ti. Aṭṭhamaṃ.

“Venerable sir, the water in the great ocean that has been depleted and exhausted is far greater. The two or three drops of water remaining are insignificant. Compared to the water in the great ocean that has been depleted and exhausted, the two or three drops of water remaining do not amount to a hundredth part, nor a thousandth part, nor a hundred-thousandth part.” “In the same way, bhikkhus… the attainment of the Dhamma-eye.” Eighth.

9. Pabbatasuttaṃ

9. The Discourse on the Mountain

82. Sāvatthiyaṃ viharati…pe… “seyyathāpi, bhikkhave, puriso himavato pabbatarājassa satta sāsapamattiyo pāsāṇasakkharā upanikkhipeyya. Taṃ kiṃ maññatha, bhikkhave, katamaṃ nu kho bahutaraṃ, yā vā satta sāsapamattiyo pāsāṇasakkharā upanikkhittā yo vā himavā upanikkhittā, himavā vā (sī.) pabbatarājā”ti?

82. At Sāvatthī… “Suppose, bhikkhus, a man were to place seven mustard-seed-sized pebbles near the Himālaya, the king of mountains. What do you think, bhikkhus, which is more: the seven mustard-seed-sized pebbles that have been placed there, or the Himālaya, the king of mountains?”

“Etadeva, bhante, bahutaraṃ yadidaṃ himavā pabbatarājā; appamattikā satta sāsapamattiyo pāsāṇasakkharā [P 2.0138] upanikkhittā. Neva satimaṃ kalaṃ upenti na sahassimaṃ kalaṃ upenti [M 1.0356] na satasahassimaṃ kalaṃ upenti himavantaṃ pabbatarājānaṃ upanidhāya satta sāsapamattiyo pāsāṇasakkharā upanikkhittā”ti. “Evameva kho…pe… dhammacakkhupaṭilābho”ti. Navamaṃ.

“Venerable sir, the Himālaya, the king of mountains, is far greater; the seven mustard-seed-sized pebbles that have been placed there are insignificant. Compared to the Himālaya, the king of mountains, the seven mustard-seed-sized pebbles that have been placed there do not amount to a hundredth part, nor a thousandth part, nor a hundred-thousandth part.” “In the same way, bhikkhus… the attainment of the Dhamma-eye.” Ninth.

10. Dutiyapabbatasuttaṃ

10. The Second Discourse on the Mountain

83. Sāvatthiyaṃ viharati…pe… “seyyathāpi, bhikkhave, himavā pabbatarājā parikkhayaṃ pariyādānaṃ gaccheyya, ṭhapetvā satta sāsapamattiyo pāsāṇasakkharā. Taṃ kiṃ maññatha, bhikkhave, katamaṃ nu kho bahutaraṃ, yaṃ vā himavato pabbatarājassa parikkhīṇaṃ pariyādiṇṇaṃ yā vā satta sāsapamattiyo pāsāṇasakkharā avasiṭṭhā”ti?

83. At Sāvatthī… “Suppose, bhikkhus, the Himālaya, the king of mountains, were to diminish and waste away, leaving only seven pebbles the size of mustard seeds. What do you think, bhikkhus, which is more: that which has diminished and wasted away from the Himālaya, the king of mountains, or the seven mustard-seed-sized pebbles that remain?”

“Etadeva, bhante, bahutaraṃ himavato pabbatarājassa yadidaṃ parikkhīṇaṃ pariyādiṇṇaṃ; appamattikā satta sāsapamattiyo pāsāṇasakkharā avasiṭṭhā. Neva satimaṃ [T 2.0168] kalaṃ upenti na sahassimaṃ kalaṃ upenti na satasahassimaṃ kalaṃ upenti himavato pabbatarājassa parikkhīṇaṃ pariyādiṇṇaṃ upanidhāya satta sāsapamattiyo pāsāṇasakkharā avasiṭṭhā”ti.

“Venerable sir, that which has diminished and wasted away from the Himālaya, the king of mountains, is indeed far greater; the seven mustard-seed-sized pebbles that remain are of a trifling measure. Compared to that which has diminished and wasted away from the Himālaya, the king of mountains, the seven remaining mustard-seed-sized pebbles do not amount to a hundredth part, nor a thousandth part, nor a hundred-thousandth part.”

“Evameva kho, bhikkhave, ariyasāvakassa diṭṭhisampannassa puggalassa abhisametāvino etadeva [V 1.0124] bahutaraṃ dukkhaṃ yadidaṃ parikkhīṇaṃ pariyādiṇṇaṃ; appamattakaṃ avasiṭṭhaṃ. Neva satimaṃ kalaṃ upeti na sahassimaṃ kalaṃ upeti na satasahassimaṃ kalaṃ upeti purimaṃ dukkhakkhandhaṃ parikkhīṇaṃ pariyādiṇṇaṃ upanidhāya yadidaṃ sattakkhattuṃparamatā. Evaṃ mahatthiyo kho, bhikkhave, dhammābhisamayo, evaṃ mahatthiyo dhammacakkhupaṭilābho”ti. Dasamaṃ.

“So too, bhikkhus, for a noble disciple accomplished in view, a person who has comprehended, by far the greater part of suffering has been destroyed and exhausted; only a little remains. What remains does not amount to a hundredth part, nor a thousandth part, nor a hundred-thousandth part when compared to the former mass of suffering that has been destroyed and exhausted, that is, the state of having at most seven more existences. So great in benefit, bhikkhus, is the breakthrough into the Dhamma; so great in benefit is the attainment of the Dhamma-eye.” Tenth.

11. Tatiyapabbatasuttaṃ

11. The Third Discourse on the Mountain

84. Sāvatthiyaṃ viharati…pe… “seyyathāpi[P 2.0139], bhikkhave, puriso sinerussa pabbatarājassa satta muggamattiyo pāsāṇasakkharā upanikkhipeyya. Taṃ kiṃ maññatha, bhikkhave, katamaṃ nu kho bahutaraṃ, yā vā satta muggamattiyo pāsāṇasakkharā upanikkhittā yo vā sineru upanikkhittā, sineru vā (sī.) pabbatarājā”ti?

84. At Sāvatthī… “Suppose, bhikkhus, a man were to place seven mung-bean-sized pebbles beside Mount Sineru, the king of mountains. What do you think, bhikkhus, which is more: the seven mung-bean-sized pebbles that have been placed there, or Mount Sineru, the king of mountains?”

“Etadeva, bhante, bahutaraṃ yadidaṃ sineru pabbatarājā; appamattikā satta muggamattiyo pāsāṇasakkharā upanikkhittā. Neva satimaṃ kalaṃ upenti na sahassimaṃ [M 1.0357] kalaṃ upenti na satasahassimaṃ kalaṃ upenti sineruṃ pabbatarājānaṃ upanidhāya satta muggamattiyo pāsāṇasakkharā upanikkhittā”ti. “Evameva kho, bhikkhave, ariyasāvakassa diṭṭhisampannassa puggalassa [T 2.0169] adhigamaṃ upanidhāya aññatitthiyasamaṇabrāhmaṇaparibbājakānaṃ adhigamo neva satimaṃ kalaṃ upeti na sahassimaṃ kalaṃ upeti na satasahassimaṃ kalaṃ upeti. Evaṃ mahādhigamo, bhikkhave, diṭṭhisampanno puggalo, evaṃ mahābhiñño”ti. Ekādasamaṃ.

“Venerable sir, Mount Sineru, the king of mountains, is indeed far greater; the seven mung-bean-sized pebbles that have been placed there are of a trifling measure.
